articles.title_zh: Chinese court sentenced former mayor of Wuhan city to 14 years in prison for bribery
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
A federal judge in California has sentenced a former Syrian prison warden to 60 years for torturing inmates and lying to immigration officials to get into the United States.
A jury convicted Samir Ousman Alsheikh, 74, in March of conspiracy to commit torture, three counts of torture, one count of visa fraud and one count of attempted naturalization fraud, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles.
Alsheikh was involved in torturing political dissidents to deter opposition to the regime of then-Syrian President Bashar Assad, according to the Justice Department.
Government officials say Alsheikh is the highest-ranking former member of the Assad regime to be tried and convicted in person outside Syria.
The Justice Department had sought no fewer than 80 years in prison, while Alsheikh requested five years, citing his age and his chronic medical conditions.
In handing down the sentence on Thursday, U.S. District Judge Hernán Vera remarked on the “utter reprehensibility” of Alsheikh’s crime, Courthouse News Service reported .
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and unspeakably violent and brutal,” the judge reportedly said.
Nina Marino, Alsheikh’s attorney, said her client plans to appeal the sentence.
In a statement, First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli said he hoped the sentence “gives some semblance of healing and closure to this defendant’s victims.”
“Criminals who inflict the type of savage brutality that this defendant did on his victims must never be granted refuge in our country,” Essayli said.
Samir Ousman Sheikh allegedly ordered inmates to a wing of a Syrian prison where they were then tortured with a device known as the ‘flying carpet.’
During Alsheikh’s trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Alsheikh ordered and participated in the torture of prisoners while he headed the Adra Prison, also known as Damascus Central Prison, from around 2005 to 2008.
Jurors heard testimony from three of Alsheikh’s victims who said they were packed into small, filthy, cold, wet cells that were infested with insects and other vermin. They described being tortured and seeing and hearing the torture of other prisoners.
The victims testified about being fastened to a device known as the “Flying Carpet,” which folded their bodies in half at the waist; about being manacled to the ceiling and suspended sometimes for days; and about being beaten while immobilized inside tires, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in L.A.
During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that when detainees refused Alsheikh’s orders to harm political prisoners, he ordered them to be sent to an underground section of the prison known as Wing 13, where they were tortured.
Prosecutors also presented evidence that Alsheikh, who came to the country in 2020, lied to U.S. immigration authorities about his background to secure a green card and also on an application to naturalize as a U.S. citizen.
Alsheikh has been in custody since his arrest at Los Angeles International Airport in July 2024.
Khaled Abdul Malek, who testified about being detained and tortured under Alsheikh’s direction, praised the sentence in a statement .
“The land of freedom will never be a safe haven for slaughterers and those who committed crimes against humanity,” Malek said. “This trial is not the end, but the first step on the road toward accountability and justice for everyone whose hands have been stained with the blood of innocent people.”

articles.title_orig: What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’?
articles.title_zh: What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’?
articles.content_orig:
It has been one year since United States President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP) brokered a “ceasefire” aimed at eventually ending Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
However, rather than receiving relief and a chance to rebuild, Palestinians in the enclave continue to face attacks and be uprooted as Israeli forces have expanded control within the territory.
Trump first proposed the BoP in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.
In November, a United Nations Security Council resolution recognised the board as a “transitional administration” in Gaza.
But what has the board achieved? Here’s what we know:
The BoP’s mission was laid out in Trump’s 20-point Gaza peace plan , as was the “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire began on October 10, 2025.
The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.
It required Israeli forces to withdraw to about 50 percent of the Gaza Strip and cease aerial and artillery bombardments. It also required Israel to release 250 Palestinian prisoners and another 1,700 people jailed from Gaza since October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas led attacks into southern Israel and Israel began the war. The plan proposed reopening border crossings to allow much-needed aid into Gaza.
The peace plan required Hamas to release all Israeli captives. It also proposed a later phase in which the group would disarm and its members would be granted amnesty or a safe exit from Gaza.
The peace plan established the BoP as a transitional governing body until the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the occupied West Bank, could take over.
An International Stabilization Force (ISF), led by the US, was supposed to take over security in Gaza from withdrawing Israeli forces, the plan stated. It also proposed the reconstruction and redevelopment of Gaza, whose people, it said, “have suffered enough”.
In February, the BoP’s members, who each joined in exchange for a $1bn annual fee, met in Washington, DC, for its first summit, at which member states pledged $7bn in funding although aid agencies said reconstructing Gaza would cost closer to $70bn.
On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, the BoP also unveiled a 66-project recovery plan worth $2.4bn.
The BoP’s achievements are tied to the success of the Gaza peace plan.
Under that, Hamas has released all 168 living captives and Israel has freed Palestinian prisoners.
Hamas has also announced the dissolution of its government in the Gaza Strip although Israel has dismissed that as a “stunt”.
Other goals under the peace plan have been only partially met.
Governance has been hampered. While a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), meant to act as the governing authority in Gaza, was founded, Israel has not granted it entry into the Strip. The NCAG reports directly to the board and is led by Chief Commissioner Ali Shaath and other Palestinian technocrats. It operates from Cairo. Israel has not stated why the committee is not permitted to enter Gaza.
Aid remains restricted. About 227 aid trucks enter the Strip daily when 600 trucks were supposed to, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) hunger monitor.
Israel has classified thousands of basic items, such as tents and essential equipment like ventilators, as “dual use” items, which means they have military and civilian applications, and has restricted their flow into the Strip. About 1.4 million Palestinians – or most of Gaza’s more than 2 million people – will suffer hunger until at least December, the IPC has noted. That is 200,000 more than those who faced hunger in May, suggesting a significantly deteriorating situation.
Observers argued that the BoP has entirely failed to secure the “ceasefire” as Israeli attacks have continued almost daily on the Strip.
Since October 10, 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians, mostly women and children, have been killed. In the three years since the war began, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, and thousands more are missing and presumed dead under the rubble.
Israel says its continuing attacks target Hamas members, but the group vehemently denies the claims.
Israel also now occupies about 60 percent of the Strip, more than the 50 percent agreed in Trump’s peace plan. The “Yellow Line”, which demarcates the area of Gaza under Israeli occupation, has been pushed farther into the Strip, causing further displacement and squeezing Gaza’s population into an ever-shrinking area. Palestinians unknowingly crossing the “Yellow Line” have been shot dead.
In December, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army “will never fully leave” the Strip.
Mohamad Elmasry at the Doha Institute of Graduate Studies told Al Jazeera that Israel is simply continuing a broader policy of “ethnic cleansing” in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. “They are making life miserable,” he said, adding: “This is all by design.”
Consequently, the BoP has also failed to ensure Hamas disarms so phase two of the peace plan could begin.
Although Hamas has agreed to hand its weapons over to the NCAG, it rejects the “disarmament” clause because Israel has not ceased its attacks or withdrawn from the Strip as agreed. At the same time, Israel has said it will not move forward with the plan if Hamas does not disarm, leaving the two sides in a standoff.
Meanwhile, no stabilisation force has been deployed. Six countries – Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania, Kosovo and Uganda – have so far committed personnel to form a security force of 20,000 soldiers and 12,000 police headed by the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM).
There has been no meaningful reconstruction in Gaza. Palestinians continue to live in tent camps infested with rodents and insects with little to shield them from intense heat, or rain.
The Trump administration and BoP have echoed Israel’s rejection of the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, or UNRWA, which has long provided lifesaving humanitarian aid, education, development programmes and social services in Gaza and employs about 11,000 Palestinians.
The BoP said last month that it will not work with UNRWA, essentially sidelining the agency.
A BoP official told The Associated Press news agency that UNRWA could continue working in Gaza if its programmes were deemed relevant but the agency’s “days are over”.
UNRWA said the move was “not logical”.
In June, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to extend UNRWA’s mandate until 2029. The BoP itself is mandated to oversee the peace process until December 2027 when its progress will be reviewed for possible renewal by the UN.
Analysts and rights groups have raised concerns that the BoP could take over all aspects of Gaza’s rebuilding. Countries too, including France and other European nations, have called out any attempts to replace the UN in the Strip.
But Elmasry said no country is willing to take action. “There are a lot of international actors that do not want to cross the US,” he said. That essentially leaves the fate of more than 2 million Palestinians to Trump, he added.
Ultimately, the BoP has “failed”, said Simon Mabon, a professor at Lancaster University.
“The failure to implement its own plan to end the Gaza conflict demonstrates its impotence and the inability to ensure that Israel and, to a lesser extent, Hamas, remain bound by their own commitments [and] has allowed the genocide to continue,” he concluded.

articles.title_orig: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
articles.title_zh: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
articles.content_orig:
For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”
In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.
Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.
Volunteers went through the same four-part sequence twice, once sober and once on psilocybin. The sequence included putting participants in four different settings or contexts: eight minutes of lying at rest, a guided meditation, an 11-minute curated music playlist, and finally six minutes of eyes-open video of clouds moving across a sky. Each participant did all four inside an MRI scanner about 80 minutes after dosing, and again on EEG about 150 minutes after.
There were no cognitive tasks researchers routinely go for in brain studies, but there was a purpose behind this omission.
“We wanted ecological validity,” Stoliker says. “We wanted to know what the brain was like when somebody was having an authentic, uninterrupted psychedelic experience. If somebody took a psychedelic in a therapeutic setting, you wouldn’t have them completing tasks.” Stoliker also points out that there’s evidence that giving someone a task mid-trip pulls them out of the state—a phenomenon researchers sometimes call grounding. “Once you introduce these sorts of tasks, you’re actually interrupting the very phenomena you are seeking to measure.” And it worked.
Half of the participants ranked their session among the most meaningful experiences of their lives, and 24 put it in their personal top five. Stolkier and his colleagues started analyzing their brain scan data to find out why.
Measuring global functional connectivity—how much influence each patch of cortex exerts over the rest—the team found that, when participants had their eyes closed, sensory regions lost sway while associative regions gained. “It seems like the brain’s ability to construct reality, or imagination, or our associations, our beliefs, our sense of self—these faculties had more dominance over sensory areas,” Stoliker says, stressing that the interpretation is a hypothetical. “This could help explain why people have meaningful, complex imagery experiences, why they have mystical experiences with imagery that is personally relevant to them.”
Another observation the team made was that connections within each brain network weakened, connections between networks strengthened. The brain’s modularity, a parameter that describes how cleanly neurons stay sorted into specialist teams, dropped across all four parts of the experimental sequence.
What’s more, researchers found that, when sober, activity in a brain with its eyes shut looked very different from a brain watching a movie. Under psilocybin, that difference nearly evaporated. In the visual network, the gap between eyes-open and eyes-closed connectivity shrank by 85 percent. The results from the EEG session independently confirmed that, with alpha-band activity (normally a marker of the brain gating visual input) reduced by nearly half.
“When somebody takes a psychedelic and they’re able to close their eyes and see complex imagery, there seems to be less boundary between the internal and external world than we ordinarily experience,” Stoliker says.
Regardless of these details, the results rather accurately reproduced the chaos in the brain so many researchers claimed psychedelics caused. This chaos, though, turned into order when the team processed their data in a slightly unorthodox way.
Scientists usually do two acts of averaging in a standard brain imaging study. The first is averaging over time. An eight-minute brain scan comprises a few hundred successive images of the whole brain. To understand how two specific regions work together, researchers conventionally average all these images down to a single number describing how well the two regions’ activity matched up across the whole eight minutes.
The problem with this analysis is that it runs the risk of missing ordered structures that appear for a brief period and then disappear into chaos.
The second analysis is averaging over people. Having produced one such number per participant, the standard approach then pools all of them into a group average, on the assumption that individual differences are noise that will be canceled out. Stoliker’s study was focused on individual experiences, so he wanted to avoid that.
Instead, the team fed the moment-by-moment activity of 332 brain regions into CEBRA, a machine-learning tool that compressed the data down to its essential structure while preserving the order of events. For each individual, it produced a trajectory—a path traced through a three-dimensional space, one point for each moment of the scan.
“When they’re not under psilocybin, the brain activity is less differentiated by context,” Stoliker says. “But under psilocybin, we see that the activity becomes organized across time and more clearly differentiated by context.” The trajectories separated into four distinct clusters corresponding to rest, meditation, music, and the movie. A classifier could read a moment of brain activity and say which one the person was in.
It turned out the performance of that classifier scaled with how profound the participants described their experience as being.
To find out which parts of the brain were doing the work, the team replaced one network’s psilocybin activity with its sober version and checked how badly the classifier degraded. The default mode network and the visual network each accounted for over 20 percent of the effect. “The default mode network is strongly associated with the sense of self: daydreaming, mind wandering, thinking about yourself. It’s often been called the narrative self,” Stoliker explains. “On the other end of this gradient, more externally oriented, is the visual system.”
Under psilocybin, the two became less differentiated, which the team thinks explains why participants reported a subjective experience of the self and the external world becoming less separate, a state Stoliker calls “embeddedness.”
“Theoretically, we could suggest that psychedelics are temporarily altering the organization of brain networks that ordinarily help maintain this separation that we experience,” he says. “It really challenges the idea of whether the internal world and external world are separate and highlights the idea that the brain may be responsible for constructing both.”
The day after the session, participants rated whether various things had shifted, like sense of connection to themselves, to others, to nature, along with peace, acceptance, and creativity, all on a scale running from –100 to 100. “For the vast majority of our participants, we found they had positive psychological changes the next day,” Stoliker says. articles.title_orig: World Mental Health Day: Eteri Liparteliani on the Mental Battle of Judo
articles.title_zh: World Mental Health Day: Eteri Liparteliani on the Mental Battle of Judo
articles.content_orig:
There are many ingredients to becoming a champion: strength, discipline, technique, passion and, of course, mental health.
On World Mental Health Day (10 October), it's a reminder that what happens in an athlete's mind can be just as important as what happens on the tatami.
That is precisely why, at the start of the competition day, Georgia's Eteri Liparteliani can be found at the edge of the mat, working through breathing exercises and visualisation techniques with her psychologist. It's part of a routine that helps her prepare for the challenges ahead.
For the -57kg 2025 world champion, this year's World Championships brought a new kind of pressure. For the first time, she was stepping onto the tatami not as a title contender, but as the defending champion.
Despite a nagging rib injury, Liparteliani showed massive judo all the way to her second world final. There, she fell to Japan's Akari Omori and settled for silver, leaving the competition with mixed emotions and yet another challenge to navigate: coming to terms with a result that fell short of her golden expectations.
The EJU spoke to the Georgian history-maker about the mental side of competition and the importance of psychological support.
"I felt really ready for these World Championships, but because of the injury, I wasn't able to show everything I can do or use all my techniques, especially in the final.
" I think it is very important for all of us to understand that there is a lot of work to be done and that we have to work hard to make sure that we get what we want.
"Special thanks, of course, to my psychologist," Liparteliani said. "She was with me last year and again this year. I'm also very grateful to my coaches. Their support helps me a lot and gives me extra motivation."
The mental battle began before Liparteliani ever stepped onto the tatami. Just two weeks before the World Championships, the world champion sustained a rib injury that threatened her chances of competing at all.
Determined to defend her title, she pushed through her preparations and competed with pain-relieving injections. But while she kept the injury from affecting her performance for much of the day, the pain eventually caught up with her.
From the outside, there was little indication that anything was wrong. Liparteliani looked sharp and confident throughout the preliminary rounds, seemingly undeterred by the injury. Mentally, she had made a conscious effort to put the pain to one side and focus on her judo.
"I tried not to think about the injury. Psychologically, I was doing my best to block it out. But in the final, I really felt the pain, and that made things difficult."
What frustrated her most wasn't just missing out on another world title, but knowing she couldn't show the full extent of her abilities when it mattered most.
Still, Liparteliani is already looking ahead. Having experienced both the joy of becoming world champion and the disappointment of falling just short, she knows setbacks are part of the journey.
"Of course, I wanted to become world champion for the second year in a row. I was very well prepared for these World Championships, but the injury may have affected my performance a little. I did everything I could, and although this year I won silver, I'll keep fighting for the highest medals."
"There will be more World Championships, and I'll be even more motivated for the next competitions. I want to improve on this result."

articles.title_orig: Pope: Art is not ‘mere aestheticism’ but a way to share the Gospel
articles.title_zh: Pope: Art is not ‘mere aestheticism’ but a way to share the Gospel
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV met with members of the Bizot Group, officially known as the International Group of Organizers of Major Exhibitions, at the Vatican on October 10. The Group brings together directors of the largest art and culture museums around the world.
The Pope highlighted how the Groupâs passion reveals that âevery museum is a place of memory, beauty and history, fostering encounters between generations and promoting culture and human creativity.â
Over the centuries, the Catholic Church has developed a deep connection with the arts in all forms. Art, Pope Leo stressed, âis the means by which persons, through their ingenuity, enhance and transfigure matterâthat is, the creation in which they dwell as made in the image and likeness of God.â
Centering on the theme of 'Materiality,' the Bizot Groupâs meeting invites a deeper exploration into the relationship between an object and art interpretation. Moreover, it plays a role in reflecting on how God chose to reveal himself in the specific quality of matter.
With this in mind, the Pope outlined three points regarding matter, beginning with how it is available to humanity as âa gift entrusted to our care.â Through an artistâs skill, they are able to turn matter into a gift for others.
He underlined that cultural activity can reveal the beauty of creation.
Furthermore, matter can be formed into whatever the artist is trying to express. Art, Pope Leo said, âis a creative process through which human beings, in imitation of Godâs work, shape matter and imbue it with a transcendent meaning.â
In this way, artwork becomes a sign of the beauty that stirs humanityâs hearts and minds, encouraging the person to look to what is above.
Thirdly, matter is memory. âThe works preserved in museums bear witness to a history that speaks to every person, from one generation to the next,â the Pope explained. Pieces in a museum offer the wisdom of the past to the present.
âThe Church, as a pilgrim through time, has understood art precisely in this way: not as mere aestheticism, but as a means of proclaiming the Gospel through beauty.â
Concluding, Pope Leo congratulated the Bizot Group for its work in directing and administering museums around the worldââsafeguarding a heritage that belongs to all humanity.â

articles.title_orig: China, Pakistan armies to conduct counterterrorism drills
articles.title_zh: China, Pakistan armies to conduct counterterrorism drills
articles.content_orig:
Chinese and Pakistani armies will conduct a joint training exercise in Korla, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, in mid-to-late October, a Chinese defense spokesman said on Saturday.
Chen Xi, a spokesman for the Ministry of National Defense, said at an online news briefing that the exercise, code-named Karakoram 2026, will focus on joint counterterrorism operations in high-altitude areas.
The training will include drone operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, as well as joint command exercises and live-force drills, Chen said.
He said the exercise will be the first joint army training between the two countries and will help deepen exchanges and cooperation while enhancing their ability to jointly respond to terrorist threats.

articles.title_orig: World Watch Day 2026: Time as Living Heritage
articles.title_zh: World Watch Day 2026: Time as Living Heritage
articles.content_orig:
Today marks the second annual World Watch Day , celebrated on October 10 in a clever nod to the familiar “10:10” depiction of watch hands. This year’s theme, “Time as Living Heritage”, puts the people of Sainte-Croix at the centre of the occasion.
A training course at Association Mec-Art
Marking the event, our founder SJX participated in a round-table discussion about preserving and passing on the skills of both watchmaking and mechanical art.
The panel included De Bethune co-founder Denis Flageollet and automaton maker François Junod, who helped establish the Association Mec-Art, watchmaker Vianney Halter, The 1916 Company’s Tim Mosso, and Karin Alexandrian of the Musée des Arts et Métiers. Europa Star ’s Pierre Maillard moderated the conversation.
Denis Flageollet of De Bethune co-founded the Association Mec-Art in 2016 with automaton-makers François Junod and Nicolas Court
The organisers, Association Mec-Art and the Musée de la Mécanique d’Art et du Patrimoine de Sainte-Croix (MuMAPS), work to safeguard the traditions explored in our earlier story on the unique skills being preserved in Sainte-Croix. These extend beyond watches to music boxes, mechanical singing birds, and automata.
Mec-Art helps keep the skills alive through creative projects and practical courses, while MuMAPS is the local museum dedicated to mechanical art and the town’s heritage. The shared challenge is to ensure that future generations can still make and repair these objects, and so that future artisans will continue to have a commercial outlet for their craft.
For more information visit worldwatchday.org and mec-art.ch .

Alonzo Lunsford said he wants to "lock eyes" with Nidal Hasan.
For two of the survivors of the Fort Hood shooting, the news that the execution of the gunman who attempted to take their lives nearly 17 years ago will be livestreamed for the public to see has unearthed complicated emotions.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed Thursday that the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in the November 2009 mass shooting , will be open to the public and livestreamed online .
Hasan, who described the shooting as an act of jihad, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3 by eight military service members -- marking the first military execution since 1961, as well as the first by firing squad since 1945.
Alonzo Lunsford had served in the Army since 1990, and at the time of the shooting was a sergeant stationed at Ford Hood. Hasan shot Lunsford seven times -- including in the head and in the stomach -- and Lunsford witnessed Hasan kill several colleagues that he had become good friends with.
Lunsford, who retired from the Army in 2013, told ABC News he plans on attending the execution in December because he wants to "lock eyes" with Hasan while he takes his last breath.
"I want him to be able to look at my eyes and to let him understand I won't be defeated, can't be defeated. I am no longer a victim, his victim. I am a survivor," Lunsford said.
Lunsford said he welcomed President Donald Trump's approval to proceed with the execution of Nidal Hasan on Monday, saying that he feels as if he and the other survivors of the shooting would finally obtain some closure. He even said that he completely agrees with the administration's selected method of carrying out the execution via firing squad.
"It's how he shot us," Lunsford said.
Even so, Lunsford says he has misgivings about the Pentagon's plan to livestream Hasan's execution, and said he believes it should only be broadcast to the survivors and the families of those who perished in the shooting.
"I don't want this to be viewed upon as a spectacle, like a pay-per-view event, or like going to a basketball tournament," he said.
Lunsford said that he believes setting a precedent of livestreaming executions for anyone to watch does not align with the responsibility of the U.S. to serve as a moral example for the rest of the world.
"We're not trying to meet a standard -- we're trying to set a standard for the free world," he said.
Some Republican and Democratic lawmakers alike condemned the Pentagon's announcement about the livestreaming of the execution, with some even likening the decision to the public executions broadcast by terrorist groups in the Middle East.
"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do," Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., a senior member of the House Armed Services Committee, wrote on X. "America is better than that."
Meanwhile, Rep. Adam Smith, the highest-ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said that livestreaming an execution "makes a mockery of our legal system."
"We are a democratic country and should take the rule of law seriously, not turn it into a spectacle," Smith wrote in a statement.
Dayna Ferguson Roscoe was just 21 years old at the time of the shooting, serving as a specialist in the Army. She was shot three times in her arm, her shoulder and her thigh, and credits her survival to a birth defect that caused one of the bullets to ricochet off of her stomach and into her thigh instead.
Roscoe said that although she did not expect that the execution would be livestreamed, she believes it follows a historical tradition.
"It's not completely shocking, given that death and war have historically always been documented through photographs and video. But it's just not something I expected to hear," she told ABC News.
"I hadn't really thought about if I agree with the decisions being made -- but it doesn't make a difference in what happens to him," Roscoe added.
Roscoe, who left the Army after she finished her four-year enlistment, is still figuring out arrangements to attend the execution.
Despite the pain that she endured at the hands of Hasan, Roscoe told ABC News that when she reflects on the day of the shooting, she is just thankful to be alive.
"I've been hurt worse in life than by Nidal. Sometimes you're just the collateral damage in someone else's warfare in their own mind," Roscoe said.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan President William Lai Ching-te says the island “cherishes peace” and will “not give up our freedom” in a National Day speech outside the Presidential Office in Taipei.
Lai made the remarks on Saturday in front of thousands of people, including foreign guests and diplomats. Fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over Taipei before his speech.
“We are open to exchanges but will not accept subordination,” he said. “Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke; rather, it is to deter war.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office condemned Lai’s speech, saying it “disregards facts, ⁠distorts the truth, misleads the public, and reveals ulterior motives”.
It said ‌Lai “stubbornly clung to ‘Taiwan independence’ separatist thinking” and exaggerated the “threat from the mainland”.
“There is only one ⁠China in the ⁠world, and Taiwan is part of China – this is the ⁠true status quo in ⁠the Taiwan ⁠Strait,” it said.
Taiwan’s future “can and must be decided jointly by ‌all the Chinese people, including our compatriots in ‌Taiwan”, ‌it also said.
The holiday marks the 115th anniversary of a 1911 uprising that toppled China’s last imperial dynasty and led to the founding of the Republic of China.
Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory, has never renounced the use of force to take it and calls Lai a “separatist”.
Beijing has rebuffed his offers of talks.
Lai said China continued to “apply pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait”.
Grey-zone tactics are actions that stop short of open war. “Peace cannot rely solely on wishes, and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggressors to encroach ever further,” he added.
Lai’s government has set aside a record 1.1 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($34.5bn) for defence in 2027, more than 3 percent of its gross domestic product.
China held war games around the island shortly after Lai’s first National Day speech in 2024 but not last year. Its last drills near Taiwan were in late December after news of an $11bn arms deal with the United States, the largest ever US weapons package for the island.
Lai said he welcomed talks between the US and China but insisted “there must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist”.
He urged democracies in the Asia Pacific to join forces to preserve peace and stability in the region.
Lai also said China has exerted pressure to try to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait and the island’s “resolve” is not just about its own survival in the face of “authoritarian expansion”. It’s also about whether the international community still believes that force cannot override rules, he added.
According to Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defence, 21 Chinese military aircraft and seven navy ships were operating around Taiwan in a 24-hour period ending at 6am on Saturday (22:00 GMT on Friday). Thirteen of the aircraft crossed the median line in the Taiwan Strait, which once served as an unofficial barrier between the two sides, and entered the island’s air defence identification zone.
Eswatini King Mswati III and Indiana Lieutenant Governor Micah Beckwith were among the foreign guests who offered their congratulations in Taiwan, Lai’s office said. Eswatini is Taiwan’s only diplomatic ally in Africa. A Japanese parliamentary delegation also visited the island and joined the National Day celebrations.
The US switched its official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago but remains Taiwan’s most important security backer.
Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan has not changed under President Donald Trump.
In May, after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, Trump suggested arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China, which set off alarm across the world.
Taiwan is now waiting for Trump to sign off on $14bn worth of weapons, including the US-made Patriot air defence system.
The dispute dates back to China’s civil war, when the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after defeat by Mao Zedong’s communists.
The Republic of China remains the island’s formal name.

articles.title_orig: From hunger to hope: Lettie's story on World Porridge Day
articles.title_zh: From hunger to hope: Lettie's story on World Porridge Day
articles.content_orig:
When Mary's Meals first met Leticia, known to many as Lettie, she was 11 years old. Recently orphaned and hungry, she had been forced to leave school and care for her two younger brothers. Her story was first shared in Child 31 , the award-winning 2012 documentary that introduced audiences around the world to the reality of child hunger in Malawi. Now, more than a decade later, Mary's Meals has returned to Lettie's story.
Their new documentary, Lettie , shares a new, very different chapter of her life.
Today, Lettie is an educated, working mother. She works for Mary's Meals Malawi, where she also serves as a Youth Ambassador, sharing the stories of children who, like her, receive a daily meal at school. Her son is thriving and neither he nor his mother are facing the hunger that once threatened to define her and her brothers' futures.
For Angela Chipeta-Khonje, Country Director of Mary's Meals Malawi, Lettie's story is both extraordinary and deeply familiar. "She is one of those children who went through hunger, but she overcame it thanks to a meal that she was getting every day at school". However, Chipeta-Khonje notes, the significance of her story goes beyond survival. "It is a story that is giving hope to so many other children in Malawi," she explains. "And it helps people understand the extent to which children are living in these situations."
World Porridge Day, marked each year on 10 October, draws attention to the importance of school meals in tackling childhood hunger and improving access to education. The day is closely associated with the work of Mary's Meals, which provides nutritious meals to children in some of the world's poorest communities. Although the documentary was released earlier this year, Lettie's story offers a reminder of the lasting difference that a daily meal can make in a child's life.
For children in Malawi, the challenges of hunger and food insecurity are particularly acute. According to the World Food Programme, 6.8 million people in the country are experiencing insufficient food consumption. Most families rely on smallholder farming and rain-fed agriculture, leaving them especially vulnerable to droughts, flooding and other climate-related shocks.
"Food insecurity has remained a significant challenge," Chipeta-Khonje explains. "Most families have been unable to recover from repeated climatic shocks and do not have adequate food production." Children are often the first to bear the consequences. Yet, in the midst of these challenges, a simple meal can become something far greater than food. Mary's Meals "is meeting immediate hunger needs," Chipeta-Khonje says, "but it is also providing the incentive and energy for education, which ultimately breaks the cycle of poverty."
Mary's Meals began serving school meals in Malawi in 2003. What started with around 200 children in a single school has grown into the charity's largest programme worldwide. Today, more than 1.3 million children receive a meal every school day across Malawi. They now operate in 16 countries worldwide. According to the organisation's 2025 impact study, 97 per cent of teachers reported improvements in literacy and numeracy linked to better attendance and reduced hunger. Every teacher surveyed reported reduced dropout rates and improved retention among pupils receiving school meals.
Chipeta-Khonje says these outcomes reveal something important. "Yes, we are alleviating hunger," she says. "But at the same time, it is an investment in human capital development." Education, she argues, is one of the most effective ways of addressing the challenges many African countries continue to face. "We need a population that is educated so that we can deal with the challenges we are seeing every day."
Lettie's story has captured international attention because her journey was documented. But Chipeta-Khonje insists that "there are so many Letties out there".
Over the last two decades, millions of children have passed through Mary's Meals programmes in Malawi. Many have returned years later to share how a daily meal at school enabled them to remain in education, find employment, support their families and build better futures. For Chipeta-Khonje, these stories reveal the true power of school feeding programmes. "They create conditions for hope," she says. "They create opportunity. They bring lasting change that is carried into adulthood and passed on to the next generation."
Chipeta-Khonje hopes that as people watch Lettie all across the world, they will see more than one woman's journey. She hopes they will recognise what can happen when people choose to respond to hunger with compassion. "It doesn't have to be huge," she says. "Small acts of love can do so much for so many children across the world".
It is a message that resonates strongly on World Porridge Day. Behind the simple act of providing a daily meal are opportunities for children to attend school, receive an education and build a better future. Stories like Lettie's remind us what this means in practice. Often, it means a future that once seemed impossible. As Lettie shows, a daily school meal may seem simple, but for millions of children, it can change everything.

Australia’s men and Japan’s women have been crowned champions of the 2026 Asia-Pacific Sixes Lacrosse Championships after two one-goal thrillers on the final day on the Sunshine Coast.
The hosts had the final say in the men’s gold medal game, holding off Japan 14-13, with Marcus Wertheim named MVP. Japan’s women denied Australia a double, winning the women’s final 9-8 behind goalkeeper Mao Kawamura, who made nine saves and was named MVP.
The Philippines men claimed bronze, getting their revenge on China with a 17-9 win, and Rylan Connors was named MVP after scoring four goals. Korea’s women took the women’s bronze with a 16-11 win over the Philippines, led by five goals from Claire Cho and four from Helen Bae.
The final two tickets to the 2027 World Lacrosse Sixes Championships were also decided. Chinese Taipei’s men edged Hong Kong, China 20-18 to finish fifth. New Zealand’s women outlasted Chinese Taipei 13-11 to claim the last women’s spot, with Alannah Mouat named MVP after scoring three goals and adding an assist.
That closes out the tournament, with 10 teams now qualified for the 2027 World Lacrosse Sixes Championships in Colorado Springs in October 2027.

articles.title_orig: China maintains stable employment growth, vows further policy support
articles.title_zh: China maintains stable employment growth, vows further policy support
articles.content_orig:
China's job market maintained stable growth in the first three quarters, and the government will continue taking active measures, including expanding vocational training programs, strengthening rights protection for gig workers and developing new occupations, to further promote employment.
Figures released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security on Saturday show that about 10.52 million people found jobs in urban areas in the first nine months of this year, achieving 87.7 percent of the annual target. The surveyed urban unemployment rate averaged about 5.2 percent in the first eight months.
To promote higher-quality employment, the ministry will step up financial and fiscal support in the coming years and actively address the impact of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, on the job market, said Li Zhong, vice-minister of human resources and social security, at a news conference in Beijing on Saturday.
The ministry will focus on stabilizing employment in labor-intensive and service industries to create more jobs, while expanding vocational training programs to address structural imbalances between labor supply and demand.
It will also improve public employment services and strengthen supervision of the human resources market to promote higher-quality employment, Li said.
"Administrative regulations and mechanisms for protecting the employment rights of workers in flexible employment and gig work will be further improved to ensure fairer recruitment, remuneration, social insurance coverage and rest periods," he said.
The ministry will also continue developing new occupations in response to technological advances and the evolving needs of industrial development, thereby expanding employment opportunities.
Vocational training is also key to addressing structural imbalances in the labor market. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), the ministry aims to provide government-subsidized vocational training to 10 million people annually and help 40 million people obtain government-recognized skills certificates over the five-year period.

articles.title_orig: A Vague, Redacted Execution Protocol in Tennessee Draws Scrutiny
articles.title_zh: A Vague, Redacted Execution Protocol in Tennessee Draws Scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
The case of Christa Pike, who survived an execution attempt in Tennessee, has been called unprecedented. It's not.
Among other failed executions, there is the case of Willie Francis in Louisiana.
In 1946, the state attempted to execute a 17-year-old who had been condemned to die for shooting a pharmacist to death. Jurisprudence was much different then. The trial of the teen concluded within two days, there were no appeals, and Willie Francis was sent to the electric chair.
News accounts described Francis convulsing and screaming as the executioner tried twice to carry out the sentence. At one point, the teen screamed, "I am not dying," and the execution was called off.
After the attempt, there were calls for the sentence to be commuted; the case eventually went before the U.S. Supreme Court, which allowed the execution to take place a year after the first attempt.
Will the state of Tennessee also get a second chance to execute Pike? That's among the many questions swirling as a strange week comes to a close.
When the week began, Pike's attorneys had been told that she was brain dead and unlikely to recover. But she regained consciousness on Tuesday, and reportedly asked for an iPad soon after waking up. By Wednesday afternoon, she had taken a few steps. And, according to a statement released by her attorneys, on Thursday, she was walking with assistance and her arms, which she had initially not been able to move, "are healing and regaining movement and strength" and she has started to eat again.
"Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.
There are many people, however, who are dismayed by it, including the family of the young woman that Pike and her accomplices killed, Colleen Slemmer, who was 19 at the time of her death.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told ABC News that she cried when she realized that Pike had survived and that she felt she had failed her daughter by not seeing justice delivered. She later told an NBC affiliate that she doesn't think the execution will take place. "It doesn't matter what I think. They're going to do what they're going to do," WBIR reported .
On the date of her scheduled execution, Sept. 30, Pike was given two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital. The same drug was administered to a convicted killer in Texas a week later, and he died within 20 minutes .
In Tennessee, it was the second failed execution this year. Gov. Bill Lee has paused other planned executions and has ordered an investigation, and the state's prison chief, Frank Strada, has resigned.
What happens next for Pike will depend on the courts and the governor.
At a hearing on Wednesday in Nashville, Pike's attorneys asked a judge to require the Tennessee Department of Correction to keep "logbooks, surveillance footage, equipment, medical records and other information related to the events that transpired before and after the failed execution," per The Washington Post.
They have not yet asked for access to the records, but are simply asking for their preservation.
Pike's legal team also asked the judge to order the removal of shackles on Pike in her hospital bed and to allow for communication with her through a tablet. The judge did not immediately rule on the requests.
Pike's attorneys have also asked the Tennessee governor to grant clemency in light of the failed execution. "She should never be subjected to another execution attempt," they said in a statement.
Lee has not responded to the request. Shortly before the attempted execution, he denied a request for clemency that her legal team submitted, citing childhood trauma, and her rehabilitation and remorse.
NewsNation's Brian Entin, who went to Nashville for the hearing, talked with criminal defense attorney Mark Geragos , who is not associated with the Pike case, about the possibility that Pike might file a civil suit against the state of Tennessee in order to receive compensation for her injuries and any psychological harm she sustained.
"I think the last of her concerns right now is to sue. If she was going to sue, it would be to stop them from another failed attempt at killing her," Geragos said. But, he added, "Look, would I be surprised, in this case? That would be one of the least surprising turns of events."
Geragos noted that Pike had originally been offered life without parole in exchange for a guilty plea, but turned it down and went to trial. And as the date approached for her execution, Pike's legal team argued that death by lethal injection would be difficult to achieve because of complexities with her veins.
It's been reported that she was stuck with seven needles and that at least one had been bent. During the procedure, she said, "The vein in my arm feels like it's about to burst open," which analysts have said was evidence that something was wrong.
"To then take somebody from the death chamber to the hospital to try to do heroic efforts to get them fit enough to kill them again, it just seems to be the definition of insanity," Geragos told Entin.
Pike's legal team seems to be laying the groundwork for a case that their client has suffered psychological harm.
In the statement released Thursday, they said, "While her physical recovery has been remarkable, significant questions remain about the long-term effects of what she endured. Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die."
In an interview with Jesse Weber of NewsNation, Bernard Harcourt, a professor of law and civil liberties at Columbia University, said he doubts that Tennessee will be able to try again.
"It's arguable that at this point, anything more would be a violation of the Eighth Amendment because there's already been just this traumatic experience that she's gone through," Harcourt said.
In a similar case, Harcourt represented Doyle Hamm, a death row inmate in Alabama, whose scheduled execution in 2018 was called off after he was still alive nearly three hours into the procedure. He later filed a civil rights lawsuit and reached an agreement with the state in which Alabama said it would not seek another execution date.

articles.title_orig: How This Tiny Startup Built the World’s Safest Bike Helmet
articles.title_zh: How This Tiny Startup Built the World’s Safest Bike Helmet
articles.content_orig:
For decades, researchers judged cycling helmets on how well they protected against direct impacts. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission ( CPSC ) still does, even though research shows the danger isn't just how hard your head hits the ground, but how violently it twists. That rotational movement can make the brain twist and stretch inside the skull, increasing the risk of concussion and other brain injuries.
Not waiting for the CPSC to catch up, the cycling industry got to work. Multidirectional Impact Protection System , or MIPS, hit the market in 2007 and is now a common feature on premium helmets . At the same time, Virginia Tech turned helmet safety into something of a competition for manufacturers. In 2018, it launched helmet STAR ratings (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk), testing beyond the legal minimum and measuring both linear and rotational impacts.
Only four of the first 30 helmets earned five stars, but by 2025, 167 of 272 achieved five stars, and Virginia Tech had to tighten its grading. That only drove competition and improved helmet technology. Suddenly, hitting the number one spot was good for business and brains.
Sitting comfortably ahead of the competition, with a 4.61 score (10.1 or lower earns a five-star rating; lower is better), is the Pikio Si Oblik road cycling helmet, featuring a new safety system called Oblik. Inspired by the headbanging, concussion-proof woodpecker, this new design has wiped the floor with the competition. For context, Pikio's 4.61 score is 2.21 points lower than the previous best Canyon Deflectr’s 6.82. That’s about 32 percent lower, a massive shift when many of the highest-rated helmets score only between 7 and 10 points.
How has this relatively obscure Vancouver startup gotten it right the first time? As founder Daniel Abram explains, it “comes from 18 years researching impact protection and helmet design.” After studying mechanical engineering, he moved into helmet research at Simon Fraser University, where he helped develop BrainShield , a system designed to reduce rotational forces during impacts. He later founded helmet technology company BiaGuard , before MIPS paid around $1 million for the patents and intellectual property in 2022.
Most bike helmets use a thin plastic shell over expanded polystyrene (EPS) foam, which crushes on impact to absorb energy before it reaches your skull. Oblik takes that familiar foam structure and breaks it into independently mounted sections rather than one continuous block.
Each section attaches to the base EPS layer with flexible connection points, allowing them to move separately or detach if the helmet takes a serious impact. Combined with dual-density foam that absorbs direct impact, the movement helps to minimize the twisting force transmitted to the head. Abram explained how, “Rather than compressing material in one direction, the system is able to deform, deflect, and detach depending on the impact's intensity, location, and direction, helping manage both linear and rotational impact energy.”
Other helmet technologies approach the problem very differently. The now-ubiquitous MIPS remains the dominant commercial system, using a low-friction layer that can move 10 to 15 millimeters during the first 5 to 10 milliseconds of an impact. MIPS Spherical uses two nested liners that rotate relative to each other, while 6D’s Omni-Directional Suspension (ODS) suspends one liner inside another. WaveCel uses an engineered cellular structure that flexes, crumples, and glides under angled impacts.
Pikio's closest rival, the Release Layer System (RLS), featured on Canyon’s Deflectr and the third-placed, 3D-printed Hexr Miden RLS , tackles rotation from the outside, using external shell panels floating on tiny polycarbonate ball bearings that can roll and detach, redirecting rotational energy before it reaches the head.
Lab testing is one thing, but real-world data is something else. If your Pikio helmet is called into serious action, you will need to replace it—as with most EPS foam designs—but the company is offering a 30 percent discount on a replacement if it can get its hands on your damaged helmet.
“So far we’ve had four helmets returned and replaced,” Abram says. “Each has proven invaluable, not least because they’ve done their job and kept riders safe.”
At $379, the Pikio is a premium choice—a cool $219 more expensive than the second-best STAR-tested Canyon Deflectr RLS. Much of the cost stems from a vastly more complicated manufacturing process. Abram says a standard cycling helmet has around eight to 10 parts, but the Pikio Si uses around 80 individual components. The separate foam sections, intricately engineered flexible connection points, and dual-density construction all add to the cost.
It’s a small price to pay if it saves your life, but how does it fare day to day? I’ve been riding with the Si Oblik for the past month and have been impressed by how few compromises there have been in the pursuit of protection.
At 279 grams (in medium size), it's respectably light, though not class-leading, and the dial-to-fit cradle hugs my head neatly without pinch points. It’s a little bulky for a road lid, but is extremely comfortable; the 17 air vents keep my head refreshingly cool, and nobody has laughed at me for wearing it (yet). I would have preferred Pikio to use a magnetic Fidlock fastening under the chin as they’re brilliant, but it is a minor complaint—which Abram quickly quashed: “Fidlock weighs around 13 grams; a buckle is just four grams.”
It’s a great helmet loaded with unique, deliberately safety-first tech. Abram was keen to point out he is not interested in what he called “crown-like cycle helmet” aesthetics, and that “form always follows function.” The Pikio lacks a little of the cool factor you’ll find with a POC or Giro helmet, but it’s certainly not ugly.
For a company most cyclists have never heard of, taking the top spot at Virginia Tech is an extraordinary result. The harder part may be persuading people to trust an unknown name with something as consequential as head protection. MIPS faced a similar problem before turning an independent safety technology into something licensed across much of the helmet industry, and Oblik could conceivably follow the same path.
Whether Pikio becomes a major helmet brand—a second design is due early in the new year—a technology supplier, or both remains to be seen. But for now, it has given the cycling industry a new number to chase.

articles.title_orig: Police arrest leader of India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement before mass protest
articles.title_zh: Police arrest leader of India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement before mass protest
articles.content_orig:
Indian police have detained the founder of a surging youth-led political movement and hundreds of protesters in a crackdown ahead of a major planned protest in the capital New Delhi.
Abhijeet Dipke was detained along with other leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party as their plane landed in New Delhi, according to the group. Footage shows Dipke shouting “go ahead and arrest us! Victory to Mother India! Long live the revolution!”
The CJP started out in May as a Gen-Z internet joke that went viral. In July, it forced the government into its biggest climbdown in years. Now the party is back for what it is billing as Season 2 of its political movement.
This time its target is the 62-year-old chief of the Election Commission that holds the keys to India’s democracy – the world’s largest – and who, the CJP alleges, is responsible for disenfranchising tens of millions of their fellow citizens.
Supporters of the movement gathered in New Delhi Saturday despite the capital turning into a fortress to keep out protesters. Mobile internet was also blocked. Many people at the protest site were detained by police, CNN witnessed.
The party quickly condemned the detention of its founders and leaders calling it an attempt to “cripple the leadership of today’s peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site.”
In a separate statement, the party said highly popular influencer and activist Dhruv Rathee – who has 33 million subscribers on YouTube alone – was detained at the protest site.
But Nitin Nabin, president of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), on Saturday lambasted the CJP.
“You cannot bear to see India moving forward as a self-reliant and empowered nation, and you are attempting to destabilize it at the behest of foreign forces,” he said on X.
The CJP takes its name from an off-the-cuff remark by India’s chief justice, who in May allegedly used the words “cockroaches” and “parasites” to refer to groups of unemployed youth in the country. He later claimed he was misquoted, but CJP founder and Boston University graduate Dipke ran with it, hailing the titular insect’s stubbornness and indestructibility.
The movement then joined nationwide protests demanding the removal of the education minister over an exam paper leaks scandal, harnessing widespread anger at the lack of opportunities for young people and sparking moments that captured India’s internet.
Reels captured everything from dancing and DJ parties at protest sites to songs mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Other clips played on FOMO and nudged friends to get off their phones and join the protests.
And there was free food. So much free food that organizers eventually had to ask supporters across the country to stop sending it.
Then, after weeks of sit-ins and marches, Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister, stepped down, a rare blow to Modi’s government, and one that more established opposition parties had been unable to land.
The focus of Saturday’s planned protest is Gyanesh Kumar, the head of the Electoral Commission that’s currently in the middle of a gargantuan exercise to remove dead, duplicate and otherwise ineligible voters from its rolls. Opposition parties say the commission is stripping out eligible voters to benefit Modi’s BJP, claims the BJP and the commission deny.
CNN has reached out to the election commission and BJP for a response.
More mainstream political parties are calling for the same thing, but Dipke had called supporters of the CJP back to Jantar Mantar, the historic protest ground in the center of the capital New Delhi, for “Season 2.”
In a statement released in the wake of Dipke’s detention, the party confirmed the march would continue. It orders its supporters, “If your movement is blocked by barricades or police personnel anywhere on the streets, do not stop—start your protest right where you are stopped.”
Organizers had been hoping tens of thousands would come out, but such crowds are yet to materialize – perhaps because of extraordinary measures taken by the government.
The CJP said on Friday police in several states were detaining thousands of its supporters, while India’s interior ministry ordered an internet blackout in central Delhi until 10 p.m. local time Saturday.
Central Delhi was sealed, with thousands of police and paramilitaries on the scene. Reuters reported that some long-distance trains to Delhi were canceled on Friday and more than 50 metro stations shut.
Muskaan, 19, a video editor based in Delhi and veteran of the first round of CJP demonstrations, was weighing whether to go again, she told CNN Friday.
Attending the first round of the protests, she had been expecting the police violence she had seen on television, she said, asking only to use her first name. She’d only gone because her friends had, she said.
“But when we went there, there was a lot of fun… People were playing songs, dancing, and really good memes on banners.”
Once she was there, she learned much more about the exam leaks and how they had affected people’s lives.
Muskaan said she was pleased when Pradhan resigned, but also disappointed that the protests ended so quickly. “I felt that it was too soon, that we should have got another chance to go again,” she said.
Chief Election Commissioner Kumar is a very different target.
Removing him would require a formal parliamentary process and a special majority in both houses. The opposition doesn’t have the numbers.
That leaves the CJP facing a different test. Its first campaign showed that an online joke could become a street movement and generate political pressure. Season 2 is asking whether that formula can work on a much bigger issue: India’s electoral system.
For a movement born from memes, this second wave of action will test whether that irreverent energy can translate into pressure on an institution at the heart of India’s democracy.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias downgraded after making landfall in Florida
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias downgraded after making landfall in Florida
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias has been downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone the day after it made landfall along the northern Gulf Coast of Florida, bringing with it heavy rains and powerful winds.
Isaias - which is the first of the 2026 Atlantic season - is still surging across south-eastern parts of the US.
Hundreds of thousands of households in Florida, Alabama and Georgia are without power, and each state has issued a state of emergency. There are currently no warnings in places after they ended on Saturday.
Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.
Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations to thousands of people due to the storm.
In Florida, those evacuations included coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"
Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.
On Saturday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the US president had approved emergency declarations for the two states to "ensure federal resources are available" for support.
Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.
It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form before October.
Ahead of the storm, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned it was likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast.
All warnings pertaining to Isaias had been discontinued on Saturday morning, the NHC said.
The post-tropical cyclone is currently moving north and is expected to cross Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley later on Saturday and Sunday, according to the National Weather Service.
Hurricane-force winds on Friday evening extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km)  from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).
However, hundreds of thousands are currently without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding.
On Saturday morning, more than 400,000 were in the dark in Florida and just over 300,000 customers in Alabama were experiencing outages, according to PowerOutage.us. In Georgia, more than 100,000 customers were without power.
Ahead of the hurricane, Pensacola resident John Guoth, told the BBC that he and his wife would remain at home despite the rest of his street having already left.
"It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said, explaining that they have "battened down" anything that "can fly".
Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".
A few households remained in the area, describing themselves as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".
People in the Florida city who had "seen bad storms before" were still "bunkering up", Brandin Ruth said. She told the BBC: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".
One indicator of a storm's severity to southern communities was Friday's closure of stalwart restaurant chain , The Waffle House.
A Waffle House spokesperson confirmed to the BBC that the chain had already closed a number of locations in the hurricane's path and "will continue monitoring conditions".
US President Donald Trump also cancelled plans to attend a major American football college game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama because of the hurricane, shifting plans to attend a rally in Tennessee instead.
Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.
Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific.
While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.
Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.
Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".
It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.
With additional reporting by Simon King and Matt Taylor, BBC Weather

articles.title_orig: SpaceX launches 21 data satellites for the Space Development Agency
articles.title_zh: SpaceX launches 21 data satellites for the Space Development Agency
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX launched a Falcon 9 rocket early Saturday carrying a batch of data satellites for the U.S. military’s Space Development Agency (SDA), five days after a last-minute abort scrubbed the first attempt.
Liftoff from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California is occurred at 12:39 a.m. PDT (3:39 EDT / 0739 UTC). The Falcon 9 took a southerly trajectory on departure from Space Launch Complex 4E, currently SpaceX’s only launch facility on the West Coast.
A launch attempt on Oct. 5 was halted by an auto-abort with 58 seconds remaining on the clock. The halt was triggered moments after the rocket’s onboard computers took control of the countdown. SpaceX said the hold was called due to “some off-nominal data on Stage Two”.
The vehicle was lowered to a horizontal position at the pad for troubleshooting the issue, and the launch was repeatedly pushed back a day at a time.
“Additional time throughout the week allowed for double checks on vehicle systems and range deconfliction,” said SpaceX launch commentator Atticus Vadera.
The range conflict is believed to have been a missile test from Vandenberg that occurred on Friday.
The mission, dubbed Tranche 1 Transport Layer A (T1TL-A), is the fourth mission sending production satellites into orbit for the SDA. This is one piece of a broad constellation — called the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture (PWSA) — designed to support the U.S. military and its allies through space-based capabilities, like missile tracking and secure communications.
The mission will used Falcon 9 first stage booster B1103. This was its sixth flight following the launches of the SDA’s T1TL-E, NROL-179, and three batches of Starlink satellites.
About 7.5 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX landed B1103 at Landing Zone 4. This was the 37th landing at LZ-4 and the 668th Falcon booster landing to date.
The T1TL-A mission is one of 23 missions awarded to SpaceX as part of the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 2 contract awarded in August 2020, which is managed by the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command (SSC). The previous missions from the SDA have already been launched:
The T1TL-B and -E missions featured satellites manufactured by York Space Systems and the T1TL-C satellites were produced by Lockheed Martin. Space Force Col. Ryan Hiserote, SSC’s division chief in Assured Access to Space, told Spaceflight Now back in September 2025 that these initial T1TL missions could be launched in any order.
The 21 satellites flying as part of the T1TL-A mission were manufactured by Northrop Grumman and delivered to Vandenberg Space Force Base on Sept. 28.
Tranche 1 is the initial component of the PWSA constellation is expected to begin providing operational capabilities to the Department of Defense beginning in 2027. When complete, T1 will consist of 126 Transport Layer satellites, 28 Tracking Layer satellites, and four missile defense demonstration spacecraft.
With the three launches completed to date, there are 63 satellites in orbit.
“In close coordination with Space Systems Command (SSC) and Space Launch Delta 30, the deployment of Tranche 1’s proliferated capability will soon deliver continuous overwatch—neutralizing any first-mover advantage by delivering data to warfighters around the world, nearly instantaneously,” said GP Sandhoo, SDA Director and Space Force Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Missile Warning and Tracking following the T1TL-E launch in July.
The SDA said the Transport Layer will consist of between 300 to 500 satellites in low Earth orbit from 750 km to 1,200 km in altitude. The SDA said once complete, 95 percent of the globe will be in view of at least two of the T1TL satellites at any given time.
“The constellation will be interconnected with Optical Inter-Satellite Links (OISLs) which have significantly increased performance over existing radio frequency crosslinks,” the SDA wrote. “LEO orbits in conjunction with OISLs will reduce path loss issues but more importantly offer much lower latencies, which are deemed critical to prosecute time sensitive targets in today’s wartime environment.”
These satellites will be able to integrate with the Link-16 and Integrated Broadcast System (IBS) to allow for “timely threat warnings and situational awareness information”.
The launches of these satellites are managed by the SSC’s System Delta 80 (SYD 80) and the Space Fore Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Assured Access to Space.
The rocket carried an unspecified number of satellites to orbit. Liftoff from pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base happened on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 6:07:56 p.m. PDT / 9:07:56 p.m. EDT on Sept. 16 (0107:56 UTC on Sept. 17).
A Falcon 9 rocket fired into a late-night sky Friday night over Cape Canaveral with a Dragon supply ship bound for the International Space Station. Eight minutes later, the booster returned to Florida’s Space Coast for SpaceX’s 50th landing of a Falcon first stage.
Marc Rayman is chief engineer on NASA’s Dawn mission, which has run out of fuel after a 11-year interplanetary journey that explored Vesta and Ceres, the two largest objects in the asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

articles.title_orig: 'No one ever heard of her': Trump rails against Nobel Peace Prize snub
articles.title_zh: 'No one ever heard of her': Trump rails against Nobel Peace Prize snub
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump overnight delivered a lengthy, scathing rant on the decision to award South African jurist Navanethem "Navi" Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize.
In a post on Truth social, Trump called the decision an "indelible stain on Norway" as he dismissed Pillay's career and touted his own diplomatic record.
"I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else! In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel," he wrote, adding: "I don’t know what the woman has done."
He went on to claim he "should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes" for having "settled 8 wars" and said he would soon "settle, or win, two more," pointing to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Trump listed the conflicts he said he had "settled" as Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Pakistan and India, Israel and Iran, Egypt and Ethiopia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, and Israel and Hamas.
Becoming increasingly irate, Trump continued to detail his perceived achievements before renewing his attack on Pillay, who he described as a "liberal person who works at the United Nations."
"The Nobel 'Peace' Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy, and enemies of civilization!" he concluded.
The post came after the president had already lambasted the award decision while speaking at a campaign rally in Syracuse, New York, on Friday, where he branded it as "disgraceful and embarrassing."
Born in Durban on South Africa's east coast, Pillay would go on to become the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2008, a post she held until 2014.
Earlier in her career, she worked as a defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists, helping establish rights for prisoners on Robben Island.
She then served as acting judge on the South African High Court and as a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.
She was also appointed as a judge on the International Criminal Court in 2003, working within the Appeals Chamber until 2008.
In 2025, whilst serving as the chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, Pillay accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.
Learning she had won the Peace Prize on Friday, Pillay appeared unable to resist taking a playful jab at Trump.
"If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she said, in an apparent nod to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, presenting her award to the American president.
It comes as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on Friday that the US would be sanctioning the International Criminal Court, which Washington has repeatedly accused of "politicised actions" and of "targeting Israel."
"We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us," Rubio said in a video address shared on social media.
"Our message is clear, the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC," he added.
