articles.title_orig: Vos claims second gravel world title with impressive performance in Australia
articles.title_zh: Vos claims second gravel world title with impressive performance in Australia
articles.content_orig:
Marianne Vos has claimed the gravel world title for the second time in her career. The Team Visma | Lease a Bike rider was crowned world champion in Nannup, Australia, after a demanding race over gravel roads and challenging climbs. With her victory, Vos adds another rainbow jersey to her impressive palmarès.
“This victory really means a lot to me,” an emotional Vos said after the finish. This year marked the first time the UCI Gravel World Championships were held outside Europe. In and around Nannup, the riders faced a demanding 125.6-kilometer course with approximately 3,180 meters of elevation gain.
"I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here."
The succession of short climbs made the course particularly challenging, requiring not only physical strength but also technical skills and good race management. On the demanding course, Vos once again demonstrated her versatility. “There was more mud than I expected. As a result, there were also some slippery sections on the course, so we had to be careful at times. Rosa was incredibly strong, especially on the climbs, where I really had to dig deep to stay with her,” Vos explained.
“It was a fantastic course here in Australia. I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here,” the Dutch rider concluded. This is Vos’s second gravel world title. In 2024, she had already claimed victory at the World Championships in Leuven. With this latest world title, Vos adds another chapter to her remarkable cycling career and brings a difficult season to a close on a high note.

articles.title_orig: U.S. official: Trump cut deal with Putin after Zelensky ignored his requests
articles.title_zh: U.S. official: Trump cut deal with Putin after Zelensky ignored his requests
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has slammed an agreement on diesel fuel between the US and Russia, casting the decision as an “investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
US President Donald Trump on Friday said he secured a deal from Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply markets with Russian diesel fuel as he works to bring down energy costs ahead of the midterm elections.
Zelensky said the move, which Trump announced as fresh Ukraine-US talks were getting underway in Miami, was “a weak decision of strong partners,” while analysts said the agreement was not likely to lower diesel prices in any meaningful way.
“We need strong signals from the United States, from Europe, and from other partners — signals in support of Ukraine and aimed at LIMITING Russia’s ability to wage war and terrorize people,” Zelensky said. Hours after Trump’s announcement Russian strikes killed at least 17 people in Ukraine.
Trump wrote on social media that Putin agreed to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel to global energy markets, with another 500,000 tons promised in November. Together, the amounts — equal to 6 million barrels of diesel fuel — would cover about a day and a half worth of US demand, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
But former US officials said it is unclear if Putin even has the amount of diesel that Trump cited to sell, as Ukrainian strikes put growing strain on the country’s oil supplies.
Just this week, Kyiv has claimed strikes on five different refineries across Russia, the latest of which were announced by Ukrainian authorities after Trump’s Friday announcement.
Trump said that millions more tons of Russian diesel would be supplied following the first tranches “based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries.”
Analysts cast doubt on the impact of the agreement.
“We are talking PERHAPS a 5-6% increase in supply between now and year end,” Dan Pickering, founder and chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners, said about the the president’s announcement.
“Bottom line — this is helpful but not a needle mover for global diesel markets,” Pickering said. “Sidenote — there is a reason Trump talked about volumes in tons instead of barrels. The tons number looks bigger to a general observer. This is more politics than a game changer.”
Russia banned exports of diesel in early July, after Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries triggered widespread fuel shortages across the country. This cut roughly 800,000 barrels per day from the global market — at a time when supplies were already tight because of the US war against Iran.
According to the Kremlin readout of the phone call between the two leaders, Putin told Trump that Russia was “ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets.”
“I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy,” Putin said, according to the Kremlin.
But analysts — and commodities traders — raised doubts that Russia would be able to live up to that promise.
At the close of trading on Friday, diesel futures were down by about 4%.
Kyiv has long advocated for tougher sanctions on Russian energy exports, arguing that oil and gas revenues are a major source of funding for Russia’s war machine.
The US president has blamed the rise in global diesel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war and called on both sides to halt strikes on energy facilities as recently as last month, to little avail.
The past few months have been brutal for Ukrainian civilians as Russia has taken advantage of Kyiv’s critical shortage of air defense missiles, launching near non-stop aerial attacks against Ukrainian cities. One such strike on a bus stop in eastern Ukraine killed more than 30 people on Thursday.
More recently, a Russian attack on Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region killed 17 people, including three children, local authorities said Saturday. Search and rescue operations are ongoing.
Zelensky has made it clear the timing of the announcement — just as a top-level Ukrainian delegation arrived to Miami for talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — makes it all the more painful for Kyiv.
“In this exact moment when our team is talking to the American team in Florida, the US President has a conversation with Kremlin leader, with the leader of this war, the leader of this aggression,” he said.
Masha’s husband was fighting on the front line. But she was the one killed by a Russian drone
Richard Nephew, a former principal deputy coordinator for sanctions policy at the State Department, noted that “the message it sends and the damage it does to the broader sanctions regime is very significant.”
“How does anyone take the sanctions regime seriously?” he questioned, noting that if the US is going to say that they need to use sanctions relief to address an economic issue, “how can we convincingly argue that anyone else shouldn’t use the same excuse?”
A former senior State Department official said it doesn’t matter if Putin can actually deliver the diesel because “now he’s achieved the result he wants” which is Trump thinking he’s gotten a pre-election bump and it might have an impact on the markets.
The timing of the call with the start of the talks with Ukraine is no coincidence.
“Putin is a lot of things, but he’s not stupid,” they said.
Trump has been working to identify ways to bring down costs, including by temporarily lifting restrictions on “red dye” diesel used in farm equipment.
Trump did not mention raising during his call with Putin the still unexplained death of a plague lab researcher.
Instead, the US president focused solely on diesel supplies, which have concerned Republicans as higher energy prices drive up other costs.
“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump wrote.
Energy analysts quickly cast doubt on that assertion.
“So assuming this happens and Putin delivers — which would mean reversing the ban on diesel exports that has been in place for several months now — it would be a bandaid, nothing more,” Gregory Brew, an analyst with Eurasia Group’s Energy, Climate & Resources team, said in an email.
“I also have a strong suspicion Putin expects Ukraine to cease its attacks on refineries in exchange for doing Trump the favor. I have a hard time seeing Zelensky cooperate on that front,” Brew said.
This story has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Victoria Butenko, Kosta Gak and Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: A US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled
articles.title_zh: A US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled
articles.content_orig:
A Palestinian mother mourns her son, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike just over a month into the ceasefire, at Al-Shifa Hospital, in Gaza City, on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death.
GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge.
Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire.
That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza.
NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos.
Palestinians returned to the ruins of Gaza City after Israeli forces withdrew and ended their ground operation on the first day of the ceasefire, on Oct. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
In Khan Younis, families greet Palestinian prisoners who were freed in exchange for Israeli hostages on Oct. 13, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
At Al-Shifa Hospital on Oct. 23, 2025, Joud Al-Angar, 12, and his younger cousin are covered in dime-sized scabs after they were wounded by a piece of shrapnel from an Israeli munition. They found it in the rubble and thought it was coal they could use to help their family cook dinner. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
The bodies of multiple people, including children, are covered in shrouds at a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital on Nov. 20, 2025, after Israeli airstrikes targeted homes and tents. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
People inspect the aftermath of a deadly Israeli airstrike that destroyed a home in Gaza City six weeks into the ceasefire on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A father and his son wade through flooded streets in Gaza City after picking up humanitarian aid on Nov. 25, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Children wear virtual reality headsets as part of a TechMed Gaza initiative that aims to help provide children with psychosocial support for trauma, in Al-Zuweida, Gaza, on Dec. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Saqer Al-Ankah holds his dying 10-year-old granddaughter, Bayan, in his arms at Baptist Hospital in Gaza City on Dec. 10, 2025, after she was shot in her tent by Israeli troops who occupy northeast Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Makeshift tents like these in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025, offer little protection from the winter cold, but the U.N. says roughly 1.5 million people have only these for shelter after Israeli airstrikes destroyed nearly all the buildings in the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Raed el-Ghazawi and his children stand in a tent in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025. The family of five says the tent is freezing cold and damp from winter rainstorms. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
On Dec. 17, 2025, Palestinian Christian children decorate a Christmas tree inside the Holy Family Church in Gaza City for the first time since the beginning of the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Fresh produce returns to Gaza City's streets on Dec. 23, 2025, after U.N.-backed experts declared a famine there amid Israeli restrictions on aid during the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Patients sit in a clinic run by Doctors Without Borders in Gaza City on Dec. 31, 2025, a day before Israel banned more than 40 international aid organizations from bringing in staff or aid to Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian female artists gather at the beach in Gaza City for the first time since the war began to paint as a form of therapy, on Feb. 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian rescue workers begin the work of retrieving corpses from under the rubble of homes bombed by Israel during the war in Beit Lahia, Gaza, on Feb. 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
The skeleton of Shawqi Abu Naser, 60, is retrieved from under the rubble on Feb. 16, 2026, more than a year after an Israeli airstrike killed 132 people from the same family in Beit Lahia. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A mother from the Abu Nasr family sits by her son's body in Beit Lahia on Feb. 17, 2026. The body was retrieved from under the rubble more than a year after 132 people were killed in a single Israeli airstrike on the family home. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians gather in an open space in Gaza City for early morning prayers that mark the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child smiles next to a man dressed as a clown on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, celebrations that mark the end of Ramadan fasting, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian boy shakes hands with Hamas militants on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, following the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians stand next to boxes of U.N. food aid in an area that aid groups need Israeli permission to enter in Jabalia, Gaza, on April 18, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A yellow block placed by Israeli forces marks the expanding territory controlled by the military in Bureij, Gaza, on May 7, 2026. Palestinians are barred from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Young Palestinian chess players gather at a coffee shop in Gaza City for the first tournament since the start of the war, on May 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child carries jugs of water as he passes by a mural of Spanish soccer star Lamine Yamal that is painted on the rubble of a home destroyed by Israeli airstrikes, in Al-Shati refugee camp, Gaza, on May 14, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A building burns after an Israeli airstrike killed Izz al-Din al-Haddad, the leader of the military wing of Hamas, his wife, his daughter and a neighbor in Gaza City on May 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Children jump on a trampoline during the Eid holidays on May 31, 2026, in Beit Lahia, which the Israeli military had deemed an "orange zone." Aid organizations are restricted from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child looks into a burned car that was targeted in an Israeli airstrike on a busy street in Gaza City on June 22, 2026. A teenage girl who was going to find internet access to take her final exams was killed in the strike. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A plume of smoke rises after an Israeli airstrike targeted a home in Gaza City nine months into the ceasefire on July 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Thousands of displaced Palestinians gather under Egyptian flags amid the rubble in Gaza City for a public screening of Egypt's match against Argentina in the World Cup on July 7, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
One-hundred corpses are wrapped in Palestinian flags in Gaza City on Aug. 4, 2026, after being retrieved from under the rubble of a building that was hit in an Israeli airstrike in October 2023. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child whose brother was killed in an Israeli airstrike cries at the door of a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on Aug. 19, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian children form a chain for a global solidarity initiative called Swim With Gaza that raises money for swimming lessons in Khan Younis on Aug. 25, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child's toys are stained with blood in Gaza City

articles.title_orig: We bought a one-way ticket to travel the world with our children
articles.title_zh: We bought a one-way ticket to travel the world with our children
articles.content_orig:
Dani and Tom Wooldridge worked hard to transform a 1970s house into a beloved family home after they bought it about seven years ago.
Dani, 39, a nurse, also ran an aesthetics business while Tom, 38, had a construction business. Three children, a close extended family and lots of friends. A happy life.
Yet in May this year, the five of them sold their possessions and home, and bought a one-way ticket heading for Indonesia, with the only things they owned in the world now stowed in backpacks in the luggage compartment.
With Olivia, 12, Morgan, seven, and four-year-old George, the Woolridges are planning to travel the world, with no endpoint in sight, hoping to see every continent.
Five months in, over a video call from the Indonesian island of Lombok, Dani and Tom explain the decisions which have brought them to the shores of south-east Asia.
Both of them had gone travelling for a period of time in their early 20s, a classic gap-year style experience, and had enjoyed taking holidays, particularly to sunny destinations.
Dani said: "It was always a conversation we had but once you start having kids and you've got the mortgage and everything like that it's kind of, 'oh it's not the right time'."
But nearly two years ago, the family took a holiday to Thailand over Christmas.
"We were fortunate enough to have a month over there, travelled round with the kids and obviously they were almost two years younger than they are now, and managed really well.
Tom added: "It all went really smoothly and it was great seeing the kids experience a completely different world to what we'd all grown up. It just felt so great exploring with them.
Dani said that sparked their interest to start researching and meeting other families who had decided to jet off.
"We made lots of lists - lots of positives, lots of negatives," she said.
"Can we do this? How are we still going to educate our children? We had a home, we had our businesses, we had careers. What do we do about all that?"
Once they made the decision, they knew they had to be "100% committed".
Dani thought at first they should rent their house out "so we've got something to come back to" but Tom wanted to sell, and the couple realised they didn't want to leave the responsibility of managing it to people back home.
The boys were excited about the idea from the start but the couple admit it was harder for their daughter.
Tom said: "Olivia was a bit nervous. She'd just started high school in the September and we left in May. She was very apprehensive about leaving all her friends.
"Morgan and George do mention their friends now and again, but they're a bit younger so they didn't have that emotional attachment as much as Olivia."
When they told their parents about their plans, their initial reaction was "why are you selling everything you've worked so hard to get?"
"Most people have got bets on when we're coming back," Dani said, laughing. Tom added: "They've all got a year each."
After selling their house at the start of the year, they lived in rented accommodation for a number of months, before heading to the airport in May for the big farewell.
Leaving was "very emotional", Dani said.
"We were very fortunate that we had a lot of family coming to the airport with us," added Tom. "We'd checked our luggage in and we got to the security gates - that was hard.
"We were so fortunate to have a close family and friendship group as well. They're the people we miss and that's what we miss from back home, the people that were in our lives. Not so much the material things we had."
However once the plane had taken off and the goodbyes were behind them, the excitement started to kick in.
"We remembered where we were going," joked Tom.
Even though they had both been to their first destination, Bali in Indonesia, before, the culture shock still hit them.
"It's just everything. Your senses are just heightened. It's the smells, seeing everything around, it's so different to home.
"We went to Bali 15 years ago when it was a lot quieter," added Dani. "People have said how busy it is now, and it was.
"The first day or two was very overwhelming. Our daughter was still a bit emotional. She was up and down with things and we were all a bit jet lagged.
"We went to Uluwatu first and it has got so busy. Even us walking down a road, I was nervous. Scooters everywhere."
But there were also upsides, Tom said. "The food instantly was amazing. And the people are just beautiful, and so kind. And just to feel the heat on our skin."
They moved to different parts of the island, swapping the beaches in the south to climb the volcanic Mount Batur in the north, and spending time in the cultural village of Ubud inland.
They then went island hopping eastwards across the Indonesian archipelago before doubling back to Lombok for a second stay.
"We were moving around quite a bit," Dani said. "So each time it was almost like that feeling of going home because we were packing up, but we weren't going home. I think it took us months to really think, 'wow, we're not actually going home'."
Leaving the UK behind has not meant abandoning education, Dani stressed.
"Even though we want our children to experience the world and have that kind of real world learning, we have said we also want them to have opportunities. So if they want to go to university and be a doctor or a nurse or whatever career path they want to go down, we still want them to have those opportunities," she added.
They have a "huge bag" full of textbooks and workbooks recommended by teachers before they left and they are following the UK teaching curriculum. Olivia has an online maths tutor, who was previously head of maths at her high school in Rhondda Cynon Taf, and had also taught Tom at the same school.
The boys have a tutor who covers the primary curriculum with them and does English and some science with Olivia.
Although the big downside to their journey is missing time with family back home, Dani and Tom say the cultural experiences and confidence the children have already gained from their travels, meeting such a wide variety of people and having the opportunity to live such an outdoor life, outweighs the negatives.
The family is due to be moving on to Malaysia after spending five months travelling around Indonesia, most recently in Lombok for a second stint, where the children have been attending a world schooling centre - which the couple described as a "lovely routine" with amazing friends.
After bringing "way too much stuff" with them initially, they have given away possessions to locals they have met along their travels and refined it down to two large 120-litre backpacks for the parents and two 100-litre rolling packs including one filled with educational materials.
"The kids will have virtually nothing on their backs, just maybe a really small backpack to get on the plane," said Tom.
"We thought the kids would be excited at carrying their backpacks. Yeah, they're not onboard with that," laughed Dani.
Among the things they have planned for Malaysia is visiting an orangutang sanctuary in Borneo and another longer stop at a world schooling centre to give the children more chances to spend time with peers.
Then they move into Thailand, where both Dani's mum and Tom's parents will make separate visits and after figuring out a good location to celebrate Dani's 40th birthday, will move through Cambodia, Vietnam and the Philippines.
With all that, they have the next year "roughly" planned out. They have allowed for contingencies and emergencies - Tom has already had to fly home once for a funeral - but don't have a firm destination in mind yet once they leave Asia, barring a likely brief visit home to catch up with family.
"We're going to do as much as we feel we want to in a continent and then go to the next one," explained Tom.
"Just keep going for as long as we can, and want to. If at some point we don't want to then we'll have explored a lot of places to pick somewhere to stop."

articles.title_orig: Trump, Putin reach deal to release Russian diesel to world
articles.title_zh: Trump, Putin reach deal to release Russian diesel to world
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release Russian diesel to US and global markets.
The move, which aims to address rising fuel costs before the US midterm elections, marks a dramatic turnaround in US policy toward Moscow since the start of the war in Ukraine .
In a social media post, Trump wrote he had made a deal with Putin during a phone call that was supposed to be about a suspected plague outbreak in Russia .
According to Trump, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
Trump wrote that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that.
The US Treasury Department issued a temporary license that will allow Russian diesel to reach global markets through April 2027.
Trump's announcement follows his signing of a broad Russia sanctions law last month. The law is intended to clamp down on Russia’s energy sector and other areas that fuel its war against Ukraine.
Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian presidential envoy, reposted the Treasury Department's announcement on X, saying that "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
Alexander Novak, Russia's Deputy Prime Minister, said that the country was ready to start supplying additional volumes of diesel to the United States and other countries from October.
He also said that Russia's exports are expected to rise further in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance.
Later, the Kremlin released a statement from Putin saying that, during their call, he and Trump had also devoted "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and had discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has condemned the agreement, saying that any easing of sanctions without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of "weakness."
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," he wrote on social media.
"Allowing Russia to ⁠sell ​petroleum products ​is an investment in a ​war that ‌must be ended, not prolonged. What ​is needed ⁠is real de-escalation with Russia ⁠on ​a reciprocal basis," the Ukrainian president stressed.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine hopes the US will have a strong conversation with Russia: "A strong one, not a weak one."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Since its 2022 full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine, Moscow has been hit with rounds of sanctions by the United States and its Western partners.
But as the war has continued with no resolution in sight, Washington's commitment to that approach has appeared to waver.
Earlier this year, temporary US sanctions waivers that allowed the sale of Russian oil raised concerns because they could hinder efforts to deprive Moscow of funds for its war in Ukraine.
Last month, Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring diesel prices, and even publicly told Zelenskyy to stop the attacks.
Trump's announcement on Friday came just as US, Ukrainian, and European officials were meeting in Miami for new diplomatic talks aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.
According to US envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian, European, US and NATO representatives held "constructive" discussions in Miami, and agreed to continue diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
According to Ines Pohl, the chief of DW's Washington D.C. bureau, the diesel deal is mainly about domestic politics.
With the midterms only weeks away, Trump is under heavy pressure over high energy prices . The deal allows him to show that he is taking action and appeal to voters who feel the rising cost of fuel directly, while the war in Ukraine seems far away.
Politically, that is significant: Trump is accepting a loosening of sanctions on Russia, even though Washington had actually wanted to increase pressure on Putin.
It also makes one thing crystal clear: when push comes to shove, Trump consistently chooses what benefits him personally over what Congress has decided .
He appears to be betting that, for many Americans, prices at the pump matter more in the end than the geopolitical consequences. Whether the promised deliveries will actually bring noticeable relief, however, remains doubtful.
Edited by: Sean Sinico, Karl Sexton

articles.title_orig: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
articles.title_zh: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
articles.content_orig:
Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday.
The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists.
The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on calls for his resignation.
The protest comes just months after the movement brought thousands of young people onto Delhi's streets in July, in demonstrations that saw violent clashes with police and forced India's education minister to resign.
Police say they have denied permission for Saturday's gathering, and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed off with huge metal barricades.
The restrictions have caused major disruption across central Delhi, with traffic diverted from several key roads. A journey that would normally take 15 minutes took more than an hour this morning.
At Jantar Mantar, police and paramilitary personnel are stationed behind barricades and ropes, preventing people from entering the protest site. Drones could be seen flying overhead.
Some protesters who arrived early were stopped and questioned by security personnel. The BBC also saw at least five people being detained near the site.
Journalists covering the protest have been cordoned off into a designated area nearby.
At a nearby roundabout, loudspeakers repeatedly broadcast appeals for people to cooperate with the police.
Delhi Police has defended the measures, saying they were necessary to maintain public safety and prevent overcrowding at Jantar Mantar, which can accommodate only 1,000 people at a time.
Several trains to Delhi have also been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering.
But Abhijeet Dipke, founder ⁠of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may".
"If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing ​Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X.
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations demanding education reforms over the summer. The resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July was seen as a major victory for the group.
CJP protesters returned to the streets last week with a rally in Mumbai to demand Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held another large rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore).
Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days.
Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups.
CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi.
In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests.
Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP.
"Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said.
Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them.
"In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied."
The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather.
At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.
For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue.
Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.

articles.title_orig: Two more world records set, as study probes freedivers’ brains
articles.title_zh: Two more world records set, as study probes freedivers’ brains
articles.content_orig:
A female and a male freediver who have dominated headlines by venturing ever-deeper in 2026 emerged from a major competition in Cyprus this week having set further depth records.
At the start of this year the women’s Free Immersion (FIM) world record stood at 103m. It has since deepened no fewer than five times , with the latest 108m absolute record dive carried out by Zsófia Törőcsik at the AIDA World Apnea 2026 Depth Championships in Limassol.
The Hungarian was also crowned Overall Women’s World Champion for the second year running in the competition and took the championship title in the FIM discipline, which involves finless freedivers descending and returning to the surface by pulling themselves along the dive-line with their hands.
Törőcsik completed her record dive in four minutes and celebrated back at the surface by throwing the retrieved depth-tag high into the air.
“My happiness was sky-high today,” she said, and later reflected: “Every time you defeat yourself, it brings you closer to that voice in your head that finally says: yes, you are indeed capable of it.”
The freediver beat her rival Natalia Zharkova of Ukraine to the FIM world record by 5m on the day. The two women had tussled in the demanding discipline throughout 2026, with Zharkova (briefly matched by US diver Enchante Gallardo) holding the record for just over two months this summer. Törőcsik had held it at 107m since early August before improving on the depth in Limassol.
Meanwhile Alexey Molchanov, diving as an independent, left it until the final day of competition to set a new Constant Weight (CWT) absolute world record with a descent to 137m.
It was his 46th career world record and the seventh time he had reset the record he has held constantly for 14 years, having taken the title from Herbert Nitsch with a 126m dive in 2012. He had set the depth to beat at 136m over the past three years.
Molchanov and his Croatian rival Petar Klovar had been within a point of one another going into the final day of the competition, but in the end Molchanov won the Overall Male World Champion title by a margin of 11 points, scoring 484 across the event’s four competitive disciplines.
The World Apnea Championships ran from 30 September and represented the fifth time that Cyprus had hosted an AIDA World Championship, with athletes from more than 50 countries competing.
As Törőcsik mused on the mentality involved in record-breaking dives to depth, a scientific study has suggested that freediving training might prompt the brain to adapt to repeated oxygen deprivation.
Neuroscientist Julia Micaux and colleagues at the University of Paris-Saclay in France studied 17 male recreational freedivers before and after seven months of structured training.
Using functional MRI scanning, the researchers found that training was associated with changes in communication between several major brain networks, including those involved in attention, movement, vision and decision-making.
The hippocampus, a brain region crucial for memory and particularly vulnerable to low oxygen, showed especially notable changes. After training, it became more strongly connected with the cerebellum but less connected with some sensory and motor regions.
These connectivity patterns were also associated with performance on tests of episodic memory, suggesting that the brain might adapt its organisation to help maintain memory during repeated bouts of hypoxia.
Importantly, an earlier part of the study found no evidence of hippocampal damage or impaired memory after the seven-month training period, compared with 20 physically active non-freedivers.
The researchers, while conceding that the study was small, say that the findings point to a form of “adaptive neuroplasticity” – the brain’s ability to reorganise itself by forming new neural connections and shifting functions to healthy areas to restore normal abilities after learning, ageing or injury. Their findings are currently a preprint awaiting peer review.

articles.title_orig: The world needs Ukraine’s grain. Its farmers are running out of reasons to plant
articles.title_zh: The world needs Ukraine’s grain. Its farmers are running out of reasons to plant
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's harvest season is moving from wheat and barley into corn, soybeans and sunflower, and farmer Oleksandr Chumak has had a strong yield so far. That should be good news.
Instead, after 11 years of growing a range of crops in the Odesa region of southern Ukraine, Chumak has had enough.
Storage facilities across both Ukraine and Russia are filled with millions of tons of produce that would normally be sent to Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Africa — but are instead trapped in the warring countries.
Russian drone and missile hits on Black Sea targets intensified over the summer and into fall, making it impossible to insure commercial ships. Kyiv's retaliatory attacks mean Russian exports are now also stuck, further squeezing global supply.
And with fatal Black Sea attacks continuing into October , prospects of a ceasefire look slim, even as Turkey ramps up efforts to broker a deal due to the risk to global food security.
Chumak says that around 80% of his grain cannot currently be sold at a profit, and he is out of cash.
A collapse in domestic prices is giving farmers like him little reason to sow for the 2027 crop in the coming months.
"For the farmers, it's very difficult because we need to pay taxes, we need to pay rent for land, and now we are not able to do this because we are not able to sell anything," said Andrii Dykun, chairman of the Ukrainian Agri Council.
"The only crops we are able to sell are rapeseeds and sunflower seeds. But still, the volume is not enough... So why should we plant if today we have no profits at all?"
"If our stocks will be full, it makes no sense to do any farm operations in the spring because then it's just a waste of time and money."
PrivatBank, Ukraine's biggest lender, told CNBC that it had disbursed 1.53 billion hryvnia ($34.2 million) in working capital finance to agribusinesses between June and August, more than double the 718 million hryvnia lent in the same period last year. Small and medium-sized producers account for 70% of its agricultural loan book.
"Funds effectively remain tied up in grain inventories, while farms still need to cover their ongoing operating expenses and secure financing for the autumn and spring sowing campaigns," said Yevhen Zaihraiev, chief corporate and SME business officer at state-owned PrivatBank.
"We are seeing different strategies among our clients. Some agricultural producers are selling their crops sooner, even at less attractive prices, in order to maintain sufficient operating liquidity. Others, particularly those with access to storage capacity, are postponing sales in anticipation of more favorable market prices," he said by email.
Ukrainian production of grains and oilseeds is forecast to increase to 85 million tonnes from 80 million tonnes this year, but carry-over stocks from the previous season are pressuring Ukraine's storage infrastructure and logistics, Zaihraiev noted. Those facilities include long plastic silobags snaking across fields and towering metal grain elevators that are themselves increasingly vulnerable to military strikes.
"We are also seeing agricultural producers gradually revise their planting plans for next year in favor of oilseeds and niche crops, whose prices are less dependent on logistics costs," Zaihraiev added.
Farmer Oleksandr Chumak said he will follow that strategy, significantly scaling back planting for next year, avoiding corn and barley altogether, and instead opt for crops which require less fertilizer — which is also facing a global squeeze following amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran .
Meanwhile, for Ukrainian farmers — those not currently being drafted to serve — the war with Russia is ever-present. "We are living and working in a place where any time you or your circle can be hit by [a] rocket or drone," Chumak said by phone. "We are sleeping in beds with explosions 300 to 1,000 metres around."
Ukraine's agricultural sector has faced farm takeovers, mines and labor shortages ever since Russia's full-scale assault began in early 2022. International bodies have struggled to preserve its export routes through various agreements, including the collapsed Black Sea initiative and the European Union's politically contentious "Solidarity Lanes."
Now, the situation inside the country and the consequences for global food chains are the most severe they have been since the war began.
Between them, Ukraine and Russia supplied the world with more than half of its sunflower oil, nearly a fifth of its barley and 14% of its wheat in the years leading up to the war, according to the UN . Ukraine is also one of the world's biggest growers of corn, with China and the European Union among its biggest buyers.
Around 90% of Ukraine's main agricultural exports typically run via the Black Sea. In August this year, its grain and legume exports totalled 981,000 tonnes, down about 58% year on year.
The risk is heightened by weakness elsewhere. Europe is expected to have a particularly poor corn harvest and needs larger imports just as its demand for feed remains high. The United States is also facing a weaker corn crop .
For now, better wheat and barley crops in Canada, Australia and Argentina, along with good harvests in the Middle East and North Africa, are cushioning the blow.
The continued blockage is supporting commodity prices outside of Russia and Ukraine, but the reopening of Black Sea ports would unleash a wave of cheap supply that would "flip the market fast... with little warning," said Benoit Fayaud, senior manager for grains and oilseeds analysis at Expana.
A deal which restores Ukrainian and Russian exports could see grains prices in other origins decrease by a few dozen dollars, he told CNBC. "They have such big stocks it will be bearish for the market all over the world," he added.
Prices for Russian and Ukrainian wheat, barley, oilseeds and other products have become so low within the countries that it has intensified the scramble to find alternative routes via rail, road and river, according to Fayaud.
But these alternative routes are "difficult and slow from both countries," he said.
Ukraine's Eastern European neighbors such as Poland and Romania are resisting a push to allow grain to transit through them — even temporarily — due to concerns about a glut destroying demand for their own crops.
Another option via the Danube river has been hampered by low water levels; and a key bridge out of Ukraine has been damaged. There are options to export via the Baltic states and through Georgia by land into the Middle East and Central Asia, but this can only cover a small portion of typical flows, Fayaud said.
Andrii Dykun of the Ukrainian Agri Council stressed that there was no alternative to the Black Sea routes when it came to pricing.
"It would always be cheaper for us, even for the farmers on the western border of Ukraine, to sell the grain to other ports from Black Sea ports because it's much more profitable for the farmers than to sell it via the border to [the] EU," he said.
"So without Black Sea ports, it will not work for us at all."

articles.title_orig: Trump hits International Criminal Court with sanctions after Nobel goes to former judge
articles.title_zh: Trump hits International Criminal Court with sanctions after Nobel goes to former judge
articles.content_orig:
When Payam Akhavan talks about the Trump administration's new, sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, the first feeling he brings up is despair.
"These institutions, which were once sacrosanct, are besieged," said Akhavan, a Canadian who was appointed as a special adviser on genocide at the ICC in 2021.
The United States government, in the words of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is now working to "dismantle the ICC, piece by piece."
But Akhavan says it's not too late to stand up for the court.
"Canada is at a historical juncture where it has to choose which side of history it's going to be on," he said.
"Will it continue not just to support the rule of international law, but to double down?"
On Friday, the U.S. announced it would cut off the ICC from American financial services, technology companies and even U.S. dollars within six months. The court investigates and tries individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity and the crime of aggression.
Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize for 'her commitment to justice and human dignity'
The U.S. has been pushing to dismantle the ICC over its investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel . U.S. President Donald Trump strongly opposes the ICC arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The U.S. has long rejected the court's authority to investigate, charge and prosecute American service members, treating it as a threat to national sovereignty.
Neither the U.S. nor Israel are parties to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC.
After the sanctions were announced, Canada released a joint statement along with Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, expressing "unwavering support for the independence, impartiality and integrity of the ICC."
Akhavan says Canada must go further. He and other Canadian legal professionals are calling on the federal government to take action to strengthen the ICC through additional funding or other measures.
The initial joint statement did not mention any concrete actions being taken.
"We remain both united in our support for the ICC and committed to engaging in constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-states parties," it said.
Heidi Matthews, who has researched international law for two decades, is scratching her head about what that could mean.
"We would assume [non-state parties] means the United States here," said Matthews, who has worked in the international criminal tribunal prosecuting human rights violations in Sierra Leone.
Trump administration hits International Criminal Court with sweeping sanctions
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay of International Court of Justice
But given "how aggressively the Trump administration has been moving against the ICC," she said holding constructive dialogue with the U.S. is "almost impossible to see."
The administration's previous moves against the court included sanctioning individual judges, such as Canadian Kimberly Prost .
Matthews says a stronger statement would have clearly recommitted the allies' support for their obligations under the Rome Statute, "including to arrest and surrender accused criminals."
The joint statement appears to instead be "an attempt to appease the Trump administration," said Matthews, and a signal that the independence of the court is up for discussion.
"If the independence of the court is on the table as something that Canada and others are willing to allow to be eroded in one manner or another, then the court is no longer worth the paper that the Rome Statute is written on."
Matthews agrees with Akhavan that Canada should put its money where its mouth is by increasing financial support for the court.
She'd also like the government to put in place legislation that would protect Canadian ICC staff by preventing Canadian companies from complying with the U.S. sanctions — similar to the EU blocking statute .
That legislation can be used to essentially stop a third party's laws from controlling activities on another sovereign territory.
Why the ICC is in the fight of its life with Trump | About That
She says Canada must provide a much stronger signal of its support for the court, whose roots go back to the Nuremberg trials that prosecuted the architects of the Holocaust.
"If we're no longer interested in prosecuting state officials who are engaged in mass atrocity, then I think we're no longer interested in what [Prime Minister Mark] Carney so happily refers to as the international rule of order."
Akhavan says the ICC does have room for improvement, such as its governance and increasing efficiency.
"The question is not that we cannot criticize the court," he said. "But to try and dismantle it as a whole I think is really an attack on the idea of the rule of international law."
Jennifer Yoon covers the latest national and international news for CBC News on television, radio and digital. You can reach her at jennifer.yoon@cbc.ca.

articles.title_orig: Large waves pummel Southern California coast, flooding homes
articles.title_zh: Large waves pummel Southern California coast, flooding homes
articles.content_orig:
A hurricane swell and an overlapping south swell, combined with high tide, flooded the streets of Newport Beach and Laguna Beach with salt water Friday morning, shutting down roadways and snarling traffic throughout the coastal towns.
City workers scrambled to pump the salt water back to the sea.
And the worst is likely yet to come. Waves are expected to get even bigger over the weekend, with tides even higher in the morning hours. Rain from Tropical Storm Rachel is also in the forecast this weekend.
The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood advisory for Orange County beaches that will remain in effect until 2 p.m. Tuesday, warning of flooding in low-lying coastal areas during high tides.
Both coastal towns have suffered severe erosion in recent months, as consistent swells have battered the coastline, eroding the beach buffer between the ocean and the roadways. Friday morning, seawater flooded nearby streets, despite city efforts to build berms, set up sandbags and hold back the ocean.
Newport Beach officials said they were declaring a local emergency Friday to get resources quickly and asked people to stay clear of the flooded areas on the Balboa Peninsula as water was drained and the aftermath of the flooding was cleaned up. Police were allowing only residents into the area.
City staffers were out Friday assessing any damage to homes, and about 40 to 50 workers had been tasked with pumping water out of the streets, city spokesperson Georgia Rios said.
Newport Beach maintains a network of 86 tidal valves designed to prevent rising ocean water from backing up through storm drains, along with 18 pumps used to remove standing water from streets near the harbor. The city has previously identified the Balboa Peninsula, Balboa Island, Newport Island and other low-lying harborfront neighborhoods as areas particularly vulnerable to flooding during unusually high tides.
Another six crews were rebuilding berms on local beaches, with more flooding anticipated through the weekend, Rios said.
Utilities Director Mark Vukojevic said an estimated 20 streets flooded Friday morning, similar to July 2020 when water from the ocean rushed into the streets during an episode of extremely high tide.
The water overtopped the beaches, flattening out the berms, then made its way to streets, he said.
Drains throughout the low-lying areas that feed out to the harbor were closed, because the tide was high. If they were opened, Vukojevic said, water would also rise up from the harbor into the streets.
“It would make the streets 10 times worse,” he said. “The water has nowhere to go, so we’re trying to pump it out. The relief comes when the tide goes down, that’s why it takes a couple hours after the tide goes down to drain out.”
A dozen more pumps have been added to the peninsula for the weekend and added crews will be on hand, he said.
Vukojevic was unsure Friday afternoon if homes flooded, but said he saw some water entering garages.
The city did not pump out any private properties, he said.
Councilmember Erik Weigand said he was stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic on Friday afternoon while trying to get onto the peninsula to meet with Brett Sanders, director of the UC Irvine Climate Collaboration, to assess the conditions that contributed to the flooding.
“We’re in a current situation that this will keep occurring the next few days,” Weigand said. “It may just be too much Mother Nature impacting us. We’re just going to keep trying everything we can. Our guys are going to be out there constantly in the next week, doing everything in their power to assist where we can.”
While the water was receding from some of the flooded areas by mid-afternoon Friday, sections from 6th to 17th streets were still underwater, he said.
Weigand wasn’t sure if homes were impacted by flooding, or how many, though he said he saw some online videos from areas around the Wedge and the upper 50th streets that showed water flooding into yards and possibly into homes.
“I think we’re doing everything in our power to make sure we can protect property if we can,” he said. “The city is doing the best it can to protect homes and utilize heavy equipment that can build up berms.”
Weigand remembered times growing up in Newport Beach when streets would flood. And then, there was July 4, 2020, when Balboa Peninsula streets flooded and cars were pushed around in the parking lot. There was also some similar summer flooding in 2010.
“But I haven’t seen it this severe,” he said of the latest flooding. “To the extent it is happening at more than one area, throughout our entire coastline, is definitely, I think, an effect of the Kelvin wave, meets swell, meets high tide. I think, overall, we have the perfect storm.”
A Kelvin wave is a warm-water anomaly that travels from around the equator and pushes water levels higher for extended periods.
And what’s on the horizon could make matters even worse — an inch of rain is forecast late Saturday through Monday morning.
Newport Beach Bike Rentals owner Dave Shaw said business was slow Friday all morning, but traffic was moving through the peninsula by the late afternoon.
One thing they aren’t renting out – electric bikes.
He’s bracing for the weekend, unsure of what is ahead. The beaches have been busy with Arizona schools out for fall break, and tourists coming to the beach to beat the heat.
“It’s going to happen all weekend,” he said of the flooding potential. “We’ll figure it out as it comes.”
Bill Sharp, who has lived in West Newport for 65 years, said he has seen streets in the low-lying areas flood over the decades. But Friday’s scene was something different.
“I’ve never seen it like this, ever,” Sharp said. “There’s been moments where it’s coming up and washed into the streets in certain spots. But this is from River Jetties to the Wedge, it’s coming over the berms and filling the streets.”
“It’s unprecedented,” he added.
Usually, the flooding comes when high tides, surf and rain combine in winter months — the rain raising the water levels — but rarely does the ocean water flow into the streets during dry summer months. The region is even on the tail end of a heat wave.
Sharp said he walked through the shin-deep water in the roadway at 51st Street Friday morning.
“It’s flowing heavily over, water rushing from the ocean to the street,” he said. “It’s going over the berms, all the way to the houses. A series of berms and dikes are diverting it to the streets.”
While houses weren’t “falling into the ocean,” he said a number of the homes had drenched front yards and water was flowing around structures and into the streets.
“There’s not massive destruction, but everyone is getting wet,” Sharp said.
At the Wedge, where the local surfing community has been sounding the alarm for months about the recent speed of erosio n, bodysurfer Sean Starkey showed videos on social media of water gushing into the yards of multi-million-dollar beachfront homes.
Starkey said he had warned the city that a steep, natural sand berm created by the waves was hard packed enough to keep the water at bay, but city crews flattened it out to create a slope. That allowed the water to run up the small sliver of sand left, he argued.
Weigand said crews have been out at the Wedge since June trying to move sand around. He wondered if there was enough sand to work with in the first place after recent erosion to create a big enough berm along the beaches.
And, beaches that have wide swaths of sand flooded over, like near Newport Elementary, he said.
“You can only protect so much with the manpower you have,” Weigand said. “We have 7 miles of shoreline; it’s impossible to protect it all, in a situation like this where it’s affecting everything. There’s swell, high tides and Kelvin waves. It’s a trifecta of trouble.”
Sharp has seen a thousand 6-foot swells, with 6-foot tides, like what showed up on Friday, he said. But this time, it was different, he said.
“It’s a foot higher than it’s supposed to be,”

articles.title_orig: Three men found guilty in the 2024 killing of Australian and US surfers in Mexico
articles.title_zh: Three men found guilty in the 2024 killing of Australian and US surfers in Mexico
articles.content_orig:
A local judge on Friday found three Mexicans guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.
The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raúl Hernández in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, alias “El Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N,” and Ángel Jesús “N” were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson and American Carter Redd Rhoad.
The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.
“Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024,” said father Martin Robinson.
The three traveled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 80 kilometers (50 miles) from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well.
García, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Irineo Francisco “N,” and Ángel Jesús “N.”
During the month-long trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that García confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9mm pistol.
‘The world has become a darker place’. Heartbroken parents of surfers murdered in Mexico remember loving sons who adored adventure
Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.
The state prosecutor’s office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and “instigated one of her companions to rob them,” which was carried out the following day.
The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims’ cell phones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to “aggravated robbery with violence” and “vehicle theft with violence” in an expedited proceeding. However, García and his two accomplices decided to go to trial.
The judge will announce the final sentence on Oct. 16. The Baja California State Attorney General’s Office requested for each defendant the “exemplary sentence” of 210 years in prison.
“No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honoring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were,” said Martin Robinson. “They will never be forgotten.”

articles.title_orig: Climate crisis is coming to crush many of world’s best surf breaks, study warns
articles.title_zh: Climate crisis is coming to crush many of world’s best surf breaks, study warns
articles.content_orig:
Changing tide levels, shifting sands and hardened shorelines put waves at risk, affecting more than just surfers
The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.
Analysis of dozens of famous waves in world surfing reserves (WSR) found more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines and shifting sands.
The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.
The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador, and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.
The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of sea-floor shape, swell direction and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a co-author of the study.
Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.
Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR programme in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”
The study, published in the journal Climatic Change , concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”
Almost 200 local experts analysed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.
A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.
Adam Hall, a co-founder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”
after newsletter promotion
He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants and car parks when the swells are good in January, February and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”
The researchers want more local surfers to use the tools developed to assess their own breaks and work with local authorities and other groups to protect waves from coastal development and climate change.
Some places already do this, such as the city of Gold Coast in Australia, which has put surf protection in planning law; New Zealand, which designates surf breaks of “national significance”; and Peru’s Ley de rompientes (law of the breakers) that protects listed surf breaks.
“Surfing is a huge driver of local economies,” Hodges said. “So whether you’re a surfer or not, that money supports local businesses, hotels, lodgings and so on.”
In Santa Cruz, surfing brings in about $200m (£151m) a year, he said.
“In the east of El Salvador, you have some of the most perfect point break waves you will find, and the entire economy there is pretty much dependent on surfing,” Hodges added.

articles.title_orig: Panama rocked by 2 powerful earthquakes and multiple aftershocks, prompting evacuations
articles.title_zh: Panama rocked by 2 powerful earthquakes and multiple aftershocks, prompting evacuations
articles.content_orig:
A major earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.7 has struck southern Panama, according to the US Geological Survey.
Several people have suffered minor injuries but so far there are no reports of fatalities or missing persons, officials said. Various homes, roads, hotels, government buildings, businesses and churches have sustained structural damage, according to the civil protection system.
The USGS had said some casualties were possible and extensive damage was probable. The earthquake was followed by 147 aftershocks, director of the Emergency Operations Center René García told CNN. Some of those aftershocks reached magnitudes of 6.1 or 6.6.
García said authorities are waiting for the tremors to subside before conducting structural inspections of damaged buildings. The most significant damage has been reported in Coclé province on the nation’s southern coast, although some has also been seen in the capital, Panama City.
Footage verified by CNN shows several damaged buildings in Penonome, some 70 miles from the epicenter. One video shows a church with a partially collapsed steeple and another building with a crumbled facade.
In the popular resort town Playa Venao, a multi-story building collapsed and crushed several cars beneath it.
Along the Panama Canal, the Centennial Bridge’s suspension cables were seen shaking as vehicles drove through.
The canal authority said operations were continuing as normal and that staff were inspecting facilities for damage.
Panama City’s public transit system has suspended service on two metro lines and evacuated passengers from some stations.
Scores of residents gathered in the streets of the capital after rushing out of their buildings in a panic.
“I am on the ninth floor here and yes it was felt strongly,” Panama City resident Kevin Cortez told Reuters.
“Everything was moving: the lamp, the chair, the table,” another resident said. “I decided to stay and wait because I knew running down the stairs was a problem. So I stayed waiting for it to pass. I had no other option. Yes, we felt it was quite prolonged. People running, shouting; not everyone takes it the same way, but well, here we are, downstairs.”
The Education Ministry has canceled classes nationwide for the rest of the day.
Panama’s main international airport was temporarily closed as a precaution and flights were diverted to other airports before operations resumed later in the day, the civil aviation authority said.
The water and sewage institute has reported interruptions at several water treatment plants due to power outages caused by the quake.
Panama’s President José Raúl Mulino has called for calm and instructed the minister of government to provide information on the earthquake’s effects. He has also mobilized resources to those affected.
Mulino visited an affected hospital in Penonome, where several patients were evacuated and have had to receive treatment outdoors.
Earlier, the US Tsunami Warning System warned of possible tsunami waves along some coasts, before saying there was no longer a threat.
This is just the latest powerful earthquake to have struck Latin America this year. Over the summer, Venezuela was hit by two powerful earthquakes that killed more than 6,400 people, while Colombia suffered a tremor that left around 300 dead.
The leaders of both countries have offered to help Panama’s government as it responds to the disaster.
CNN’s Mauricio Torres contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: GM China sales top 358,000 in third quarter as NEV share exceeds 60%
articles.title_zh: GM China sales top 358,000 in third quarter as NEV share exceeds 60%
articles.content_orig:
General Motors reported its third-quarter 2026 sales in China on October 9, with new energy vehicles accounting for a growing share of deliveries even as its overall sales declined from a year earlier.
· GM and its joint ventures delivered more than 358,000 vehicles in China during the quarter. New energy vehicles accounted for over 60% of the total, a record share for a third quarter.
· Deliveries were notably lower than the nearly 470,000 vehicles sold in the third quarter of 2025, when sales rose 10.1% year on year.
· The Buick Electra E7 plug-in hybrid midsize SUV recorded sales of more than 13,000 units, making it one of the brand's main volume contributors.
Image source: General Motors
· SAIC-GM-Wuling remained a major source of GM's NEV sales, led by the Binguo family with more than 57,000 units and the Hongguang MINIEV family with over 34,000 units.
The Buick GL8 family sold more than 22,000 units during the quarter. Its cumulative sales had exceeded 2.2 million units as of August this year.
Cadillac delivered more than 9,000 XT5 vehicles in the third quarter. The China-developed XT5 PHEV, hitting the market in September, expanded the brand's electrified lineup and features an assisted-driving system based on Momenta's R7 world model.
Image source: ﻿General Motors
Within SAIC-GM-Wuling's portfolio, the Wuling Xing Guang L plug-in hybrid SUV sold nearly 19,000 units, while Huajing S sales approached 22,000. The Binguo Pro contributed nearly 40,000 units to the Binguo family's quarterly total.
The higher NEV share indicates some progress in GM's product transition in China. However, with total deliveries under pressure, the key test will be whether the changing sales mix can translate into sustained volume growth and improved profitability.
John Roth, GM senior vice president and president of GM China and Asia, said the company's evolving product mix was building momentum for profitable growth in key segments.

articles.title_orig: Newport Beach declares local emergency after coastal flooding on Balboa Peninsula
articles.title_zh: Newport Beach declares local emergency after coastal flooding on Balboa Peninsula
articles.content_orig:
The city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency after ocean water surged onto streets and properties in the Balboa Peninsula community Friday.
The National Weather Service issued a coastal flooding advisory that remains in place through Tuesday. A coastal flood warning expires at 3 p.m. Sunday.
City officials said during an evening news conference that crews will work through the night and into the weekend to rebuild sand berms as the threat of flooding continues.
"Our goal is to reinforce as many vulnerable locations as possible before the next high tide," said Newport Beach City Manager Seimone Jurjis.
Friday evening, residents near the water in Newport Beach took precautions.
"We are just going to fortify the entry to our home and then the back entry," said Josh Pham.
"We have some sandbags that we got from the city from the fire station," said April Witting. "A friend got extra; we are going to borrow some from him and fill it with sand."
Officials said the emergency response would continue through the weekend, with crews monitoring ocean conditions and deploying additional resources as needed. Temporary street closures and parking restrictions may be implemented if conditions worsen, according to the city.
"These Kelvin waves are real," Newport Beach City Councilmember Erik Weigand  said. "It's not a wave like you would see with swell, but it's a tidal push, and we're projecting those to be 20 inches greater than what high tides projected."
Every high tide is expected to be higher than normal, especially at the south-facing beaches, like parts of Newport, Long Beach, Dana Point, and Laguna Beach.
Flooding risks are highest on Sunday, with tides likely 1 to 1 ½ feet above astronomical tide charts, according to NWS.
Aerial footage over the Balboa Peninsula showed people wading barefoot on sidewalks and streets, some knee-deep in rain boots and vehicles nearly half-submerged.
"Do not drive through flooded streets. Use alternate routes, exercise caution, and follow directions from public safety personnel," the city of Newport Beach wrote in a statement.
Newport Beach Fire Department Chief Jeff Boyles advised the community not to drive, walk, or bike through the water, as some places along Balboa Boulevard are submerged in nearly 2 feet of water.
"We're prepared, and we already know that Sunday morning will likely be a little bit worse with the higher tide and larger swell expected," Boyles said. "We're experiencing some unprecedented flooding ..."
By the afternoon, the water had receded, leaving businesses to clean up. Gus Orozco of Balboa Fun Tours was busy cleaning saltwater off beach cruisers.
"All the water started rising little by little," he said. "By 10 o'clock the water was like a lake. The street was flooded, flooded like a lake."
It wasn't just business owners cleaning up; homeowners were, too. Musician Jennifer Trevour waded through chest-high water in her garage on West Balboa Boulevard to save her keyboard.
"All the stuff in the garage is holding me in, and I'm just like praying like I can get through it, and I push through," Trevour said. "I got the keyboard out, but nothing else."
The city is providing free sandbags at its Corporation Yard at 592 Superior Ave. This location will remain open overnight. Newport Beach police say Peninsula residents can also pick up sandbags at Marina Park. Lifeguards on the Balboa Peninsula also have sandbags available in their vehicles.
Orange County launched a website today that provides residents with emergency information and resources related to El Niño. The website, ocgov.com/el-nino , serves as a central source for updates on the county's response to storm-related issues.
The site also includes links to local government resources and information about preparing for dangerous weather.

Europe has called on China to voluntarily reduce hybrid car exports into the continent, but authorities in Beijing had reportedly slapped down the request , according to the Financial Times.
The widening trade surplus between the EU and China has been a point of contention, with Germany and France previously having called on Brussels to develop a "last-resort" trade instrument to address imbalances.
Sefčovič said Friday that the final decision would still need Brussels' approval. Overall, he cast the two days of talks with China's Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Beijing as a positive first step, following a summer of rising tensions between China and the EU.
China's Commerce Ministry on Friday released a list of 16 "'consensus outcomes."
They included licenses for rare earth and permanent magnet export licenses to the EU. Sefcovic did not elaborate on a timeline for the rare earth exports.
