articles.title_orig: Teacher Reacts to Khloe Kardashian Making Fun of Him for Flirting
articles.title_zh: Teacher Reacts to Khloe Kardashian Making Fun of Him for Flirting
articles.content_orig:
Originally appeared on E! Online
Jacob Myers-Norys doesn't necessarily think he got schooled by Khloe Kardashian .
Nearly a year after the Khloé in Wonder Land podcast host sparked headlines by leaving a flirty comment on the high school teacher's Instagram, she addressed the "cute" moment on the season eight premiere of The Kardashians .
"On his Instagram he highlighted some of his great characteristics, and then in the caption something like, 'I can't wait for a woman to ask me how my day was,'" Khloe recalled on the Oct. 8 episode. "I thought it was wholesome. I just wrote in the caption, 'How was your day?' It was that innocent."
However, the 42-year-old clarified, "Do I think I'm gonna go and marry this young man? Absolutely not."
Still, Khloe noted the situation unexpectedly "took off like wildfire."
"I have like 15 DMs from him that have gone unresponsive," she explained during the confessional, before reading the messages to camera. "'If anything, I just want to say thank you for everything.' 'I know it was just a comment.' 'Love to hear how your day was.' 'Just shooting my shot once again.' 'I would love to meet you and talk about how your day was.'"
See Jessica Biel, Justin Timberlake's Son Make His Acting Debut in Matchbox: The Movie
George Clooney Addresses Death of Cindy Crawford, Rande Gerber's Son Presley Gerber
Kaitlyn Bristowe Says Brian Austin Green "Humiliated" Sharna Burgess by Complaining About DWTS
In response to the unrequited texts, Khloe had a message for Jacob, whose social media handle uses "Yacob."
"Calm down, Yacob. Just be cool," she said. "And his name is Yacob? Yacob, please, get a J."
Following the episode, Jacob had a hilarious reaction to being discussed on The Kardashians .
Jacob Myers-Norys/Instagram; Disney
In an Oct. 9 TikTok, he drank from a coffee mug and stared stoically at the camera as an audio clip played featuring laughter and a voice sarcastically saying, "Oh no, I'm devastated."
Plus, atop the clip, Jacob compared the moment to his job, writing, "When they try to roast and embarrass me on The Kardashians , but I get roasted by high schoolers every single day."
That's why Jacob is able to look at the bright side, despite Khloe shutting him down.
As he wrote in the caption of his TikTok, "Hey, at least I can say I made it onto The Kardashians ."
While Khloe and Jacob may not be going on a date any time soon, read on to take a deep dive into the love lives of the Kardashians stars.
Why, yes, Kris Jenner and longtime love Corey Gamble are still doing amazing, sweetie. In 2014 , the music industry insider approached the world's most famous momager at fashion designer Riccardo Tisci 's 40th birthday bash in Ibiza and "I just tried saying, 'You're beautiful. I'd love to get to know you,'" he shared on the family's OG series, Keeping Up With the Kardashians , "and it went from there."
More than a decade in, Kris gushed about her "ride or die" in a 2025 birthday tribute , writing, "Thank you for all you do every single day, for the love you give, and for always being there for all of us. I'm so blessed to have you by my side."
With all due respect for all the small things, Kourtney Kardashian 's husband has made some pretty grand gestures throughout their yearlong marriage. Take her 44th birthday that saw her and Travis Barker take a trip up the California coast to Santa Barbara. The Blink-182 drummer marked the occasion by filling their room at the famed Kennedy Cottage with rose petals and gifting her with a $161,819 piece by artist Yoshitomo Nara . The Poosh founder has fully embraced her new life as the girl at the rock show. And in November 2023, she and Travis welcomed their first child together, son Rocky Thirteen Barker .
As Kim Kardashian put it in The Kardashians trailer, "Things change really quickly." When season two wrapped, the SKIMS founder was still with then- Saturday Night Live standout Pete Davidson .
She got fans hoping she was getting back in the dating game with retired NFL quarterback Tom Brady .
Alas, the mom to North West , Saint West , Chicago West and Psalm West —with ex-husband Kanye West —wasn't on the hunt for a new teammate, a source telling E! News in May 2023, "They have friends and business partners in common."
By early 2026, she was racing into a new romance with Lewis Hamilton , hard-launching her relationship with the F1 driver that June.
After her divorce, she told The Times in October, "I wanted to completely heal and just work on myself. I wasn't ready to open up. I really wasn't even thinking about it. The universe works in your favor when you just allow it to."
In a 2023 episode , Kris shoots her shot while chatting with Khloe Kardashian about Tristan Thompson , asking, "How's everything going with Tristan?" Safe to say the Good American founder has the basketball player benched for now. Though the exes have worked out a game plan for raising daughter True and son Tatum , Khloe shot down the idea that they're back together in May 2023, calling the narrative "tiring."
She's more interested in starting a fresh story. After meeting Love Is Blind star Alexa Lemieux the following April, Khloe pitched a winning idea to Netflix, writing on Instagram , "I think some of us single K sisters should go on LIB . What do you think?"
Months after Kendall Jenner 's split with NBA guard Devin Booker in fall 2022, the model's love life got an assist from friends Justin Bieber and Hailey Bieber . The married duo were spotted enjoying a double date with the reality star and musician Bad Bunny in February 2023. The following December, it was reported that the two had called it quits .
Then in the spring of 2026, fans started to wonder if a new romance was in bloom as Kendall was spotted hanging out with Jacob Elordi . The Euphoria alum was among those cheering for the model when she walked in Milan Fashion Week in September 2026.
Seems Kylie Jenner has found herself a new beautiful boy . Last seen publicly with rapper Travis Scott —dad to her daughter Stormi and son Aire —at an Art Basel party in December 2022, the beauty mogul, has first linked to Oscar-nominated actor Timothée Chalamet in April 2023.
Now, rise and shine because you don't want to miss the glimpses they've given us of their romance at New York Fashion Week and the US Open, as well as live on TV, when they showed PDA while seated together at the 2024 Golden Globes and 2025 Oscars .
Then, while accepting Best Actor at the 2026 Critics Choice Awards in January, he thanked his "partner of three years," for the foundation she provides, adding, "I couldn't do this without you. Thank you from the bottom of my heart."

articles.title_orig: World's Longest-span Steel Arch Bridge Rises with Digital Tech
articles.title_zh: World's Longest-span Steel Arch Bridge Rises with Digital Tech
articles.content_orig:
High above a deep gorge in southwest China's Chongqing, the final concrete deck panel of a bridge was lowered into place with millimeter precision. On June 12, the steel-concrete composite girder of the Fenglai Daxi River Grand Bridge was officially completed. With a main span of 580 meters, it is now the world's largest-span steel arch bridge.
Standing over a deeply incised tributary of the Wujiang River, the bridge is both an engineering marvel and a dialogue across 1,400 years â blending the ancient wisdom of the Zhaozhou Bridge, a stone arch bridge built 1,400 years ago, with modern digital technology.
"This is a typical deep V-shaped gorge with limited space, huge height differences and fierce valley winds," explained Chen Kejian, deputy chief engineer of China Railway Eryuan Engineering Group. Suspension and cable-stayed bridges need towering pylons, which would be extremely difficult to erect here and costly. Arch bridges offer rational force distribution and the V-shaped cliffs in the area serve as natural abutments. A disadvantage thus became an advantage.
The first challenge was sheer weight: 25,800 tonnes of steel, equivalent to 3.6 Eiffel Towers. Traditional solid abutments would crush the load-bearing foundation.
The design team drew inspiration from the Zhaozhou Bridge. Its pioneering "open-spandrel" design reduced weight by hollowing out the spandrels. The team adapted this into an "inverted Ï-shaped" hollow foundation, standing on two "legs" to distribute pressure.
The 580-meter span also introduced a new mechanical problem: lateral forces. Traditional small-span arch bridges are controlled mainly by vertical forces, but here the arch foot is controlled by both lateral and vertical forces.
"We broke convention and, for the first time globally, adopted active control of arch ring internal forces using cables," said Zhang Chao, project design lead. This transferred pressure from the lower chord to the upper chord, solving the anchoring problem and cutting steel consumption by 37 percent compared with similar bridges of smaller span.
Digital 'twin' fixes pre-assembly
The second challenge was pre-assembly. Hundreds of thousands of high-strength bolts had to pass through holes with only a three-millimeter gap. "It's like assembling hundreds of tonnes of Lego at 100 meters high and threading hundreds of thousands of screws through needle eyes," said Huang Jian, technical lead at China Railway No. 8 Engineering Group.
Worse, the only pre-assembly yard was less than 90 meters of usable length. Multi-round assembly would cause errors to snowball, potentially leading to deviations of over 10 centimeters.
Professor Zhou Jianting's team at Chongqing Jiaotong University provided the key: digital pre-assembly. Each steel component is "CT-scanned" with holographic laser scanning, and the point cloud data are stitched into a millimeter-precision 3D "virtual twin."
"A single truss segment is 18 meters high, 39.5 meters long, and weighs 425 tonnes. We control bolt hole reconstruction within one millimeter and overall segment accuracy within two millimeters," said Zhou Yin, deputy director of the university's large-span arch bridge intelligent construction institute. Unlike ordinary building information modeling, this is a "force-form coupled" dynamic simulation that calculates deformation during assembly.
The team also developed "N+1 pre-assembly control technology," locking errors into the manufacturing stage. This cut pre-assembly time by 25 percent and raised full-arch alignment from centimeter to millimeter precision.
A dynamic 'brain' for high-altitude assembly
The third challenge: cantilever assembling 10,000 tonnes of steel at 310 meters high, amid gorge winds and 20-centimeter temperature deformation between day and night.
"The steel arch expands tens of centimeters in the sun and contracts at night," Huang said. "With a fully bolted structure, a one-millimeter deviation in the first segment could lead to centimeter-level errors later."
The team deployed an "original shape reset installation control method" and a "digital twin control platform." The reset method gives each suspended segment a 3D millimeter-level target, so it fits "right the first time." The twin platform captures every deformation in real time and predicts invisible internal forces, ensuring adjustments when the sun or wind is present.
The system improved high-altitude alignment efficiency by 50 percent. "The pass rate for high-strength bolts and first-time weld inspection both exceed 99.5 percent," Huang said.
The project has produced more than 10 innovative technologies, including active control design, stress-free closure, digital pre-assembly, and environment-adaptive installationâclearing key obstacles for assembled construction of long-span arch bridges in mountainous regions.
With the girder joined, the bridge has entered its final sprint. This red arc across the Daxi River Gorge is both a tribute to ancient bridge engineering and a powerful calling card for China's infrastructure.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has sent a congratulatory letter to the Science and Technology Daily on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of its founding.
As artificial intelligence continues to advance, robots are moving beyond laboratories and exhibition halls to take on an expanding range of tasks once performed entirely by humans. From everyday services to industrial production, intelligent machines are increasingly being put to practical use, helping improve efficiency, consistency and hygiene while addressing challenges in traditional industries.

articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has told Donald Trump about Iran's position on a possible Mideast peace deal, the Kremlin said Saturday.
The Kremlin said Tehran's stance was relayed in a phone call held between the two leaders on Friday. It did not say how Trump responded, nor elaborate on Iran's position.
Diplomatic efforts to end the Iran conflict, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have been at an impasse since the summer.
Putin met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan earlier this week, where the Russian leader expressed an interest in helping broker peace.
"In coordination with the Iranian president, Putin conveyed the Iranian side's views on a possible resolution to the conflict to Trump," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Saturday, according to Russia's state RIA news agency.
During a rally in upstate New York, President Trump said, "Iran will be very quick, one way or the other. Either they give us everything, or they don't exist any longer. They know that"
The president made the comments while criticizing the Nobel Peace Prize committee for not awarding him the prize — a frequent complaint by Mr. Trump. Calling the body "crooked," Mr. Trump attacked it for giving the prize to former International Criminal Court Judge Navanethem Pillay, whom the president called a "mystery person."
"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision," he said. "The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said Saturday it destroyed more than 100 military targets in a "large-scale operation" against the Iran-backed group.
"We are carrying out a large-scale operation targeting the personnel and capabilities of the Houthi terrorist militia," Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi coalition, wrote on X.
"We destroyed 136 military targets in areas controlled by the Houthi terrorist militia," he said in a separate post.
The Houthi's Almasirah TV channel reported that Saudi missiles targeted areas in the northwestern Yemeni governorate of Saada.
The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government — which Saudi Arabia supports — reignited in July, and has since spilled over into the neighboring kingdom.
In addition to seizing territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have attacked transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world's largest crude exporter with drones and missiles.
President Trump said Russia has agreed to provide the world with millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months in a bid to decrease skyrocketing global prices.
In a Truth Social post, the president said he had just gotten off the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately. He said another 500,000 tons of diesel would be released in November, followed by 1 million tons in December.
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump continued.
The Treasury Department also announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
Mr. Trump had earlier Friday teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks at a Columbus Day celebration.
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.
President Trump teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks Friday at a Columbus Day celebration, but offered little information to speculate on what the announcement would be about.
Mr. Trump pointed out Energy Secretary Chris Wright and said he was "doing a great job."
"We have, I think, some big news on that diesel situation," the president said. "It's gonna — we're gonna be knocking the hell out of it. And remember, what have we done? We stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That's big time. And the prices — the prices will come tumbling."
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA , which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.
Diesel had never previously crossed $6 a gallon until just before Labor Day weekend. The record, hit on Sept. 22, was $6.53 per gallon. Diesel is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, so it's a factor for nearly every type of good, including groceries.
The Trump administration has looked into several ways to lower diesel prices, most recently signing an executive order this week allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways. Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.
Sri Lanka's government says it has no immediate plans to help 19 Iranian ships that have been anchored in the international waters near the island nation facing food, water and fuel shortages.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo said Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States.
He said, however, there hasn't been any communication from the U.S. warning of repercussions should Sri Lanka decide to help.
Rodrigo said the ships are stationed 24 nautical miles from Sri Lanka's coast and have reported shortages of food, water and fuel.
Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath told local Sunday Times newspaper the ships are Iranian oil tankers and they have been anchored off Sri Lanka for the past several months after the U.S. resumed its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving dozens of Iranian vessels stranded and unable to return home.
The U.K., France, Germany, Australia and Canada have advised their citizens against travel to parts of Saudi Arabia following a wave of Houthi attacks, including one that killed three civilians at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.
The U.K. Foreign Office now advises against all but essential travel to the Riyadh region, Najran, Jizan and Aseer provinces, Taif city and Taif International Airport, and against all travel within six miles of the Yemeni border.
France says travel to Najran, Abha, Khamis Muhsait and Djizan in the south of the kingdom " remains strongly discouraged ," and Germany , Australia and Canada have all advised against all travel to the country.
The U.S. has also tightened restrictions , requiring government employees to obtain special authorization to use Riyadh airport, and barring them from all travel within 20 miles of the Yemen border. U.S. government employees also require "special authorization for travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu, and Taif."
There is currently no warning for U.S. nationals more broadly to avoid Saudi Arabia, but the U.S. embassy in Riyadh urged Americans across the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance due to the complex security environment."
Yemeni government forces, backed by air support from the Saudi-led coalition, have taken control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Mayyun Island from the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, a Saudi diplomat said Friday.
Saudi Arabian Ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed Al Jaber, said in a post on X that the strait had been "cleansed" of remaining Houthi forces.

articles.title_zh: China, EU agree to keep bilateral trade ties stable, hold next meeting in March 2027
articles.content_orig:
The agreement will see Chinese hybrid vehicle exports decline by ‘several million cars’ in the coming years, EU trade chief says
The European Union and China have “reached an understanding” that will cut Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc by “more than a half”, in a temporary salve to trade tensions that have threatened to boil over into a full-blown trade war.
Speaking after marathon trade talks in Beijing, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said the deal would see China slash its hybrid car exports “by several million cars” over a four-year period.
“This is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tensions, and I very much appreciate that,” Sefcovic told reporters in the Chinese capital.
The sides also agreed to expedite EU applications for rare earth mineral export licences and improve market access for goods including car parts, olive oil and textiles, which Sefcovic said could be worth “almost €4 billion” (US$4.5 billion) in current export value.

articles.title_orig: What share of plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
articles.title_zh: What share of plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
articles.content_orig:
Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:
Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.
The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.
The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.
From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.
People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
But it tells us none of that.
It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index.
When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable.
As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most.
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
When people think about global oil, their minds often go toward countries in the Middle East.
But it’s the United States that is the world’s largest oil producer.
The chart shows oil production by country since 1990. As you can see, the US has been the largest producer for the last nine years, since it overtook Saudi Arabia.
Production in the US gradually declined during the 1990s and early 2000s, then increased sharply after 2010 and is now at an all-time high.
This data comes from the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy .
In 2025, the amount of foreign aid given by the world’s richest countries fell by almost a quarter . That amounted to a reduction of roughly US$50 billion.
Aid cuts in the United States — and the shutdown of its agency for international development, USAID — got the most attention, and for good reason: the US is the world’s largest aid donor in dollar terms, so its contributions make a huge difference to the global total.
But many other countries cut their aid contributions, too. In the chart, you can see the change among the largest 10 donors (in dollar terms) from 2024 to 2025. This is given as a share of their gross national income.
Contributions fell in eight of the ten countries. Only Sweden and Italy increased their budgets.
The countries shown are the largest donors in dollar terms; some others not shown contribute far more in relative terms: Norway, for example, was the only country to give more than 1% of its national income to foreign aid.

articles.title_orig: South Korea, U.S., Japan join push against China's overcapacity
articles.title_zh: South Korea, U.S., Japan join push against China's overcapacity
articles.content_orig:
Oct. 9 (Asia Today) -- South Korea, the United States, Japan and other major economies have joined a coordinated effort to address global industrial overcapacity, as Chinese manufacturers increasingly turn to European and emerging markets amid U.S. trade restrictions.
The initiative reflects growing concerns that China's vast production capacity, low manufacturing costs and competitive pricing could undermine industries in other countries.
According to Beijing-based sources familiar with international economic developments, 15 participating economies issued a joint ministerial statement Tuesday at the headquarters of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development in Paris.
Participants included South Korea, the United States, Japan, the European Union, Britain, Canada, Australia and India.
The statement described structural global overcapacity as a significant threat to the world economy and called for action against nonmarket policies and practices, including subsidies that distort competition and sustain excess production.
The initiative focuses on five industrial sectors: automobiles and electric vehicles, batteries, chemicals, commodity semiconductors and solar panels.
Participating economies plan to establish sector-specific working groups to assess excess production capacity, examine its effects on global markets and discuss possible responses.
Although the statement did not explicitly identify China as the source of overcapacity, the initiative is widely seen as targeting Chinese manufacturing.
China has rapidly expanded its global market share in industries such as electric vehicles and batteries, supported by large-scale production and aggressive pricing.
According to recent Chinese media reports, including those from the Beijing News, China produced approximately 16.63 million new-energy vehicles in 2025, an increase of 29% from the previous year.
The category includes battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids.
Production reached approximately 12.6 million vehicles during the first nine months of 2026, putting the country on course to manufacture around 17 million vehicles for the full year.
Chinese exports have also increased substantially.
About 2.62 million new-energy vehicles were exported in 2025, representing approximately 15.7% of total production.
Exports of battery-electric vehicles alone reached about 1.65 million units.
That figure approached the European Union's approximately 1.88 million electric vehicle sales last year and exceeded the roughly 1.27 million sold in the United States.
U.S. trade barriers, however, have made access to the American market increasingly difficult for Chinese manufacturers.
In response, Chinese companies have accelerated efforts to expand sales in Europe and emerging economies.
The shift has heightened concerns among other industrialized countries that Chinese production could overwhelm domestic manufacturers and intensify price competition.
Similar pressures are emerging in other sectors covered by the joint initiative, where Chinese producers have expanded output and pursued low-price strategies.
With China's excess industrial capacity expected to persist, participating economies face the challenge of developing coordinated responses while protecting their domestic industries.
-- Reported by Asia Today; translated by UPI

articles.title_orig: Conway Sport Clips races for world record haircuts, all to help local veterans
articles.title_zh: Conway Sport Clips races for world record haircuts, all to help local veterans
articles.content_orig:
by Kylon Williams | Isley Gooden
Faulkner County is in the home stretch of a busy, feel-good world record attempt, and it comes with a side of support for local veterans. (PHOTO: KATV)
CONWAY, Ark. (KATV) — Faulkner County is in the home stretch of a busy, feel-good world record attempt, and it comes with a side of support for local veterans.
Sport Clips Conway is trying to break the world record for the most haircuts completed at a single location in one week, with the effort benefiting local veterans. Store manager Danae Bell said the community response has been strong.
“Well, it’s actually been really great,” Bell said. “We are super excited for everyone to come out, and all the people that we have seen, and the new clients that we have been able to see, and we have just really been touched by the amount of you know stuff we have been able to give back to the veterans and the first responders here in our community.”
Earlier this week, the store also welcomed soon-to-be 101-year-old veteran Floyd Brantley for a haircut, a moment Bell said captured what the week has been about.
“Yes, it has been so rewarding,” Bell said. She said Sport Clips supports the military through its Help A Hero Foundation, but doing it locally has been especially meaningful. “But just being able to do it on a community level and in actually inside my store has has been so rewarding.”
Bell added that surprising service members and first responders with a haircut has been a highlight.
“The look on the police officers and the military people’s faces is when they don’t even know that they’re coming in to get a haircut is is just amazing,” she said. “I’m really grateful that I’m able to give back just a little, little something to them for all that they have done for us and our country.”
As of Friday, Bell said the record to beat is 1,600 haircuts in one week.
“Right. So the record currently is 1,600 haircuts in one week. We are over 600, so we still got a ways to go,” she said.
Bell said the store has also been collecting donations for UCA’s Veteran Affairs Foundation and the Help A Hero Foundation.
People still have time to take part. Bell said the store is “open today until 8 o’clock tonight,” and “open tomorrow from eight to eight as well.” And if customers keep coming, she said the clippers will keep buzzing.
“And as long if y’all keep us busy past 8 p.m. tomorrow night, we will continue to cut hair until there are no more heads to cut,” Bell said.
For updates and more information, Bell said people can find the store on Facebook.
“Yes, so we have a Facebook page. It is Conway Sport Clips of haircuts, and it’s on Facebook,” she said. “And there are so many videos. We’ve been having lots of fun making videos and sharing information.”

articles.title_orig: Dread Scott Imagines a World Without America
articles.title_zh: Dread Scott Imagines a World Without America
articles.content_orig:
When I stepped inside Brooklyn-based artist Dread Scott’s latest exhibition at Yerba Buena Center for the Arts , I was terrified.
A man in military fatigues armed with an M4 carbine loomed in the corner, guarding an American flag hanging from a short flagpole. When I approached the man, he jerked to life and admonished me, “Halt, stand back from the perimeter. I’m defending the flag. The flag of the U.S. must be respected at all times.” It wasn’t clear when or how I had crossed some invisible boundary, only that he had the power to decide. Artists push back against state power all the time — but it isn’t every day that that role is reversed inside an art gallery.
Defending the Flag is a new commission for the YBCA show The Body Politic , and it’s in direct dialogue with the artwork that put Scott on the map nearly 40 years ago, while he was still a student at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
The 1988 installation What Is the Proper Way to Display a US Flag? consisted of a flag that viewers could step on while writing their reflections of the experience in a guestbook, below a photomontage of the flag desecration. Vietnam veterans, calling themselves “defenders of the flag,” called for Scott’s death. President George Bush Sr. called the piece “disgraceful” and Congress outlawed the work. Then, in 1989, Scott was arrested for burning a U.S. flag on the steps of the Capitol for a photography project, which led to a landmark decision , confirming citizens’ rights to desecrate the flag under the First Amendment.
In a 2018 TED Talk detailing the experience, Scott stated that he does not “accept the economic foundation, the social relations or the governing ideas of America.” That holds true today, he tells KQED, but adds that, “Long-term, I look forward to a day when people have gotten beyond America — including the foundation of capitalism America rests on.”
The first piece visitors to The Body Politic encounter hangs both outside YBCA as a vinyl banner and outside the exhibition’s main gallery. It visualizes this fantasy of a decentered United States. The 2025 screen print shows a black and green world map with America moved to the margins, overlaid with the phrase “imagine a world without America,” which also serves as the work’s title.
A similarly straightforward 2022 triptych of altered photographs titled Obliterated Power shows the Capitol, Pentagon and Supreme Court buildings — three major sites of governmental power in the United States — erased by black ink, manifesting, on a national level, Scott’s ideal of a vanquished America. For now, we can only imagine such erasure. As long as America persists, the power of the state is enacted on the bodies of its citizens — and non-citizens.
“America is becoming fascist and nationalist,” Scott says, “and who is and who is not an American can determine if you live or die. Those who can’t claim citizenship basically have no rights whatsoever.”
Bodies take center stage in the rest of the show, which consists of several of Scott’s ghostly sepia body prints, at once detailed and abstract, but no less direct in their messaging. In Fight the Power and Hands Up , both 2023, clusters of hands take on different meanings: fists clench in gestures of revolution, fingers spread in pleading. The diptych Mugshot (2023) features Scott posed in profile and face-forward, holding an identification card typical of an arrest photo.
The method of body printing Scott uses was pioneered, along with Yves Klein and Jasper Johns, by David Hammons in the 1960s and 70s, who used it to make similarly politically charged work around issues of the Civil Rights movement. By repeating the motif today, Scott draws a clear parallel between the urgencies of that era and current American political pressures, reminding viewers that the struggle for liberation continues.
The largest work on view, another commission for the show, is Life/Death/America , a roughly 14-by-35-foot piece. In it, 32 body prints scatter across four canvas panels as though in free fall. The individuals, friends and friends of friends of the artist, range in age, race, gender and class, highlighting the social range of a democratic society. The way in which they are depicted varies too, and was determined by each participant, some wearing business suits, others keffiyehs. In emphasizing representation and diversity, the piece reminds us of the freedom of identity and expression Scott and many others are fighting for.
Without direct artistic visualizations of both what we stand to lose and what shedding the current power structures might look like, it can be difficult to maintain a clear picture of the collective future Scott puts forward. Sometimes, in the face of censorship and federal defunding of the arts, it feels like the current administration understands the importance of the arts better its opposition does. Imagination is a powerful weapon in the war against fascism — and one we mustn’t forget. Art like Scott’s reminds us of its potency.
“Art itself doesn’t make political change,” Scott says. “But there hasn’t been a progressive movement I know of that hasn’t had art at the foundation of it in some way. It helps people see the world in a new way and stand strong in the face of their oppressors.”
‘ Dread Scott: The Body Politic ’ is on view at Yerba Buena Center for the Arts (701 Mission St., San Francisco) through Jan. 31, 2027.

articles.title_orig: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
articles.title_zh: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
articles.content_orig:
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."
He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."
The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.
The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.
Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.
The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest.
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.
But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.
Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.
"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.
But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.
Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.
"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."
The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.
More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.
But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.
The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.
Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.
Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.
Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.
Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.
He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.
Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are l

articles.title_orig: 7.7-Magnitude Panama Earthquake Sets Off Series of Aftershocks
articles.title_zh: 7.7-Magnitude Panama Earthquake Sets Off Series of Aftershocks
articles.content_orig:
A major earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.7 has struck southern Panama, according to the US Geological Survey.
Several people have suffered minor injuries but so far there are no reports of fatalities or missing persons, officials said. Various homes, roads, hotels, government buildings, businesses and churches have sustained structural damage, according to the civil protection system.
The USGS had said some casualties were possible and extensive damage was probable.
Footage verified by CNN shows several damaged buildings in Penonome, some 70 miles from the epicenter. One video shows a church with a partially collapsed steeple and another building with a crumbled facade.
In the popular resort town Playa Venao, a multi-story building collapsed and crushed several cars beneath it.
Along the Panama Canal, the Centennial Bridge’s suspension cables were seen shaking as vehicles drove through.
The canal’s authority said operations were continuing as normal and that staff were inspecting facilities for potential damage.
Panama City’s public transit system has suspended service on two metro lines and evacuated passengers from some stations.
Scores of residents gathered in the streets of the capital after rushing out of their buildings in a panic.
“I am on the ninth floor here and yes it was felt strongly, it was felt strongly,” Panama City resident Kevin Cortez told Reuters.
“Everything was moving: the lamp, the chair, the table,” another resident said. “I decided to stay and wait because I knew running down the stairs was a problem. So I stayed waiting for it to pass. I had no other option. Yes, we felt it was quite prolonged. People running, shouting; not everyone takes it the same way, but well, here we are, downstairs.”
The Education Ministry has canceled classes nationwide for the rest of the day.
Panama’s main international airport was temporarily closed as a precaution and flights were diverted to other airports before operations resumed later in the day, the civil aviation authority said.
The water and sewage institute has reported interruptions at several water treatment plants due to power outages caused by the quake.
Panama’s President José Raúl Mulino has called for calm and instructed the minister of government to provide information on the earthquake’s effects. He has also mobilized resources to those affected.
Mulino visited an affected hospital in Penonome, where several patients were evacuated and have had to receive treatment outdoors.
Officials have reported more than 40 aftershocks, including one with a preliminary magnitude of 6.6, according to USGS.
Earlier, the US Tsunami Warning System warned of possible tsunami waves along some coasts before saying there was no longer a threat.
This is the latest powerful earthquake to have struck Latin America this year. Over the summer, Venezuela was hit by two powerful earthquakes that killed more than 6,400 people, while Colombia suffered a tremor that left around 300 dead.
The leaders of both countries have offered to help Panama’s government as it responds to the disaster.

articles.title_orig: North Carolina World War II veteran, who treated wounded soldiers, celebrates 104th birthday
articles.title_zh: North Carolina World War II veteran, who treated wounded soldiers, celebrates 104th birthday
articles.content_orig:
George Chall's life has brought him around the globe.
From World War II battlefields to Pittsboro, North Carolina, where Chall turned 104 years old surrounded by friends, family, and community who came to honor the veteran's milestone.
Chall, a New York native, served in the U.S. Army's 110th Evacuation Hospital unit during World War II. He arrived at the beaches of Normandy several weeks after D-Day and treated wounded soldiers on the front lines, including during the Battle of Metz and the Battle of the Bulge.
"I think of some of the people I helped in significant ways, and some who I was not able to help," Chall said. "I think more of those I was unable to help, of those who made it through."
He still remembers how his unit saw some of the earlier applications of penicillin in the field, and the schedule he kept to keep soldiers alive.
"Twice a day for 24 hours, at midnight and noon, we’d administer the penicillin," he said. "It was so new and not yet full strength that we had to do it twice in 24 hours to save a life."
According to the Institute of Biomedical Science , enough penicillin was made available to treat all Allied forces by D-Day.
Chall, who moved to North Carolina in 2014, celebrated his 104th birthday at his Pittsboro home.
Pittsboro's mayor honored Chall with a proclamation, dedicating October 9, 2026, as "Dr. George Chall Day."
According to the National World War II Museum, there are roughly 30,000 surviving World War II veterans. There are fewer than 900 still surviving in the state of North Carolina.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias now a major hurricane as it closes in. These cities will be hit hard.
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias now a major hurricane as it closes in. These cities will be hit hard.
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring heavy rain, damaging winds and life-threatening storm surge to the northern Gulf Coast when it makes landfall late Friday or early Saturday.
According to the National Hurricane Center, Isaias remains a Category 3 storm with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph, which forecasters consider a "major hurricane."
As of 5 p.m. ET, the storm was located about 90 miles south of Pensacola, Fla., and roughly 125 miles south-southeast of Mobile, Ala., moving north at 17 mph. It is expected to approach the northern Gulf Coast this afternoon and make landfall near the Alabama-Florida state line tonight.
The governors of Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared states of emergency, along with several Mississippi counties, urging residents to take the first hurricane of an unusually quiet season seriously. Thousands of National Guard soldiers are being deployed.
Is the storm headed your way? Follow it in real time on the new Yahoo Weather app.
Mandatory evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Florida's Walton, Escambia, Okaloosa and Franklin counties. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey also ordered nonresidents to evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island.
Heavy rain and flooding could extend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina through the weekend. There's also a risk of tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle into southern Georgia.
Follow live updates on Hurricane Isaias below.
Areas experiencing increased tornado risks on Friday caused by Hurricane Isaias
The National Weather Service warned Friday that strong winds from Hurricane Isaias are increasing the risk of tornadoes in areas impacted by the storm.
"The greatest risk will be east of the center, particularly across the Florida Panhandle into southern Georgia," the NWS wrote in a public advisory Friday afternoon.
Forecasters expect tornado risk to continue into Saturday as the storm makes its way inland, spreading to new areas across Georgia and into the Carolinas.
According to the most recent advisory from the National Hurricane Center, as of 5 p.m. ET on Friday:
Hurricane Isaias was about 90 miles south of Pensacola, Fla., and roughly 125 miles south-southeast of Mobile, Ala.
The storm had maximum sustained winds of 115 mph
It was moving north-northeast at 17 mph
Isaias is expected to make landfall in the western Florida Panhandle later tonight.
"Little change in strength is expected before Isaias makes landfall this evening," the NHC said. "Weakening is expected to begin tonight after landfall, and Isaias is forecast to become post-tropical on Saturday."
President Trump is shown on the jumbotron before a college football game between Texas and Tennessee at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville on Sept. 26.
President Trump announced Friday that he will not be attending Alabama's pivotal college football matchup against Georgia in Tuscaloosa, Ala., on Saturday because of Hurricane Isaias.
"It is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!" Trump wrote on Truth Social .
Earlier in the week, Trump had told reporters that he still intended to travel to the game, despite the impending storm.
"I love Alabama. I got to go to a game like that," he told reporters on Wednesday, but added that he would consider changing his plans "if there's an emergency."
There had been some speculation that the game might be postponed or relocated because of Isaias, but organizers have said it will be played as scheduled.
According to the most recent forecasts, Isaias will likely be downgraded to a tropical storm by the time it reaches Tuscaloosa on Saturday. The heart of the storm is expected to have moved north of the city by the time the game is scheduled to kick off at 7:30 p.m. ET.
Instead of traveling to Alabama, Trump said he will hold a rally in Tennessee on Saturday in support of Republican candidates for House, Senate and governor in the state.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced on Friday that the state had opened a hotline where residents can report "unconscionable increases in prices" by retailers in the hurricane's path.
"Protecting Floridians isn't a seasonal job," Uthmeier said in a press release . "Whether it's a storm, a scam, or a greedy corporation, our office will enforce the law."
Florida law prohibits price hikes on "essential commodities and services" that may be needed to prepare for or recover from a major storm, including food, water, ice, gasoline, lumber, equipment and hotel rooms.
Violators can be fined $1,000 for a first offense, with penalties increasing to $25,000 and potential criminal sanctions for severe offenders. Floridians can report suspected price gouging through MyFloridaLegal.com or by calling 1-866-9-NO-SCAM.
With Hurricane Isaias expected to make landfall on the northern Gulf Coast near the Alabama-Florida line, coastal Mississippians may be thinking they caught a break. But the state's governor doesn't want residents to let their guard down.
"We are still expected to receive some effects from the hurricane including 3-5' of storm surge in and around Biloxi through Jackson County and a strong risk of flash flooding throughout the eastern part of our state," Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves wrote in a post on X. "Continue to stay vigilant and weather aware, Mississippi!"
According to t he most recent advisory from the National Hurricane Center, as of 2 p.m. ET:
Hurricane Isaias was about 145 miles south of Pensacola, Fla., and roughly 125 miles southeast of the mouth of the Mississippi River
It had maximum sustained winds of 120 mph
It was moving north-northeast at 16 mph
Isaias is expected to approach the northern Gulf Coast this afternoon and make landfall somewhere near the Alabama-Florida line tonight.
"Fluctuations in intensity are possible through this afternoon, but Isaias is expected to be at or near major hurricane strength when it makes landfall this evening," the hurricane center said. "Weakening is expected beginning tonight after Isaias makes landfall, and the storm is likely to become post-tropical by late Saturday."
Want to know how to pronounce Isaias? Don't ask Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.
While delivering an update on preparations for Hurricane Isaiah, DeSantis said didn't know how to correctly pronounce the storm's name — and wasn't about to try.
"I don't know how to pronounce this because it's not normal," DeSantis said. "So, you know, I'm calling it Isaiah. You guys can call it what you want. I know that's not how you pronounce this. It's something else. But it's weird and I'm just going to keep butchering it for the next 72 hours."
For the record: Isaias, the Spanish form of Isaiah, is pronounced "ee-sah-EE-ahs."
In a livestream update from the National Hurricane Center in Miami, NHC Director Michael Brennan said tropical storm-force winds from Hurricane Isaias will begin reaching the Florida Panhandle within the next few hours.
"So if you are in these evacuation zones and you've been asked to leave by your local officials, please get out as soon as you can before conditions deteriorate," Brennan said.
A storm surge of up to 9 feet is likely, and rainfall totals of up to 15 inches are possible in the western Florida Panhandle, southwestern Georgia and southern Alabama.
He also urged those in the storm's path to use extra caution after it passes.
"Be careful with chainsaws," Brennan said. "Don't push yourself if you're out there in dangerous conditions. Please take care of yourself. And make sure if you're operating a generator, do it well away from your home and vent it away from your home to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning. So please stay safe."
Hurricane Isaias was the first to form in this year's Atlantic season, which begins in June and runs through November. It was one day shy of tying a 121-year-old record for the basin's latest-forming hurricane, accord

articles.title_orig: Human Rights Lawyer Navi Pillay Is Awarded Nobel Peace Prize
articles.title_zh: Human Rights Lawyer Navi Pillay Is Awarded Nobel Peace Prize
articles.content_orig:
Cleary is an editor at TIME, based in the London bureau.
Cleary is an editor at TIME, based in the London bureau.
Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African jurist and former U.N. high commissioner for human rights, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”
“Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation, and exclusion,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
“A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.”
Pillay, 85, is a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide. She was also chair of the ⁠U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that concluded last year that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. (Israel at the time dismissed the report as "scandalous" and “fake.") Israel's Foreign Ministry criticized Pillay's win, referring to it as a "grotesque weaponization" of the award.
In "historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence," Frydnes said, referring to Pillay as "one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time."
Reflecting on her win, Pillay said she is often asked when she will stop working. "I can’t obviously stop my work in support of the Nuremberg Principles, because of the people we meet here," she said.
Born in South Africa in 1941, Pillay was the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in the country, according to the U.N.
In those early years of practicing law, she acted as a defense attorney for anti-apartheid activists.
Pillay has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, and the International Criminal Court (ICC) throughout the course of her career.
She was the U.N. human rights chief from September 2008 to August 2014. Volker Türk, who currently holds that position, said Pillay's Nobel recognition is "particularly poignant" as it comes "at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power."
“It is an award to all those who around the world dedicate their lives to the defense of human rights, often at great risk to their security," he added.
Pillay is the fifth South African national to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. She follows in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela, FW de Klerk, Archbishop Desmond ​Tutu, and Albert Luthuli.
Pillay dedicated her Nobel Peace Prize to “all of the survivors of international crimes” and people defending international criminal justice, “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign.”
During a press conference at the International Nuremberg Principle Academy, in the German city where the trials of Nazi leaders showcased the enforcement of international law, Pillay referred to the award as a "wonderful surprise" and the "highest honor."
Using her platform to spotlight the international justice system, Pillay told reporters: “We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack... This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."
She added that the Nobel recognition has strengthened her "conviction that we must stand together in ‌defense of the rule of law, ​in defense of independent courts, and an international legal order ⁠based on principle."
When asked during a press briefing if the award sends a message to those who question or sanction international courts, Frydnes told reporters: “This is definitely a message to those who are attacking, undermin[ing] the international system, the international rules-based system, and the institutions."
U.S. President Donald Trump last month called for countries to "immediately" resign from the International Criminal Court (ICC), amid a broader push by the Trump Administration to dismantle the institution it accuses of unfairly targeting the U.S. and Israel. His call was firmly rejected by European leaders.
The Trump Administration has criticized the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli leaders, including ​Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and former investigations into the actions of American soldiers in Afghanistan.
Hours after Pillay's win, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the Trump Administration is placing sweeping new sanctions on the ICC. It has previously imposed sanctions on the court's prosecutors and judges, but these new measures go a step further.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us,” Rubio said . “The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”
As a result of the sanctions, and "subject to applicable licenses and exceptions, all property and interests in property of the ICC that are in the United States or in possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control," read a notice from the State Department.
Rubio claimed both Republicans and Democrats have concerns about the court overstepping its jurisdiction, but said only Trump is willing to take action. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," he warned.
In response, the ICC's deputy ​prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan condemned the sanctions and vowed the court's "work will ​continue ⁠across all our situations, our ⁠investigations, ​and our ​prosecution."
The Foreign Ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the U.K. have also denounced the sanctions.
In a joint statement that expressed "unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," the officials said the sanctions "will have a significant impact on the [ICC's] work, its dedicated staff, and their families."
Pillay referenced Trump and his well-documented campaign to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize when she reacted to her own recognition on Friday morning.
In a video shared by Agnes Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, Pillay could be seen entering a room at Nuremberg Court to resounding applause from her peers. "If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she joked.
The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado , famously gave her medal to Trump in January as she pressed the U.S. to support democracy in Venezuela.
While the Norwegian Nobel Institute doesn’t release a shortlist of its contenders each year, the leaders of Israel , Cambodia , and Pakistan have all previously said they nominated Trump. The institute registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s prize, including 208 individuals and 79 organizations.
Trump said earlier this week it would be a “ great discredit ” to the Norwegian Nobel Committee if they did not announce him as this year's recipient.

articles.title_orig: Southern California braces for Tropical Storm Rachel. 'This is not even the worst,' official says
articles.title_zh: Southern California braces for Tropical Storm Rachel. 'This is not even the worst,' official says
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Coastal communities from Newport Beach to Long Beach were hit by significant flooding from large waves on Friday as Southern California braces for the arrival of Tropical Storm Rachel, which is expected to make landfall near the California- Mexico border early Sunday.
Rachel’s arrival brings the potential for strong winds, rain and more damaging coastal flooding. If the current storm trajectory continues, Rachel’s effects will be felt mostly in San Diego County. However, Orange and Los Angeles counties are still forecast to see widespread rain and isolated coastal flooding as a result of the system, according to the National Weather Service.
“Even though the center of Tropical Storm Rachel will be well south of Los Angeles County, the significant swell in the ocean coming initially from the south, and then also phasing with a swell from the west, will bring coastal flooding concerns from any time from now through Tuesday, peaking on Sunday,” said National Weather Service Meteorologist-in-Charge Ariel Cohen.
The National Weather Service office in San Diego on Friday issued a rare tropical storm watch for most of San Diego County, including areas like San Diego, Chula Vista, Carlsbad and Oceanside, meaning that tropical storm-force winds are possible somewhere in the area over the next 48 hours. It’s only the second time a tropical storm watch has been issued in California.
The incoming storm could damage porches, awnings, carports, sheds and unanchored mobile homes, and snap off large tree branches, posing a safety risk, the weather service office said. It warned of hazardous driving conditions on bridges and other elevated roadways.
Predictions that Rachel, currently spinning about 800 miles off the coast of San Diego, will actually strengthen as it approaches the West Coast is unusual and remarkable, said UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain.
Typically, once storms enter the cooler water in the eastern tropical Pacific they weaken significantly. But a marine heat wave and El Niño conditions — bringing ocean temperatures 10 to 13 degrees higher than normal — have provided a more conducive environment for Rachel.
“It’s notable that this is an unusual event that’s being made possible by both coincidence of this early arriving low-pressure trough off the coast of California and the record warm — and I do mean record warm — ocean temperatures off the coast of California right now,” Swain said during a briefing Friday.
Forecasters are warning that south-facing beaches in Southern California could be particularly at risk of flooding on account of Tropical Storm Rachel this weekend.
On Friday morning, Southern Californians got a preview of what’s to come with Rachel’s arrival.
Streets on the Balboa Peninsula in Newport Beach were flooded with at least a foot of water during high tide, with the police department advising residents and motorists to avoid the area. The flooding was remarkable even in a neighborhood that has been prone to regular water inundations in the past, particularly during El Niño.
“This is the worst I’ve seen it in my 20 years on the Peninsula,” said Councilman Joe Stapleton.
Water from a massive swell — double the size that was initially predicted — blasted through 20-foot berms erected at the Wedge and washed out roads from about 21st Street to 6th Street, officials said.
“This swell was very unprecedented coming up that high,” said Georgia Rios, a spokesperson for the city of Newport Beach. “We knew we were going to have a high swell due to Tropical Storm Rachel, but along with El Niño it really has been a combination force here in Newport.”
The city declared a local emergency Friday and urged residents to pick up sandbags to protect their homes over the weekend. City crews are pumping out water on the streets, rebuilding beach berms and opening tide valves to help mitigate water intrusion.
“This is not even the worst that is expected,” Rios said. “It’s forecast to get even worse on Sunday with rain.”
In Laguna Beach, Coast Highway and Broadway was inundated with water from big waves and high tide. The typically sandy sections of Main Beach — where locals often gather to walk along the sand and play beach volleyball — were transformed into a sea of water.
At San Onofre State Beach, the road that surfers and beachgoers use to access the iconic spot was damaged resulting in a myriad of parking issues. The beach has  been undergone significant coastal erosion in recent years and advocates say it could be hit hard this winter.
Hurricane Isaias will not be the only tropical system affecting the U.S. in the coming days. Moisture from T.S. Rachel will create the potential for locally heavy rainfall and bring the risk of flash flooding Saturday-Monday from Southern California into Utah. pic.twitter.com/2n3dZ8qbHI
In Long Beach, which has been hit hard this season by a series of back-to-back distant hurricanes, powerful waves crumbled large sections of the boardwalk on the peninsula and left several homes with severe structural damage. Video showed waves slamming against the bulkhead that protects beachfront homes.
The city has already been besieged by an unusually active, El Niño-fueled hurricane season, taking damage from Hurricane Marie over Labor Day weekend and Hurricane Polo last month.
“We’ve had three storms back pretty much back to back to back,” said Laath Martin, a spokesperson for the city. “This is definitely not something that we see very often.”
Officials have red-tagged two properties, including a duplex with three units. Three buildings have also been yellow-tagged after sustaining damage from Hurricane Marie ahead of Rachel’s arrival.
Long Beach has already distributed more than 7,500 sandbags, as residents prepare for what could feel like a very long weekend.
“It’s hard to predict exactly what will happen, but just based on forecasts, we’re preparing for more damage,” Martin said.
Across Southern California, the highest chances of rain are between Sunday morning and Monday night, forecasters say. In Los Angeles County, rain is expected to be light to moderate, ranging from about a quarter of an inch to an inch across much of the region. A bit more rain is expected in the San Gabriel Mountains, according to the weather service office in Oxnard.
Rain rates are probably going to be a quarter of an inch per hour or less, making debris flow and landslides unlikely.
“There will be a couple thunderstorms out and about, especially later on Sunday. But we’re not looking at any long duration excessive rainfall,” Cohen said on Friday.
A bit more rain is expected in Orange and San Diego counties with coastal areas receiving  half an inch to an inch over the weekend and into early next week. Higher elevations, including Big Bear and Julian, could get up to an inch and a half of precipitation.
While tropical moisture from the remnants of Rachel is expected to deliver only light rain to much of Southern California, the Mojave Desert and the Inland Empire could see more significant precipitation.
The weather service is warning that there is a moderate, or 40% chance, of excessive rainfall that could lead to flash flooding in places like San Diego, El Cajon, Chula Vista, Escondido, Palm Springs and Twentynine Palms. A moderate risk means that numerous flash floods are likely, and that many streams may flood. There is a potential that the San Diego River near Fashion Valley could reach minor flood stage.
There’s also a 15% chance of that occurring in Oceanside, San Clemente, Laguna Niguel, Riverside, San Bernardino, Las Vegas and the California-Arizona border; and a 5% chance in places like Huntington Beach, Santa Ana, Long Beach, Anaheim, Pomona, Victorville, Barstow, and most of Arizona and southern Utah.
