articles.title_orig: Tech giants Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys and 5 others lose ability to sponsor African and other foreign workers for US green cards
articles.title_zh: Tech giants Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys and 5 others lose ability to sponsor African and other foreign workers for US green cards
articles.content_orig:
The United States has suspended Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services and four other major technology companies from a key employment-based green card programme, affecting skilled foreign workers, including Africans seeking permanent residency through employer sponsorship.
The other affected companies are Cognizant, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini, with the US Department of Labor suspending all eight firms from the Permanent Labor Certification programme, commonly known as PERM, amid allegations of misuse and fraud.
PERM is part of the process employers use to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based permanent residency in the United States.
The suspension applies to workers of all nationalities , including African professionals whose green card applications depend on sponsorship from the affected companies.
However, the measure does not stop the companies from recruiting Africans for jobs in Africa or other markets, but restricts their use of the PERM programme to sponsor foreign workers for US permanent residency.
DON'T MISS: 7 US multimillionaire donors gave $189 million to universities in 2026, far more than Africa’s 23 billionaires publicly gave to science and research
The decision comes as the Trump administration increases scrutiny of companies that use foreign labour while cutting jobs in the United States.
Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft during a news conference, claiming the company had laid off 6,000 American workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 permanent residencies.
“Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said.
“You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants,” he added.
Across the US technology sector, more than 131,000 workers have been laid off in 2026, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job cuts in technology companies and start-ups.
Microsoft disputed the administration’s account of its visa use, saying most of its recent filings involved workers already employed in the United States.
“80 percent of the visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees,” Microsoft said.
“The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company added.
Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling said the eight companies had requested almost three million foreign workers since 2009, secured more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and obtained more than 100,000 permanent labour certifications.
The Department of Labor also said it had uncovered $22 billion worth of alleged visa fraud.
“Today we are protecting something far more valuable than any dollar amount. We are protecting the American worker,” Sonderling said.
Employment-based immigration has provided a route to US permanent residency for thousands of Africans.
US Office of Homeland Security Statistics data shows that 11,694 African-born people obtained permanent residency through employment-based preference categories in fiscal year 2022, while 89,571 received green cards that year across employment, family, diversity visa and other categories.
In fiscal year 2023, the number of African-born people obtaining permanent residency across all categories rose to 105,520, accounting for about 9% of new permanent residents.
Nigeria accounted for 15,790 of those recipients, although available data does not show how many Africans were sponsored specifically by the eight suspended companies.

articles.title_orig: BIDMC Researchers Conduct First Real-World Study of Safety and Quality of Patient-Facing AI in Primary Care
articles.title_zh: BIDMC Researchers Conduct First Real-World Study of Safety and Quality of Patient-Facing AI in Primary Care
articles.content_orig:
BOSTON — The aging population, workforce changes, and patients’ increasingly complex medical needs are all factors straining primary care systems around the world. Artificial intelligence tools have emerged as a potential means of extending the capabilities of health care workers, including in primary care settings. Large language models (LLMs), also known as chatbots, have performed extremely well in simulations. However, little is known about how these systems perform with real patients.
Researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) have conducted what they believe is the first prospective real-world study of a patient-facing conversational AI system in primary care, taking an important step toward evaluating the technology through the same kind of rigorous clinical testing used for other health care interventions. The findings appear in The Lancet .
“Despite the theoretical performance of patient-facing AI in experimental settings, it is unclear how conversationally safe these encounters are in a real-world setting," said Adam Rodman, MD, Director of AI Programs at the Carl J. Shapiro Institute for Research and Education at BIDMC. "Before we begin evaluating them as workload interventions, AI tools must first be shown to operate safely and acceptably in real care workflows. With this research, we set out to assess whether this kind of technology could improve both patient and physician experience."
Rodman and colleagues in collaboration with researchers at Google evaluated the Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE), a medical AI chatbot that patients used from home after scheduling an urgent primary care appointment with a BIDMC physician. Through a secure text-chat interface, the system asked patients about their symptoms, gathered medical histories, provided possible diagnoses for patients to review with their doctor, and generated a summary for clinician review prior to the visit.
Conducted between April and November 2025, the study enrolled 114 patients, 98 of whom completed both the AI interaction and their primary care appointment. Every conversation was monitored in real time by a board-certified internal medicine physician who could intervene if a patient appeared at risk of harm, experienced significant emotional distress, asked to end the session, or if the physician identified a potential safety concern — such as the need to clarify symptoms, provide emergency care instructions, or address concern about a serious possible diagnosis.
Across all 98 completed encounters, none of the conversations required a safety-stop intervention. Supervising physicians identified one hallucination and provided additional clinical clarification in five cases.
"This study helps establish the baseline characteristics of such real-world conversations,” said co-first author Peter Brodeur, MD, a clinical fellow in cardiovascular medicine at BIDMC. “These baseline characteristics provide a foundation for all future prospective trials aimed at discovering when human-on-the-loop workflows may be appropriate.”
Patients appeared receptive to the technology. Patients rated the quality of AMIE's conversations favorably — as did physician evaluators — across most measures. Moreover, patient attitudes toward AI improved after interacting with the chatbot and remained elevated following their appointment with a clinician.
"One of the most important questions was simply how patients would engage with a conversational AI system in a real clinical setting," said co-first author Jacob Koshy, MD, MPH, a hospitalist in the Division of General Medicine at BIDMC. "By prospectively observing these interactions, we were able to better understand both the opportunities and the limitations of the technology in the context of routine patient care."
While patients gave high marks to the system's ability to listen, explain information, and help them feel at ease, concerns remained around two areas: trust in the confidentiality of information shared with the system and trust in the chatbot's honesty and trustworthiness. Researchers said those findings underscore the importance of continued work to build patient trust as AI tools move into clinical care.
"Research suggests that patient trust in medical AI systems flows from relationships with their human providers," said Rodman. "Future research will need to explore which interaction characteristics can build patient trust and how AI interactions can enhance the patient-physician relationship."
The findings also suggest the technology may have practical value in clinical workflows.
Primary care providers were able to review an AI-generated transcript or summary before seeing their patients for 44 cases. In 75 percent of cases, physicians said doing so helped them prepare for the visit and in 57 percent of cases, they reported it may have influenced their clinical approach. In only one case did a provider report the interaction as somewhat harmful, citing concern that a patient may have experienced anxiety after AMIE included lymphoma among its possible diagnoses.
Rodman and colleagues emphasized that the study was designed to evaluate feasibility rather than to determine whether AI improves health outcomes.
“Our primary care practice — and our hospital — has a long history of rigorously monitoring the safety of the clinical care we provide, and this study serves as an exemplar of how the safety of AI may be assessed prior to clinical implementation,” said co-senior author Marc L. Cohen, MD, Clinical Chief of Primary Care, Division of General Medicine at BIDMC. “We believe the future involves continued involvement of human clinicians in patient care, but see a future where the triad of patient, human clinician, and AI help to provide our patients with the very best evidenced-based care possible," said Cohen.
Co-authors included Ava Homiar, BS; Charles Wu, MD; Hannah M. Ferrera, MD; Lindsey Crowley, MD; Christine G. Kohn, MD; Vinay Kadiyala, MD; Wendy Du, MD; David Feinbloom, MD; Jonathan X. Li, MD; Spencer E. Rittner, MD; and Rob Fields, MD of BIDMC; Selena K. Zhang, BS, of Harvard Medical School; Anil Palepu, PhD; Roma Ruparel, MPH; Joseph Xu, PhD; Amy Wang, MD; Jihyeon Lee, MS; Ellery Wulczyn, MS; Kavita Kulkarni, MS; Jessica M. Williams, BS; Renee Wong, BEcom; Petar Sirkovic, PhD; Alessio Orlandi, PhD; Christopher Semturs, MS; Yun Liu, PhD; Juraj Gottweis, MS; Dale R. Webster, PhD; Katherine Chou, MS; Avinatan Hassidim, PhD; Yossi Matias, PhD; James Manyika, DPhil; and Mike Schaekermann, PhD, of Google Research; and Khaled Saab, PhD; Ryutaro Tanno, PhD; David Stutz, PhD; Wei-Hung Weng, MD; David Barrett, PhD; Elahe Vedadi, PhD; S. Sara Mahdavi, PhD; Tao Tu, PhD; Joëlle Barral, PhD; Pushmeet Kohli, PhD; Vivek Natarajan, MS; and Alan Karthikesalingam, PhD, of Google DeepMind.
This study was funded by Alphabet. Adam Rodman, MD, served as a visiting researcher at Google during part of the study. Full disclosures are available in the published manuscript.
Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center is a leading academic medical center, where extraordinary care is supported by high-quality education and research. BIDMC is a teaching affiliate of Harvard Medical School, and consistently ranks as a national leader among independent hospitals in National Institutes of Health funding. BIDMC is the official hospital of the Boston Red Sox.
Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center is a part of Beth Israel Lahey Health , a healthcare system that brings together academic medical centers and teaching hospitals, community and specialty hospitals, more than 4,700 physicians and 39,000 employees in a shared mission to expand access to great care and advance the science and practice of medicine through groundbreaking research and education.

articles.title_orig: Wall St climbs as oil slips; SpaceX spectrum deal weighs on telecoms
articles.title_zh: Wall St climbs as oil slips; SpaceX spectrum deal weighs on telecoms
articles.content_orig:
Telecommunications stocks sold off on Friday after Elon Musk 's SpaceX announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio , aiming to expand its Starlink internet into mobile service.
Verizon was down roughly 7% on the news, and is pacing its worst day since 2002. Shares of T-Mobile were down 12% while AT&T fell around 10%. SpaceX stock climbed slightly, around 1% for the day.
The deal includes acquiring the spectrum from Grain Management, which SpaceX described as a "license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band," in a Thursday statement.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whose agency will oversee approval of the deal, said that competition in the spectrum market was "really good news for the American consumers" in a CNBC interview.
"We're probably going to bring over $100 billion of spectrum into the market over the next two years, so we're seeing a lot of competition," Carr told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Friday.
"There's going to be moves in the market. People are going to try to out-compete, out-innovate, and I think that's great. We're going to see how this plays out. It's not for us ultimately to pick winners and losers," he added.

Earlier this week, Aaron Perris discovered code references to a new feature where “nearby smart home accessories could show controls in the Dynamic Island.” Now, @itspdfu has found even more details about how this feature will work.
In a new social media post today, pdfu says Apple’s “second-party” home accessories co-developed with LG will support this new “Proximity Control” feature.
When you tap or bring your iPhone near one of LG’s accessories, a notification will pop out of the Dynamic Island. The notification will show an “Open Controls” button for accessories like thermostats. For cameras and doorbells, you’ll see a “camera viewer.”
You’ll also see feedback in the Dynamic Island as iPhone launches setup when you first tap the accessory to pair it.
Behind the scenes, the accessory writes an “apple-deviceid” in the Matter payload stored on its NFC tag that helps iOS identify it when tapped. It also broadcasts a Bluetooth Low Energy advert for Apple Proximity Control.
You’ll seemingly have the option to turn this feature off in the Home app. As always, features referenced in Apple’s code might not ship, or they could work materially differently when they do launch.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
articles.content_orig:
The ⁠ICC’s deputy prosecutor condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal’s work
Navi Pillay has begun giving a press conference after the declaration that she has won this year’s Nobel Peace prize. She began by saying she dedicates the award to “survivors of international crimes”.
She called on people to stand together in the defence of rule of law.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today .
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza ( 11:02 , 11:04 , 11:06 , 11:11 ).
In her first reaction, Pillay specifically paid tribute to all people defending human rights everywhere, as she joked to her associates that “if you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump” ( 11:53 , 12:02 ).
Her win was widely celebrated by senior judges and human right campaigners, who offered their congratulations ( 11:33 , 12:06 , 12:17 , 12:21 , 13:22 , 15:25 ), including the president of the international court of justice, of which she is a former judge ( 12:58 ).
But Israel reacted angrily to the award, saying that “it’s the grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice” ( 13:52 ).
US president Donald Trump also reposted a critical comment saying the Nobel committee “shamed itself beyond repair and demeaned” the prize ( 16:06 ).
Just hours after the announcement, which was explicitly meant as the Nobel Committee’s backing for the international court of justice, the US has imposed sanctions on the court ( 16:20 ).

When the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not.
Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect.
A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government.
A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel. Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%.
Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion. Five countries chose to boycott the Eurovision song contest this year over Israel’s participation, after organisers declined to exclude it over its conduct in the Gaza war and rising violence in the West Bank. Organisers have now decided that broadcasters will no longer be eligible to host the song contest if their state is involved in an armed conflict or sensitive geopolitical situation.
More than 74,000 people, including at least 21,200 children, have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its war in retaliation for the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, in which the terrorist group killed 1,209 people – including 36 children – and took 251 hostages, inflicting a nationwide trauma .
Gaza remains a humanitarian catastrophe , with people facing acute shortages of water, nutritious food and medical equipment and medicines, while contending with disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the threat of death or injury. Israel’s airstrikes continue: the death toll includes 1,400 Palestinians killed since a ceasefire was declared a year ago.
The EU talks on the Middle East will focus on the conflicts in Iran and Yemen, but ministers will also discuss the situation in Gaza and the West Bank in the context of elections in Israel on 27 October and the first legislative elections in Palestine in 20 years, which are expected by late November.
The discussion is expected to expose familiar fault lines in the 27-member EU. One group of countries are vocal supporters of the Palestinian cause: Spain and Ireland were the first to call for a review of whether Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war was in breach of the human rights requirements of its association agreement with the EU, which covers the €68bn (£58bn) trade relationship, cooperation in research, environment and energy.
A second group consistently opposes targeting Israel’s government: Germany and Austria are close allies for historical reasons, while Czechia and Italy are ideologically aligned with Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration.
Among a third, larger group of countries in the middle are several, such as France and the Netherlands, that are increasingly critical of the Netanyahu government’s conduct in Gaza and its plans to build the vast E1 settlement, which threatens to critically damage the two-state solution.
Czechs go to the polls on Friday at the start of two days of voting to fill one-third of the seats in Parliament’s upper house, the Senate, and elect local representatives, AP reported.
The elections are the first test for populist billionaire Andrej Babiš since he returned to power after a decisive victory in parliamentary elections in October 2025.
His centrist ANO (YES) movement hopes to make gains in the 81-seat Senate, which is controlled by pro-western opposition parties. Twenty-seven Senate seats are up for grabs in the two-round election, with runoffs scheduled for next week. First-round results are expected on Saturday.
Babiš has formed a governing coalition with two small political groups whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine and rejecting some key European Union policies.
Unlike the government, the opposition and president Petr Pavel remain firm supporters of Ukraine following Russia’s invasion.
But Pavel – an avid biker – attracted a lot of attention in the build up to the vote as it emerged that he would miss the vote due to a long-planned motorcycle trip in Morocco. After days of relentless pressure, he eventually cut the holiday short and reported to vote, acknowledging his original “error” in scheduling.
“Some mistakes can be corrected relatively easily, others with more difficulty, and some cannot be corrected at all.
Fortunately, a mistake in planning can be remedied by changing the plan. Admitting a mistake is not easy, but if a politician values people’s trust, he must prove it.
I know what responsibility is and that any trust is hard to earn, but terribly easy and quick to lose. You pay for mistakes, and I have learned from this one of my own.”
The European Union is granting temporary trade preferences to Armenia following trade restrictions recently imposed by Russia.
In a move which shows how flexible the EU can be, it said the temporary trade preferences “will help alleviate the difficult situation faced by Armenian producers and exporters and support the resilience of Armenia’s economy by facilitating access to the EU market.
The measures, which will enter into force tomorrow for a period of two years, temporarily allow 80% of Armenian exports to the EU, including almost all exports of fresh fruit, vegetables and flowers affected by the Russian measures, as well as over 91% of exports of beverages and spirits.
Armenia is not an accession state, but has been singled out for support as part of the EU a broader solidarity support package

articles.title_orig: End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to life
articles.title_zh: End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to life
articles.content_orig:
Barbican theatre, London With a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicorns
H ow to stage Haruki Murakami’s epic, dual-narrative novel without leaving the audience in a muddle? Director-choreographer Philippe Decouflé goes big, filling the enormous Barbican stage with a kaleidoscope of dream worlds for Ako Takahashi’s adaptation. It could have become a scramble of stories and inquiries into memory, technological advances in society and the imagination. Instead, it is turned into one long immaculate coup de théâtre.
There are two versions of the protagonist, Watashi (Tatsuya Fujiwara) – one is in Tokyo, the other in a world comprising dreams. The city is noirish while the latter is beautiful but dangerous, with a complicated storyline involving the sundering of humans from their shadows, a walled city, roaming animals and a professor (Narushi Ikeda) who collects their skulls to channel past experiences through sound.
The professor’s 17-year-old granddaughter (Miu Tomita) accompanies Watashi in Tokyo and appears like a kitsch version of the prophetess who goes with Aeneas into the underworld. Watashi seeks escape, so he can be reunited with his shadow (Shuntaro Miyao), but is drawn to this strange world too and has a romance with a librarian (Misato Morita).
Initially, it spirals into a rabbit hole of wonderlands, with kooky humour and references to western canonical and pop culture, as is Murakami’s way, from ancient myth to Lewis Carroll’s Alice and Luis Buñuel’s Un Chien Andalou. A playful set, designed by K Ishihara, shows its own theatrical construction with cheeky playfulness.
The visual pyrotechnics suck you in, from big projections to the speed, flow and agility of dancing that gestures at anime. They bring forth Murakami’s many creatures, from underground “murks”, with porcupine spikes, who flip and cartwheel, to a herd of balletic unicorns.
Decouflé’s choreography is unsurpassable in its elastic grace and athleticism without seeming circus-like. The aesthetics on the whole are so ravishing that it doesn’t matter if the story is not easy to grasp in the first half. At least not for some because, while Murakami fans will know that the unity of the story is to come, initiates to his work may be left punch-drunk and befuddled by the onslaught of worlds and images.
It becomes clear after the interval that this is controlled and deliberate confusion, reflecting Watashi’s state of mind. The dance becomes imbued with feeling as Murakami’s world reveals its underlying themes of loneliness, grief, the fear of disappearing and of death.
But the story of lost shadows, representing the “true” self, bears bigger socio-political echoes that feel contemporary, and even prescient (the book was published in 1985). This world looks like Neo’s in The Matrix, and its technology chimes with ideas in Naomi Klein’s book, Doppelganger: A Trip into the Mirror World . The sinister side of the perfectionism that this dream society has cultivated could be a comment on postwar Japan, or on our world of AI, real and fake selves, code and machine-constructed subjectivity.
At almost three hours, it leaves you with the sense that you have been dreaming, collectively, about a world of dead animals, lost shadows and unfeeling humans, but also of unicorns, impossible beauty and an ocean-like imagination. It is both of our world, and other.

articles.title_orig: French student protesters vow to keep up their fight after scoring first win
articles.title_zh: French student protesters vow to keep up their fight after scoring first win
articles.content_orig:
France has been struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades .
The protests started last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb, where students joined their striking teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff were sent to the school, the strike ended.
But shortly after that, students in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances to their schools. Within days, similar scenes were reported across the country. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police have led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close, and thousands of people have been taken into police custody over the past few weeks — most of them minors with no previous criminal records.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. Following a massive day of protests on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron demanded “empathy” from police forces facing student protesters.
In an address to the nation Wednesday, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said parliament next month would debate a budget proposal that includes 64 billion euros ($71.6 billion) in funding for education, a slight increase from last year. He also said the government has launched five initiatives to respond to students’ needs.
But there has been little sign that school blockades will halt in the meantime. Student unions have called for a day of protests on October 17.
Here are some of the stories that made headlines over the past week, as well as some photos that caught our eye.

articles.title_orig: As World Health Summit opens, IRC warns global health investment in fragile states is declining as disease outbreaks pose growing threat
articles.title_zh: As World Health Summit opens, IRC warns global health investment in fragile states is declining as disease outbreaks pose growing threat
articles.content_orig:
More than 70% of epidemic-prone diseases now occur in fragile and conflict-affected countries, where weak health systems allow diseases like Ebola to spread undetected and cross borders, as global health funding collapses to 15-year low.
Progress is possible: the IRC and partners have delivered over 40 million vaccine doses to underimmunized children in crisis settings.
The IRC urges decisionmakers gathered at the World Health Summit to restore health funding to crisis settings, release pledged Ebola funds and partner with humanitarian organizations to reach communities beyond the reach of traditional health systems.
Berlin, Germany, October 9, 2026 — As global health leaders gather in Berlin for the World Health Summit, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) warns that a sharp retreat in global health spending is putting lives and hard-won health gains at risk in the world’s most fragile and conflict-affected states.
The consequences of that retreat are increasingly urgent. In eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), an outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola–for which there is no approved vaccine– has spread across seven provinces and into neighboring Uganda and Kenya. Since the first case was confirmed in May, nearly 8,500 people have been infected and more than 4,000 have died.
“Every dollar cut from health in fragile states is a risk to lives and livelihoods not just locally but globally,” said Alyoscia D’Onofrio, vice president and head of technical excellence at the IRC. “Resilience is built in the places where crises begin. We have shown that it’s possible to cost-effectively vaccinate children even in the most hard–to-reach places if we have the resources.”
IRC has proven progress in fragile and conflict-affected states is possible. The Gavi-funded Reaching Every Child in Humanitarian settings (REACH) consortium, led by the IRC, has now delivered more than 40 million vaccine doses to children in six conflict-affected countries, up from 20 million a year ago . REACH was built for communities that government health systems cannot safely reach, some of which had not seen a vaccine in more than a decade. When it launched in 2022, humanitarian organizations could access just 16% of its 156 target communities; today they reach all of them.
Those hard-won gains are now at risk as donors cut health budgets to a 15-year low - widening the gulf in health equity and outcomes between fragile and stable settings. In Afghanistan alone, the number of health facilities the IRC supports fell by 70% in 2025. Fragile and conflict-affected settings experience more than 70% of global outbreaks of epidemic-prone diseases such as cholera, measles and meningitis. One in five of the world’s children now live in these countries, where children face a mortality rate three times higher than their peers in stable settings, and are three times less likely to receive any routine vaccines. The maternal mortality ratio for a woman living in a fragile or conflict-affected setting is five times higher than her peers in stable settings.
The IRC is calling on governments, donors and multilateral institutions at the World Health Summit to:
The IRC is a global leader in delivering essential health services and building resilient health systems in fragile and conflict-affected areas. The IRC's health programs are designed to address both immediate crises and long-term challenges faced by vulnerable populations worldwide, focusing on foundational primary health care programming – ensuring we continue to deliver lifesaving services during crisis and recovery, while building resilient health systems. In FY2025, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) delivered vital health services to nearly 17 million people.
The International Rescue Committee responds to the world’s worst humanitarian crises, helping to restore health, safety, education, economic wellbeing, and power to people devastated by conflict and disaster. Founded in 1933 at the call of Albert Einstein, the IRC works in more than 40 countries and in 30 U.S. cities helping people to survive, reclaim control of their future, and strengthen their communities. Learn more at www.rescue.org and follow the IRC on Instagram , Facebook , TikTok , LinkedIn and Bluesky .

articles.title_orig: Two men deny Iran-backed surveillance of Jewish and Israeli sites in London
articles.title_zh: Two men deny Iran-backed surveillance of Jewish and Israeli sites in London
articles.content_orig:
Two men have pleaded not guilty to carrying out surveillance on Jewish and Israeli sites across London on behalf of Iran's intelligence service.
Nematollah Shahsavani, 41, and Alireza Farasati, 22, are accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service under the National Security Act 2023.
Prosecutors allege the pair carried out hostile reconnaissance at several locations between 9 July and 15 August last year.
Targets allegedly included the Israeli embassy and consulate, a woman said to be of interest to Iran, a college, and Britain's oldest synagogue.
Both defendants entered their not not guilty pleas during an appearance at the Old Bailey on Friday. Farasati appeared in person in the dock, while Shahsavani attended via video link from HMP Pentonville.
The court previously heard that police confiscated electronic devices from Farasati, a barber, when he was stopped on 14 August last year.
Prosecutors allege that Shahsavani directed Farasati to monitor and gather intelligence on London's Jewish and Israeli communities. Shahsavani, who works as a car salesman and delivery driver, was allegedly acting on instructions from Iranian intelligence.
Shahsavani, a dual British-Iranian national and father of two from North Finchley, north London, has lived in the UK since 2009.
Farasati, an Iranian national living in Colindale, north-west London, arrived in Britain as a 17-year-old in 2021.
Mrs Judge Cheema-Grubb scheduled a further pre-trial hearing for 12 February, with a full trial due to begin at the Old Bailey on 26 April next year.
Both men, who were detained in March, remain in custody.

articles.title_orig: ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting
articles.title_zh: ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting
articles.content_orig:
Immigration officer shot man in car where five-year-old child was sitting, sparking fierce protests
Leading New York Democrats expressed anger and demanded curbs on Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) violence after a federal officer shot a man driving a car in which his five-year-old son was sitting, sparking fierce protests .
At least seven shots were reportedly fired and the man was hit in the neck late on Thursday afternoon as children were coming home from school in the busy Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City. Marble Hill considered part of Manhattan, but is physically located in the Bronx.
Federal authorities on Friday morning identified Oscar Belgal as the man shot, saying he was undocumented, from the Dominican Republic and had a felony record and gang affiliations.
Marcos Charles, a senior ‌ICE official, said Belgal refused ​to exit his car when approached by ‌federal officers who were trying to arrest him, and then accelerated, ‌struck two ICE vehicles and drove towards other officers. An ICE officer then shot Belgal and Charles said the wound was “superficial”.
Footage showed a man in a high-visibility construction vest, possibly with a badge on a lanyard, carrying an assault-style rifle and standing close to Belgal, who is sat on the street, while another officer appears to hold a hand to his neck and shoulder area.
New York police officers in uniform shortly afterwards carry the man to an unmarked car and lay him in the back seat, handcuffed behind his back.
But Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York congresswoman, and Zohran Mamdani , the city’s mayor – all of whom are Democrats – led strong condemnation of ICE’s conduct.
Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic New York candidate, rushed to the protests and was knocked over in the chaos as local police and demonstrators clashed.
The wounded man was conscious and hospitalized, authorities said .
A joint statement from Manhattan and Bronx borough presidents Vanessa L Gibson and Brad Holyman-Sigal, respectively, said the man then was “reportedly transferred to a detention facility out of New York state”.
“Today, the Bronx and Manhattan stand united in outrage” over the case, Gibson and Holyman-Sigal’s statement said. “The frustration, pain, anger and trauma stoked by this incident extends far beyond an individual.”
Mamdani called the incident “unconscionable” and said on Thursday night that ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), had “whisked him away” from the New York-Presbyterian Allen hospital in upper Manhattan.
A similar incident occurred in Texas last month after a man was shot by an ICE officer in Austin and despite a bullet lodged in his back was taken by the federal authorities from a local hospital to ICE detention about 140 miles away.
Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani demanded ICE be abolished.
Both Hochul and Mamdani spoke to Donald Trump and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, by phone on Thursday night.
“I have been on ​the phone with President Trump and Secretary Mullin negotiating ‌the release of the man ICE agents ‌shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani told a press conference. He demanded from the Trump ‌administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. “ICE is rotten to its core,” he said.
ICE has been stepping up arrests all year despite withdrawing massed militarized ranks from Minneapolis in January and adopting a more covert approach to enforcement .
Both Hochul and Mamdani demanded that ICE cease enforcement operations in New York and the governor said she expressed outrage to the Trump administration on behalf of all New Yorkers. Hochul added that the incident could easily have ended in tragedy.
“No child should ever have to experience the terror of gunfire,” she said. The child was being looked after by his family on Friday.
The streets where the shooting and protests took place were calm on Friday morning but many residents remained shocked and angry.
“Here’s an innocent child that was caught in the crossfire,” said Calvin Hayden, a south Bronx native. “That child could have been killed.” Hayden heard about the shooting the night before and said he was immediately disturbed. He came to Marble Hill, the northernmost part of Manhattan, to see the aftermath.
“I don’t believe ICE has any reason or right to be in New York City,” he said, adding he thought New York was already equipped on its own to handle immigration disputes without ICE presence.
“There’s a lot of individuals who are not committing crimes and they just want to make a better life for themselves,” he said.
Some drivers on 225th Street yelled anti-ICE sentiments as they drove past the scene.
Mullin said on Friday morning that the ICE officers involved in the shooting did not know there was a child in the vehicle and defended the agency’s actions. But he pointed out that Belgal would have obviously known the child was in his car when he drove it at officers. The exact sequence of events leading up to the shooting have not yet become clear.
Mullin said that Hochul had asked the DHS for a pause on enforcement in New York.
“No, we are not putting a pause on enforcement,” he said.
Mullin criticized New York’s “sanctuary” policies , ​which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authoritie.
Belgal, 28, has prior convictions, was serving five years of probation for felony grand larceny and was also arrested on drug charges in 2025, a case that is still pending, according to the New York police department.
“What happened today was an outrage,” Mamdani said late on Thursday, adding: “When ICE agents opened fire, a five-year-old child – a five-year-old child! – was in the back seat of that car. Thank God that child is physically unharmed.”
Witnesses told local media they heard the child yelling at the officers after the shooting. At least 20 people have been shot by federal immigration agents under the second Trump administration, as well as a rise in deaths in detention.
“ICE is a rogue, lawless and paramilitary surveillance agency. It does not belong in New York City and it should not exist in the United States of America. Abolish ICE,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement.
The representative also condemned the retail company Target for allowing federal enforcement teams to use its parking lots as staging areas from which to launch arrest operations.
Protesters held signs saying:“Jail all killer ICE agents” and “Leave our neighbors alone.”
“ICE, get the fuck out of our neighborhood,” shouted Gibson, the Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here … We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.” She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing ICE, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.”
Protesters gathered at the hospital where Belgal was taken. The police set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with officers in a chaotic scene.
Demonstrators banged drums and shouted: “Shut it down,” and “ICE out!” as cars driving by honked in support.
Standing outside the hospital, Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, said he wanted to see an independent investigation into the shooting led by New York officials.
“The pain that you’re witnessing is people who are witnessing their neighbors, their family members, their friends being ripped away,” he said.
ICE has arrested more than 19,500 people in New York and nearly 18,000 in New Jersey during the second Trump administration, mostly Latin American immigrant men without criminal histories, Gothamist reported earlier this week using government data, adding that those totals were more than double the number of such arrests in the last 18 months of the Biden administration.
Lex McMenamin and Joanna Walters contributed reporting

SpaceX (SPCX) could need to build a ground-based mobile network to compete with established U.S. telecom operators following its latest spectrum acquisition, JPMorgan said on Friday.

The stock was up 3.7% in pre-market trading, while SPCX was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing.
On Thursday, SpaceX announced an agreement to acquire Grain Management's nationwide portfolio of 800 MHz wireless spectrum licenses, covering up to 14 MHz of paired spectrum. Grain confirmed that SpaceX would acquire its entire portfolio, subject to Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approval.
SpaceX said that the frequencies address an important technical gap in Starlink Mobile's push to become a major mobile carrier.

Goldman Sachs echoed the sentiment, saying it expects SpaceX to deploy the 800 MHz spectrum via cell towers in major cities and other urban areas to strengthen its mobile network coverage.

articles.title_orig: China Wants to Sell The World on Xinjiang-Farmed Fish
articles.title_zh: China Wants to Sell The World on Xinjiang-Farmed Fish
articles.content_orig:
When Chinese state television hailed inland salmon as a miracle in 2018, many viewers saw something more familiar: not a wonder, but a sales pitch.
The segment, aired by China Central Television that May, celebrated salmon farming in western China . Over images of sleek fish cutting through clear water, the narrator marveled that “a precious fish like salmon, which typically lives in the open ocean,” could now be raised inland, in the country’s barren western hinterland. The message was unmistakable. Technology had made the improbable possible. “The land is the same land, and the people are the same people,” the program declared, “but when technology is brought in, miracles are born.”
Online, viewers began poking at the claim almost immediately.
Was that salmon at all, many asked, or just rainbow trout dressed up as something fancier? On Chinese social media, the mood turned from curiosity to irritation. “People expect Atlantic salmon, but we’re getting freshwater rainbow trout that costs half as much,” one Beijing-based WeChat account complained. “How could you not be angry?” Science writer Fang Shimin dispensed with niceties: “This is cheap rainbow trout being passed off as expensive salmon. If you don’t want to deceive consumers, just call it rainbow trout.”
Such anxieties would only grow larger as China worked to sell an idea that, not long ago, might have sounded implausible: seafood from the desert. As China has rapidly expanded its fish farms as part of a state policy aimed at self-sufficiency, it has developed at least 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang, a historically restive region located in the country’s mountainous and desert inland. The Outlaw Ocean Project , a news organization in Washington, D.C. that I founded and run, mapped these farms as part of a sweeping investigation showing how much seafood is reaching the U.S., including government facilities, in violation of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA).
The distrust was not irrational. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said this year that while there is no official global estimate for seafood fraud, empirical studies suggest it may exist in up to 20% of the worldwide trade, sometimes appearing as species substitution and other kinds of misrepresentation.
For most people, seafood comes with an expected geography. Salmon belongs to Norway or Alaska. Cod evokes the cold North Atlantic. Shrimp suggests warm coasts and estuaries. Xinjiang, by contrast, calls up deserts, surveillance, cotton fields, and the Chinese government’s mass detention, forced-labor, and assimilation campaign against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities, along with the long, hard distances of the country’s far west. The most landlocked patch on the planet, Xinjiang is among the last places many people would associate with premium fish.
And yet for years, Chinese officials, state media, and seafood companies have been trying to teach consumers to do exactly that. They have promoted “Xinjiang seafood” as one of the small wonders of a new China: fish raised in glacial meltwater, in cold mountain reservoirs, in alkaline lakes, and at farms built against the edge of the desert. The imagery is always some variation on the same promise. Geography is no longer destiny. Harsh landscapes can be made productive. A remote frontier, disciplined by engineering, can become a source of delicacy and pride.
In that sense, Xinjiang seafood is not merely an agricultural product. It is a narrative achievement. The state-led campaign to create that narrative matters because it offers a rare window into Beijing’s worries about food security and its methods for redirecting Western attention away from its human rights problems. It also showcases China’s larger ambitions of using industry to help settle a historically restive region. This campaign saw its zenith in 2023, when Xinhua News Agency reported that the “Xinjiang seafood” label had surged in prominence on Chinese social media. Government data from that year show Xinjiang as China’s second-largest producer of “salmon,” trailing only Qinghai Province on the Tibetan Plateau. Its success is also relevant to what Americans eat, as the Outlaw Ocean Project found that seafood from Xinjiang ends up in the U.S. in violation of federal law. One company, called Tianyun, now ships to 14 countries, including the U.S., and distributes to food companies that supply military bases, public schools, and U.S. congressional cafeterias, according to Bait to Plate , an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.
Xinjiang Tianyun said in a statement that claims of systemic forced labor “are completely factually unfounded” and described the UFLPA as an unreasonable and politically motivated framework that violates the principles of fair international trade. Xinjiang Tianyun insists that it strictly abides by China’s laws on labor and contracts and resolutely protects the legitimate rights and interests of every employee.
The 2018 salmon dispute exposed how fragile China's narrative of achievement in Xinjiang can be. To some consumers, the issue was simple: they feared they were paying salmon prices for a cheaper fish. But the outrage ran deeper because it also touched food safety. That same year, the Chinese food-safety expert Zhong Kai warned against serving trout raw, citing parasite risks common in freshwater fish. “I do not recommend eating it raw,” he said, advising thorough cooking. Online commenters accused state media of misleading the public. This was “not the salmon ordinary people think of,” they wrote. Masami Takeuchi, a food-safety officer at the FAO, noted that illnesses caused by eating raw freshwater fish can be serious, even when symptoms arrive late or are hard to trace.
The fear, then, was not simply that consumers were being overcharged. It was that they were being sold an aspirational image that obscured material differences in the fish itself.
That anxiety found ready soil in a country where food scandals have repeatedly taught the public to distrust official reassurance. China’s aquaculture industry has expanded at staggering speed, and with that expansion have come the familiar pressures of industrial animal farming: crowding, disease, waste, chemical intervention, and a recurring mismatch between the pastoral language used to market food and the industrial realities that produce it. A 2020 study in Nature found that aquaculture has the highest antibiotic-use intensity per kilogram of biomass among major animal-production sectors, exceeding use in both humans and land-based livestock.
Chinese researchers have warned for years about severe antibiotic abuse in the industry. Sedatives have posed another problem. Diazepam, sometimes used to calm fish during transport, has repeatedly shown up in official inspections despite being prohibited. In 2021, China’s Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs began requiring routine diazepam testing, and a 2023 paper in China Food Hygiene Journal described diazepam residues as “widely detected” in water and seafood products. In 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an alert after detecting residues of prohibited substances—including malachite green, a carcinogenic veterinary drug—in seafood shipments from China, citing “significant public-health concerns.”
None of this proves that Xinjiang seafood as a whole is fraudulent or unsafe. But it helps explain why the category has struggled to inspire a durable sense of consumer trust. In a food system often shadowed by contamination scares and labeling disputes, grand claims end up feeling less like reassurance than marketing. The more insistently officials and companies promoted inland salmon, trout, whitefish, caviar, and other products from China’s far west as a new high-value frontier, the more some consumers wondered what, exactly, they were being asked to believe.
The answer, in part, was a story the state had been helping

articles.title_orig: What Microsoft’s green card suspension means for Seattle-area workers
articles.title_zh: What Microsoft’s green card suspension means for Seattle-area workers
articles.content_orig:
India called comments by U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance about immigrants from the country "deeply offensive" in an official government statement published on Friday.
Vance said on Thursday that the Trump administration wants foreign and local companies to "employ American workers," and that they "cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants."
He was speaking as the U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft , Adobe and several major Indian information technology companies from its Permanent Labor Certification program, meaning they cannot apply for permanent residency for their employees on H-1 B visas.
Around 70% of H-1B beneficiaries in 2025 were born in India , per official data .
In a statement on Friday, India's Ministry of External Affairs accused Vance of using " terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations."
"Such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem," the statement said.
Vance's office did not immediately respond to a comment request from CNBC.
Vance was critical of Microsoft, accusing the company of replacing 6,000 laid-off workers with people on H-1B visas.
The Indian foreign ministry assured its citizens that measures announced by the U.S. will not affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents.
"Talent mobility adds value to both economies," the statement said, adding that the suspensions "do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries."
The Indian companies affected by the ban include Cognizant , Infosys , Capgemini, Tata Consultancy Services , Wipro and HCL .
NASSCOM, the IT industry body, said in a statement that Indian technology companies have "significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas" over the last few years, and are expanding domestic hiring to their U.S. workforces.
The largest Indian IT company, Tata Consultancy Services, said its H-1B applications were in "single digits" in the last two years, and it intends to hire another 15,000 people in the U.S. over the next five years.
In June, a federal judge blocked the $100,000 H-1B visa fee U.S. President Donald Trump imposed last year.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest penguin colony suffers steep decline in numbers
articles.title_zh: World’s largest penguin colony suffers steep decline in numbers
articles.content_orig:
Subscribe today from as little as £2 / $2.70 a month! Find out more
Subscribe from £2 / $2.70 a month! Find out more
Occupied chinstrap nests on Zavodovski Island have fallen by 63% since 2011, scientists say, with warming seas pushing the penguins' krill prey out of reach
The world’s largest penguin colony has lost its title after a steep decline in chinstrap penguins on a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, according to new research by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).
The study, published in the journal Current Biology, found that the number of occupied chinstrap nests on Zavodovski Island, in the South Sandwich Islands, fell by 63% between 2011 and 2025. The island now has the highest rate of chinstrap decline anywhere in the world, and the title of largest colony passes to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea, more than 5,000km away.
In 2011, Zavodovski was home to an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said Prof Norman Ratcliffe, the BAS penguin ecologist who led the research.
The researchers say the cause is climate-driven change in the Southern Ocean. Chinstraps have a specialist diet and prefer cooler water, and tracking data showed they forage to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill. As the water warms, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
“Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food,” Ratcliffe said.
The island’s macaroni penguins, which have a broader diet and can switch to fish and crustaceans when krill become scarce, increased by 28% between 2011 and 2016 and have been stable since. Tracking data showed them foraging in warmer waters to the north-east. Ratcliffe described the shift as the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica.

The team travelled for 15 days by yacht to reach the island, which is more than 2,000km from the nearest permanent human settlement. They used drone surveys, aerial photography from an RAF aircraft based in the Falklands, and tracking devices fitted to penguins.
The scientists ruled out several other explanations. Zavodovski’s volcano, Mount Curry, erupted in March 2016, but the decline began years earlier and has been steady, and the researchers say it is not to blame. They also dismissed competition between the two penguin species for nesting space, and krill fishing, because harvesting is banned in the marine protected area surrounding the island. However, it is unclear how krill fishing in areas connected by currents to the protected area might be affecting wider food supplies.
The South Sandwich Islands hold around 30% of the world’s chinstrap population. The researchers say the declines here, together with those elsewhere in Antarctica, could tip the species into the “Endangered” category on the IUCN Red List.
Ratcliffe warned that the loss of chinstraps could have wider consequences for marine food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely,” he told the Guardian.
Peter Fretwell, a BAS researcher who specialises in remote sensing of penguins, said the findings showed that even the most remote places were affected by climate change. “Not even they can escape the impacts of climate change,” he said.
The study comes six months after emperor penguins were declared an endangered species because of sea ice loss.

articles.title_orig: Jane Doe texted with Cornell frat bro to find ‘jealous’ rat gossiping about them: ‘Stupid bitches like to yap’
articles.title_zh: Jane Doe texted with Cornell frat bro to find ‘jealous’ rat gossiping about them: ‘Stupid bitches like to yap’
articles.content_orig:
The Cornell student accusing seven frat brothers of gang raping her had worked with one of them to try to find the “rat” talking about them having sex at a party — claiming they needed to “grow up” and be more open-minded about what went on, according to a fresh batch of text messages.
Just four days after the Chi Phi fraternity party where the student now claims she was drugged and raped, Jane Doe texted student Matthew Ingalls in a panic claiming “everybody knows” about them having sex , leavin her “incredibly stressed out,” messages obtained by TMZ show .
Ingalls sympathized after the accuser complained about some  “random bitch” telling her friends.
“Dude I have no f—king idea, this sh-t is incredibly frustrating and I know how fast nonsense spreads at this school,” responded Ingalls, who later claimed he was the one assaulted while too drunk to consent .
“It’s fan behavior from everyone talking about it. Boring people who have nothing to do with their time,” texted Ingalls, who Doe later said instigated the alleged 2024 gang rape .
Doe said the rumors were “f—king RUINING my life” and that she wanted to sniff out “the rats.”
“My reputation is destroyed and i’m utterly ashamed. i’m f—king pissed because this many people shouldn’t know and i feel like i know who some of the rats in the room were,” she texted him.
She added that the rumors were not only spreading like wildfire but were growing “crazier every f—king day.”
“Stupid bitches like to yap, and the fact they’re doing it shows that they’re jealous of you for any number of reasons,” Ingalls shot back.
“The only shameful thing is how this spread and how much people won’t shut up about it — which just reflects poorly on them tbh,” he added.
Doe agreed that the gossips are “jealous” and threatened to beat up anyone who gives them “sh-t” about what happened while also opening up how she’s “open-minded” about sexuality.
“…but also like everyone needs to grow up cause sexuality and sex and sh-t is changing and stuff like this is going to become more common,” she said, while adding that she is “also really open minded tho.”
Doe later said she suspected of another Cornell fraternity brother she accused of partaking in the sexual assault, Jonathan Newell, of having loose lips.
“Jonathan def told people. I heard something today and i know he told people,” she texted Ingalls.
Ingalls denied Newell said anything , and suggested some upperclassman may have been spreading the word.
Doe responded that a female student who confronted her “wouldn’t tell me who she heard it from cause it’s one of her friends.”
Ingalls apologized and promised “these idiots will move on and it’ll be done with.”
More than a week later on November 7, Ingalls tells Doe that his ex-girlfriend told him he’s now been labeled a sexual abuser on campus — and asked if Doe had made those allegations against him.
Doe said she’s stayed mum but added  “people are changing the narrative because like in any sexual scenario w one woman and many men the woman was probably victim.”
“I know there are rumors I was gang banged,” she said.
That same day, Doe requested a rape kit at an emergency room and reported the alleged rape to campus police the following day , according to her lawsuit.
Ingalls and Newell were two of the seven fraternity brothers named in Doe’s lawsuit who were eventually expelled from the Ithaca, New York Ivy League school.
No criminal charges were brought at the time.

articles.title_orig: Webb Telescope Detects Galaxy Origin Of The Farthest Fast Radio Burst We've Seen To Date
articles.title_zh: Webb Telescope Detects Galaxy Origin Of The Farthest Fast Radio Burst We've Seen To Date
articles.content_orig:
And the data it provided sheds light on the origins of fast radio bursts.
Back in 2024, scientists detected the farthest fast radio burst we've ever seen to date, thanks to observations by the MeerKAT ground telescope array. Fast radio bursts are ultra-fast radio waves from deep space, which last a fraction of a second but release as much as energy as what the sun emits in three days. They were first discovered in 2007, and not much is known about them. Now, astronomers have used the James Webb telescope to pinpoint the origin of the burst detected in 2024, and it could shed light on the phenomenon's origins.
Webb's near-infrared instruments detected a galaxy in the right location from where the burst had come. Based on measurements from the way its light stretches, the fast radio burst occurred just 3 billion years after the Big Bang. Its origin galaxy existed way back when star formation was at its peak in the universe. In addition, the galaxy that produced it is also 1,000 times smaller than expected. The previous fast radio bursts we've detected took place billions of years later in massive, star-forming galaxies.
There are a couple of theories on how fast radio bursts are produced. One proposes that they're generated by the merger of two neutron stars. But it takes billions of years before two neutron stars — the collapsed cores of massive supergiant stars — collide, which means that bursts can only come from older galaxies.
Another theory suggests that the bursts can come from massive stars exploding in a supernova and leaving behind magnetars , which are rare type of neutron stars that have highly powerful magnetic fields. "Our work suggests that it's very unlikely that this [fast radio burst] was produced by a merger," said Manisha Caleb from the University of Sydney, Australia, who served as lead author on the study published in Science . In other words, their work shows that the origin of this burst was likely a supernova, providing support for the theory that fast radio bursts can come from a certain type of star explosion.

articles.title_orig: Return of USS Abraham Lincoln and mudslides in Chile: photos of the day – Friday
articles.title_zh: Return of USS Abraham Lincoln and mudslides in Chile: photos of the day – Friday
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in San Diego on Thursday, bringing dances of joy from the homebound sailors, praise for the crew’s extended service and questions about the poor conditions they endured during the record length of time the ship was away from port supporting the Iran war.
Scores of new fathers kissed their babies for the first time, couples cried and embraced and hundreds of parents let out a collective sigh of relief as the crew disembarked on the north end of the Coronado peninsula.
The ship departed from Southern California last November and was rerouted to the Middle East after the U.S. led attacks on Iran in February. Crew members have been away from their families for 321 days and set a modern record for 265 consecutive days at sea without a port visit.
The exceptionally long deployment has drawn concern over reports of deteriorating conditions on board as crew members became emblems of the sacrifices made by Americans to sustain President Trump’s conflict with Iran.
This summer, news reports revealed that multiple sailors had attempted to jump overboard amid shortages of fresh food , disruptions to hot water and laundry services and exhaustion. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao then told Congress that at least eight strike team members had attempted suicide during the deployment.
When asked Thursday about the toll on sailors, Commanding Officer Daniel J. Keeler said that everything crew members went through was “in the normal spectrum of what you might expect you see on an aircraft carrier.”
“I had all the supplies I needed to conduct combat,” he said. “We never missed a mission. I also never missed a meal.”
He said the ship deployed with five chaplains and a well-staffed mental health team.  “We got our sailors any care they needed and got them back in the fight when it was appropriate,” he said.
On Wednesday, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth presented the crew with the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest unit-level military decoration awarded by the United States.
For weeks, Trump has been threatening that a post-midterm election escalation in the seven-month-old war remains a viable option, despite his initial promises to Americans of a military campaign that would last a matter of weeks.
The aircraft carrier traveled more than 85,000 nautical miles carrying around 5,000 sailors during its 10-month deployment, described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era” by U.S. Central Command Commander Adm. Brad Cooper.
“Our epic deployment ends today and what this team achieved is amazing,” Keeler said Thursday. “Lincoln Nation conducted major combat operations, enforced naval blockade and demonstrated the presence and power of the carrier strike group and multiple numbered fleets, all while keeping up unprecedented operational tempo.”
Cooper visited the ship in August and noted it had among the lowest numbers of mental-health-related cases out of the Navy’s 11 active carriers, but “this doesn’t mean that all is perfect.”
Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) said in a statement Thursday that while he celebrated the ship’s return, he was acutely aware of the burden such a long deployment put upon crew members and their families.
Schiff said one of his constituents, identified only as Doug, wrote him a letter expressing concern about conditions aboard the ship after his son was medically evacuated due to a collapsed lung.
“After time in the ICU [abroad], he returned home to us as a shell of the son who had left,” Doug wrote. “He is 6’5″ and left weighing 210 pounds; and he returned closer to 180 pounds. He resembled a starved prisoner of war. What he told me as a father and veteran turns my stomach and must be brought to light.”
San Diego resident Annabelle Loma told the Military Times in August that her husband was among the sailors who attempted to jump overboard.
“He thinks he’ll get a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out, his 13-year-old career is ruined, just like that,” she said. “That’s not fair, that’s not right.”
Schiff said he hopes these tales of hardship resonate with the Trump administration, arguing that “with no clear objective and no measurable progress,” the war on Iran must end, not only  because of high costs imposed on the American people but also because of the high price paid by service members.
More than 860 troops have been wounded and 19 have been killed since the start of the conflict, according to data published by the Defense Department.
No casualties were reported aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
“The most important statistic, the one that I am most proud of, is zero,” Keeler said. “Zero lost aircraft, zero combat damage, zero lives lost. Every single sailor and Marine that left on this deployment is going home.”
Trump told a Texas rally that the U.S. would not allow Iran to strike Los Angeles or San Diego, two days after his remarks on the subject stirred outrage among California leaders.
The ship’s return to San Diego comes just days after the president’s controversial remarks suggesting that if Iran were to “take out” San Diego or Los Angeles it would be a “very small price to pay” to keep the world and country safe. White House communications director Steven Cheung criticized the “media freakout” over the comments, saying that the president was pointing out how American cities would have been threatened if it were not for U.S. military intervention.
Trump appeared to backpedal his bellicosity at a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday, saying he was not going to let Iranian missiles strike U.S. cities.
Nonetheless, the damage was done, with California leaders from both sides of the aisle criticizing the implications of the president’s speech.
“We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay,’” San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria posted on X . “Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”
Jim Desmond, a Trump-endorsed Republican candidate running to represent San Diego in California’s hotly contested 48th Congressional District , said he vehemently disagreed with the president’s comments.
“America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests,” the Navy veteran wrote on social media, “but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland.”
The USS Abraham Lincoln is not the only aircraft carrier to have completed an exceptionally long deployment amid the continued conflict. The USS Gerald R. Ford set a post-Vietnam War record when it returned to Naval Station Norfolk in Virginia in May from a 326-day deployment, which also earned the team a rare Presidential Unit Citation.
Last week, another crew on the USS Theodore Roosevelt and its carrier strike group left San Diego, seemingly headed to support military operations in the Middle East.
In a social media post Thursday, Trump said that his team was engaged in productive talks with Iran and he does not intend to resume military strikes on Iran before November’s midterm elections. Negotiations appeared to have stalled after Trump rejected Iran’s proposal last month to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under certain conditions.
